eras.name: Banchi di scritta
eras.subtitle: The bench on the Rialto
eras.intro: Under the porticoes of San Giacomo di Rialto, bankers sit at benches with a ledger open. Merchants hold accounts and pay one another by a spoken order to the scribe; no coin moves. The deposits are lent — to merchants fitting out galleys for the Levant, to the Commune in wartime, and into pepper and copper on the banker's own account. The Church forbids interest, so profit hides inside the bill of exchange. Banks fail often, and when they fail the state does not save them.
eras.source: Mueller, The Venetian Money Market (1997); Lane & Mueller, Money and Banking in Medieval and Renaissance Venice

eras.name: The Medici century
eras.subtitle: Branches, partners and princes
eras.intro: Florence shows how a house grows: not one firm but a parent partnership holding majority stakes in separately capitalised branches — Rome, Venice, Bruges, London, Lyon — each with its own manager holding a minority. Limited partnership by accomandita keeps a foreign branch's debts away from the parent. The temptation is the same everywhere: a prince who wants money and will remember who gave it. Lending to princes was banned in the Medici until 1471; seven years later Bruges was gone.
eras.source: de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank 1397–1494 (1963)

eras.name: Princes and fairs
eras.subtitle: Habsburg asientos and the Genoese
eras.intro: Silver from the Americas and a Habsburg empire that never has enough of it. The Fuggers finance Charles V and are gutted by Spain's stop of 1557; the Genoese take the crown's debt through asientos and juros and run their own exchange fairs, where Europe's bankers meet four times a year to net their bills with almost no coin. Philip II stops payment in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1597. Antwerp is the centre until the Spanish Fury of 1576; then the money moves north. Venice gets its first bank supervisor in 1524 and its first public bank in 1587, after its last private one dies in a run.
eras.source: Drelichman & Voth, Lending to the Borrower from Hell (2014); Ehrenberg, Capital and Finance in the Age of the Renaissance

eras.name: The northern shift
eras.subtitle: Wisselbank, goldsmiths and the Bank of England
eras.intro: Amsterdam founds its Wisselbank in 1609 on the Venetian model and gives the Dutch a unit of account the whole world trusts. The East India Company sells shares to the public. In London goldsmiths become bankers: they take deposits, issue notes against them, and lend to the Crown against next year's taxes — until Charles II stops the Exchequer in 1672 and the greatest of them go down. The answer, in 1694, is a bank of the state's own, on the Amsterdam pattern. Interest is now lawful, but capped.
eras.source: Quinn & Roberds on the Wisselbank; Winter, Goldsmith Banking: A History; Kynaston, Till Time's Last Sand

eras.name: Country banks and the City
eras.subtitle: Bubbles, bills and the Bank Charter Act
eras.intro: London is the centre now. The South Sea Bubble bursts in 1720 and the Bubble Act freezes the joint-stock company for a century. Merchant houses — Barings from 1762 — trade goods, then accept bills, then float sovereign loans; the Louisiana Purchase is a Barings bond. Country banks spring up on a landowner's name and a printing press: the Ayr Bank's notes are two-thirds of Scotland's currency when it fails in 1772. The panic of 1825 closes a tenth of them, and Parliament answers with joint-stock banks, then in 1844 with Peel's Act fixing the note issue to gold.
eras.source: Pressnell, Country Banking in the Industrial Revolution; Kosmetatos, The 1772–73 British Credit Crisis

eras.name: Lombard Street
eras.subtitle: The lender of last resort
eras.intro: Overend Gurney asks the Bank of England for help on 9 May 1866 and is refused as insolvent; the next day it stops, Peel's Act is suspended, and the lender of last resort is born — Bagehot writes it down in 1873. Only one joint-stock bank in six founded since 1844 survives the year. Limited liability arrives by statute; City of Glasgow in 1878 shows what the unlimited kind does to shareholders. Barings is rescued by a guarantee fund in 1890. In 1914 the Stock Exchange shuts for five months and the Bank buys the accepting houses' bills. Sterling leaves gold in 1931.
eras.source: Bagehot, Lombard Street (1873); Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2016 Q4, 'The demise of Overend Gurney'

eras.name: From Eurodollars to Basel
eras.subtitle: Deregulation, capital rules and the G-SIB
eras.intro: The Eurodollar market makes London the world's offshore banker from the late 1950s. Competition and Credit Control in 1971 lets credit loose and the secondary banking crisis follows; the clearers' Lifeboat lends 40% of their capital to keep the fringe afloat. Big Bang, 1986. Basel I in 1988 is the first capital rule a British bank ever had: 8% of risk-weighted assets. BCCI, Barings, 2008, ring-fencing. From 2011 the FSB names the banks whose failure would matter everywhere, and charges them for it. That list is where this game ends.
eras.source: Capie, The Bank of England 1950s to 1979; Reid, The Secondary Banking Crisis; BCBS 1988; FSB G-SIB methodology

cities.name: Venice
cities.blurb: The Rialto. Giro banking, the Levant galleys, forced loans to the Commune.

cities.name: Florence
cities.blurb: The super-companies, then the Medici. Papal banking and the wool trade.

cities.name: Genoa
cities.blurb: Rival of Venice; from 1557 the Habsburgs' bankers and masters of the exchange fairs.

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: The Curia's banker collects tithes across Christendom and moves them without coin.

cities.name: Bruges
cities.blurb: The north's exchange, until the Zwin silts and Antwerp takes the trade.

cities.name: London
cities.blurb: Wool, then the Crown's debts, then everyone's. Lombard Street is named for your predecessors.

cities.name: Avignon
cities.blurb: The popes are here from 1309 to 1377, and so is their money.

cities.name: Lyon
cities.blurb: Four fairs a year; the French crown's banker and the Italians' clearing house.

cities.name: Antwerp
cities.blurb: The Bourse of 1531, the pepper and silver trade, and the Fuggers' counter. Sacked in 1576.

cities.name: Augsburg
cities.blurb: The Fuggers and the Welsers: Tyrolean silver, Hungarian copper, the Emperor's election.

cities.name: Seville
cities.blurb: Where the silver fleets land, and where the Crown impounds them.

cities.name: Amsterdam
cities.blurb: The Wisselbank, the VOC, the first stock exchange and the first bubble.

cities.name: Frankfurt
cities.blurb: The Rothschilds' first house; later the Bundesbank's and the ECB's city.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Law's Mississippi scheme, the haute banque, the Crédit Mobilier.

cities.name: Edinburgh
cities.blurb: Free banking, the Ayr Bank, and the City of Glasgow's unlimited shareholders.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: Wall Street. After 1914 the dollar's centre; after 1945 the world's.

cities.name: Hong Kong
cities.blurb: Ceded by the Treaty of Nanking in 1842: the China trade, then Asia's dollar market.

cities.name: Singapore
cities.blurb: The Asian dollar market from 1968; where Barings' Leeson sat.

cities.name: Zürich
cities.blurb: Neutral money, private banking, and the Basel Committee's neighbours.

cities.name: Lisbon
cities.blurb: The Tagus and the Casa da Índia: after 1498 the pepper of Malabar lands here first.

cities.name: Alexandria
cities.blurb: Where the Red Sea's spices meet the Venetian galleys, under the Mamluk sultan's customs.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Venice's quarter and Genoa's Pera; after 1453 the Sultan's capital and the Black Sea's market.

cities.name: Hamburg
cities.blurb: The Hanse's North Sea gate; its Bank of 1619 copies Amsterdam's; Berenberg since 1590.

cities.name: Goa
cities.blurb: Albuquerque takes it in 1510: the Estado da Índia's capital and the Carreira's eastern end.

cities.name: Canton
cities.blurb: Through Macau from 1557, then the Thirteen Factories: China sells tea and silk and wants only silver.

cities.name: Batavia
cities.blurb: Coen founds it in 1619 as the VOC's Asian headquarters: nutmeg, cloves, and the inter-Asian trade.

cities.name: Bombay
cities.blurb: Catherine of Braganza's dowry, leased to the Company in 1668: cotton, opium for China, and later the Raj's port.

cities.name: Calcutta
cities.blurb: Job Charnock's factory of 1690; after Plassey in 1757 the capital of the Company's Bengal.

cities.name: Sydney
cities.blurb: A penal colony in 1788; wool, then gold in 1851, and the Bank of New South Wales from 1817.

cities.name: Buenos Aires
cities.blurb: Independent from 1810; Barings' loan of 1824 defaults in 1827, and the boom of the 1880s is Barings' undoing.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: Edo renamed in 1868: the Meiji state, the zaibatsu banks, and from 1980 the world's largest lenders.

cities.name: Dubai
cities.blurb: A pearling town that became the Gulf's financial centre; the DIFC from 2004.

techs.name: Giro transfer
techs.text: Transfer between accounts by book entry on a spoken order. The thing a banco di scritta is.
techs.source: Mueller (1997): tabulae cambii on the Rialto from the 13th century

techs.name: Bill of exchange
techs.text: Pay here, collect there, in another coin at a rate you set. The Church sees exchange, not interest. Lets you earn on money without a usurious loan, and makes a foreign branch worth having.
techs.source: de Roover, 'cambium per litteras'; Cajetan, De cambiis (1499)

techs.name: Double-entry bookkeeping
techs.text: Every entry twice, debit and credit, so the books must balance and a branch manager's lies show. In Genoa by 1340; Pacioli prints it in 1494.
techs.source: Genoese massari ledgers 1340; Pacioli, Summa (1494)

techs.name: Marine insurance
techs.text: Premium contracts on a hull and its cargo. Genoa and Florence by the 1350s; your merchant borrowers stop drowning with their ships.
techs.source: Earliest surviving premium policies, Genoa 1347

techs.name: Parent and branch partnerships
techs.text: The Medici design: a parent partnership in the seat city holds the majority of each branch, the local manager the minority, each branch with its own capital and books. Prefigures the holding company.
techs.source: de Roover (1963), ch. 4

techs.name: Limited partnership (accomandita)
techs.text: Florentine statute of 1408: a sleeping partner is liable only for what he put in. The Medici used it for branches they did not trust. A branch can now fail without taking the house with it.
techs.source: Florentine statute on accomandita, 1408; de Roover

techs.name: Exchange fairs
techs.text: Geneva, then Lyon, then Besançon and Piacenza: bankers meet four times a year and net every bill against every other with almost no coin. Your bills become something you can turn into money.
techs.source: Boyer-Xambeu, Deleplace & Gillard, Private Money and Public Currencies

techs.name: Syndicated sovereign loans
techs.text: The Genoese asiento: a consortium lends the Crown against named revenues, and a stop becomes a negotiated rescheduling into juros rather than a total loss. Defaults still hurt. They stop being fatal.
techs.source: Drelichman & Voth (2014) on the Genoese asientos

techs.name: Joint-stock company
techs.text: The VOC sells transferable shares to the public in 1602. You can raise equity from strangers, and they can sell it on. In England the Bubble Act of 1720 takes this away again for a century.
techs.source: VOC charter 1602; Bubble Act 1720; its repeal 1825

techs.name: Banknotes
techs.text: Goldsmiths' receipts that pass hand to hand become money you print. The cheapest funding there is, and the most runnable. Peel's Act of 1844 ends new issue in England.
techs.source: Winter, Goldsmith Banking; Bank Charter Act 1844

techs.name: Bill discounting
techs.text: Buy a bill before it falls due at less than face. The London discount market, and Overend Gurney's whole business.
techs.source: King, History of the London Discount Market (1936)

techs.name: Acceptance business
techs.text: Put your name on another merchant's bill for a commission and it becomes a bank bill, discountable anywhere. The merchant bank's trade, Barings to Kleinwort. In 1914 the Bank of England bought all of them.
techs.source: Chapman, The Rise of Merchant Banking (1984)

techs.name: Clearing house
techs.text: The London bankers' clerks stop walking between counting-houses and meet in one room. Settlement risk falls, and so does the size of the till you need.
techs.source: London Clearing House, Lombard Street, 1773

techs.name: Sovereign bond underwriting
techs.text: Instead of lending the Crown your own money, sell its bonds to the public and keep the commission. Barings and Hope do it for Louisiana in 1803; Rothschild does it for everyone after Waterloo.
techs.source: Ziegler, The Sixth Great Power; Ferguson, The House of Rothschild

techs.name: Telegraph
techs.text: Dover–Calais cable 1851, Atlantic 1866. A branch manager can be asked a question and answer it the same day. The information lag that let Portinari ruin Bruges is over.
techs.source: Submarine Telegraph Company 1851; Atlantic cable 1866

techs.name: Limited liability
techs.text: Companies Act 1862, extended to banks: a shareholder loses his shares and nothing else. Investors come who would never have risked their houses. City of Glasgow's shareholders in 1878 had not registered — and lost everything.
techs.source: Joint Stock Banks Act 1858; Companies Act 1862; Turner, Banking in Crisis (2014)

techs.name: Branch banking at scale
techs.text: Hundreds of branches, one balance sheet. Deposits from the public at large, diversified by town and trade. The clearing banks' century.
techs.source: Capie & Collins on the amalgamation movement

techs.name: Eurodollar market
techs.text: Dollars held outside America, lent from London, beyond the Fed's reach. The thing that made the City a world centre again.
techs.source: Schenk, 'The origins of the Eurodollar market in London 1955–1963'

techs.name: Swaps and derivatives
techs.text: IBM–World Bank currency swap, 1981. A markets business, and with it counterparty risk, CVA, and the trader who hides his losses in account 88888.
techs.source: ISDA history; Barings 1995

techs.name: Securitisation
techs.text: Pool the mortgages, tranche the pool, sell the tranches. Frees capital — until 2007, when no one will buy them and the pool comes home.
techs.source: Northern Rock's Granite programme; the 2007 ABCP freeze

techs.name: Value at risk
techs.text: One number for the whole trading book, 99% of the time. RiskMetrics, 1994. Regulators let you use it for capital in 1996. It does not cover the other 1%.
techs.source: J.P. Morgan RiskMetrics (1994); Market Risk Amendment (1996)

techs.name: Internal ratings-based models
techs.text: Basel II: your own PDs and LGDs set your risk weights, with permission. Capital falls — and the output floor of 2027 says it cannot fall below 72.5% of the standardised number.
techs.source: BCBS Basel II (2004), UK implementation 2007; PRA PS1/26 output floor

techs.name: Stress testing
techs.text: The Bank's annual scenario. Can your capital take it? If the answer is credible, so is your franchise when the next one is real.
techs.source: Bank of England concurrent stress tests from 2014

borrowers.name: Coin in the till
borrowers.text: Earns nothing, answers every withdrawal. The share of deposits you keep here is the oldest decision in banking.

borrowers.name: Loans to merchants
borrowers.text: Advances to traders against goods and reputation. Under the usury ban the return has to be dressed as exchange, or it is sin.

borrowers.name: Bills of exchange
borrowers.text: Drawn in one city, payable in another. The exchange rate carries the interest. Short-dated, self-liquidating, and the core of a merchant bank.

borrowers.name: Loans to princes
borrowers.text: The best rate in the market and the worst collateral: a king's word. Edward III, Charles the Bold, Philip II, Charles II. Brings standing at court — and the king's enemies for yours.

borrowers.name: State debt
borrowers.text: Venice's Monte, Castile's juros, England's consols, gilts. Funded debt of a state that taxes. Safer than a prince's promise because it is everyone's.

borrowers.name: Trade on own account
borrowers.text: Pepper, copper, alum, wool, bought with depositors' money and held for the price. What the Rialto banks were doing in the 1340s when they could not pay out. Venice banned it for bankers in 1467.

borrowers.name: Discounted bills
borrowers.text: Buy a bill at a discount, hold it to maturity or rediscount it at the Bank. The most liquid earning asset there is — until 1866, when the Bank would not.

borrowers.name: Acceptances
borrowers.text: Your name on a merchant's bill, for a commission. Off your balance sheet until the merchant fails; then on it, all at once. In August 1914 every accepting house in London was insolvent on paper.

borrowers.name: Foreign loans
borrowers.text: Latin American republics in 1825, Argentina in 1890, Russia in 1917, Mexico in 1982. You underwrite, you hold what you cannot place, and the country does not pay.

borrowers.name: Property and mortgages
borrowers.text: Lending on land. Slow, safe, and the thing that sinks banks when prices turn: 1866, 1973, 1990, 2008.

borrowers.name: Industrial lending
borrowers.text: Mills, railways, shipyards, then everything. Term loans against the enterprise rather than the goods.

borrowers.name: Retail banking
borrowers.text: Overdrafts, personal loans, cards. Granular, sticky, and from 2019 behind a ring-fence you cannot reach across.

borrowers.name: Syndicated and Euromarket loans
borrowers.text: Dollars lent from London to corporates and sovereigns in a syndicate. The recycling of petrodollars, and the Latin American debt crisis of 1982.

borrowers.name: Markets and trading
borrowers.text: Rates, FX, credit, equities, on your own book and your clients'. The highest return and the fattest tail. FRTB prices the tail from 2027.

basel1.name: Basel I
basel1.text: 8% of risk-weighted assets, four buckets: 0% OECD sovereigns, 20% banks, 50% mortgages, 100% everything else.

basel2.name: Basel II
basel2.text: Three pillars; the standardised grid gets finer and the IRB banks model their own. Tier 1 could be 2% CET1. Which is why 2008 went the way it did.

basel3.name: Basel III / CRD IV
basel3.text: CET1 of 4.5% plus a 2.5% conservation buffer, a countercyclical buffer, and a G-SIB surcharge. Leverage ratio and LCR beside it. The MDA caps your dividend inside the buffers.

basel31.name: Basel 3.1
basel31.text: PRA PS1/26, 1 January 2027: the revised standardised approach, unrated corporates at 65%/135%, FRTB, and an output floor so IRB cannot fall below 72.5% of standardised. Where the Kingsgate model lives.

gsib.text: Size, interconnectedness, substitutability, complexity and cross-jurisdictional activity, 20% each. 130 bps and you are on the list, with a 1% surcharge; each bucket above adds 0.5%.

events.title: A bench on the Rialto
events.text: The house opens its ledger at San Giacomo. Thirty accounts, a cassa of coin, and a reputation to make.

events.title: The Sultan's customs at Alexandria
events.text: Pepper, cinnamon and ginger come up the Red Sea to Mamluk Egypt and are sold at Alexandria to whoever has silver. Venice's state galleys come for them every autumn. A banker with a factor here finances the cargo both ways.
events.source: Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973), ch. 9

events.title: The Papacy moves to Avignon
events.text: Clement V settles on the Rhône. The Curia's revenues — tithes from every diocese in Christendom — now need moving to Provence, and the Italian houses that can move money without moving coin get the business.

events.title: The King of England wants money against wool
events.text: Edward II's agents offer the customs on wool as security for a loan. The Frescobaldi of Florence hold the farm now; they will be expelled within the year.

events.title: Edward III goes to war with France
events.text: The Hundred Years' War opens. Edward needs more money than any English king has ever borrowed, and he borrows it from Florence: the Bardi and the Peruzzi advance him the wool customs and more. He pays with promises.

events.title: The Rialto banks fail
events.text: Thirty years of lending deposits into pepper and copper on the bankers' own account come due. One bank after another cannot pay out. The Commune does not step in; it never did.
events.source: Mueller, The Venetian Money Market, ch. 3

events.title: The Peruzzi fail
events.text: Edward III owes the Peruzzi 600,000 florins and does not pay. The second-largest company in Florence is bankrupt. Whoever holds the King of England's paper discovers what it is worth.
events.source: Hunt, The Medieval Super-Companies (1994)

events.title: The Bardi fail
events.text: 900,000 florins owed by Edward III. The largest bank in Europe stops. Florence's third company, the Acciaiuoli, goes with them though they never lent Edward a florin: depositors do not distinguish.

events.title: The Black Death
events.text: Half of Venice dies in eighteen months. Debtors die with their debts, depositors' heirs want their money, and the galleys sail half-crewed. Trade will recover; the labourers who survive will be paid more than their fathers.

events.title: Venice rejects a public bank
events.text: Michele Morosini's committee proposes a bank of the state to replace the failing private benches. The Senate refuses. The Rialto stays private, and so do its failures, for another two centuries.

events.title: The War of Chioggia
events.text: Genoa's fleet is in the lagoon. The Republic levies forced loans on every estate and the Monte Vecchio's bonds fall by half. Bankers are told what they will lend.

events.title: Giovanni di Bicci founds the Medici bank
events.text: A new house in Florence with a Roman branch and the Curia's account. It will be the model of the century: one parent, many partnerships, and a rule against lending to princes.

events.title: Florence legislates the limited partnership
events.text: The accomandita: a partner who does not manage is liable only for his stake. Branches can be built that cannot bring down the house.

events.title: Lyon's fairs are chartered
events.text: The French crown grants Lyon its fairs; by mid-century the Italians have made them the north's money market.

events.title: The Curia wants a depository
events.text: Eugenius IV offers the Apostolic Chamber's account to a house that can advance against next year's tithes. The Medici have it; they would rather no one else did.

events.title: Constantinople falls
events.text: The Ottomans take the city. Venice's Levant trade will be fought over for three centuries, and every galley now sails with a risk premium.

events.title: Venice forbids bankers to trade on own account
events.text: The Senate bans Rialto bankers from dealing in copper, tin, silver and the rest. The lesson of the 1340s, taken 120 years late.

events.title: The Medici lift their ban on lending to princes
events.text: Sassetti persuades Lorenzo. Tommaso Portinari in Bruges lends Charles the Bold more than twice his branch's capital, unsecured, within the year.

events.title: Charles the Bold dies at Nancy
events.text: The Duke of Burgundy is killed outside Nancy. His debts die with him; his successor Maximilian borrows more and pays less. The Medici's Bruges branch is insolvent by the following year.
events.source: de Roover (1963), ch. 13

events.title: Mary of Burgundy dies; the Low Countries pass to the Habsburgs
events.text: Charles the Bold's daughter falls from her horse hunting near Bruges. Her son Philip inherits under the regency of his father, Maximilian of Habsburg; Bruges rises against Maximilian in 1488 and holds him prisoner. The Burgundian court is over. The Netherlands are the Habsburgs', and from 1556 Spain's.
events.source: Blockmans & Prevenier, The Promised Lands (1999), ch. 7

events.title: The Medici fall
events.text: Charles VIII marches into Florence, Piero flees, the bank is sacked by the mob and dissolved. Pacioli publishes the Summa the same year. One era's bookkeeping outlives its greatest house.

events.title: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
events.text: Round the Cape and across the Arabian Sea in ten months. When he returns to Lisbon his pepper pays for the voyage many times over. The spice route no longer has to pass the Sultan, or Venice.
events.source: Subrahmanyam, The Career and Legend of Vasco da Gama (1997)

events.title: A run on the Rialto
events.text: The Garzoni bank fails in February, the Rizo brothers with it; in May Lippomano stops; the next morning, when Alvise Pisani opens his bench, 'with a huge roar a mighty crowd came running to get their money.' War with the Turk and the loss of the fleet at Zonchio are the cause; the state's own borrowing from the banks is the mechanism.
events.source: Mueller; Sanudo's diaries

events.title: The Indies trade is Seville's
events.text: The Casa de Contratación monopolises the American trade. Silver will come, and the Crown will spend it before it lands.

events.title: Lisbon wants a loan against the next pepper fleet
events.text: The Crown of Portugal holds the pepper monopoly and needs silver to buy it in Cochin before it can sell it in Antwerp. The Affaitati, the Welsers and the Fuggers all take the contract at one time or another.

events.title: The Ottomans take Egypt
events.text: Selim I destroys the Mamluk sultanate. Alexandria and Constantinople now answer to one Sultan, who wants money for wars on two fronts.

events.title: The Emperor's election is for sale
events.text: Charles of Habsburg needs 850,000 florins to buy the electors. Jakob Fugger lends most of it. The Fuggers will be the Habsburgs' bankers for forty years; it will not end well.

events.title: Venice appoints the Provveditori sopra Banchi
events.text: Three magistrates to watch the Rialto banks: sureties, inspections, limits. The first dedicated bank supervisor anywhere.

events.title: Antwerp builds its Bourse
events.text: A building for the purpose: bills, bonds, commodities, and the Crown's loans, traded daily. The centre of gravity is here now.

events.title: Philip II stops payment
events.text: Spain's first bankruptcy. Short-term asientos are converted by decree into long-term juros at a fraction of their value. The Fuggers are gutted; the Genoese step into the gap.
events.source: Drelichman & Voth (2014)

events.title: The Genoese offer a place in the asiento
events.text: A consortium lends Philip against the silver of the next fleet, at the fairs' rates. Join and you are in the richest business in Europe, with the worst-paying borrower in it.

events.title: Philip II stops payment again
events.text: September 1575: all asientos suspended. Castile's credit markets freeze for two years; the Army of Flanders, unpaid, mutinies.

events.title: The Spanish Fury
events.text: The unpaid army sacks Antwerp: three days, seven thousand dead, the Bourse looted. The trade goes north to Amsterdam and never comes back.

events.title: The fairs move to Piacenza
events.text: The Genoese fairs of Besançon settle at Piacenza. Four times a year the bankers of Flanders, Germany, France and Spain clear their bills here with almost no coin: the largest money market in Europe.

events.title: The last private bank in Venice fails
events.text: Pisani-Tiepolo, propped by the Mint in 1576, succumbs to a run. There are no private banks left on the Rialto.

events.title: The Banco della Piazza di Rialto
events.text: Venice founds a public bank of deposit and transfer, guaranteed by the state. It takes the giro business; a private house in Venice is a lender now, not a payment system.

events.title: Philip II stops payment a fourth time
events.text: 1557, 1560, 1575, 1596. Defaults are not an accident of the Spanish system; they are how it works. The Genoese have learned to price them.

events.title: The East India Company is chartered
events.text: Elizabeth I grants 218 London merchants the monopoly of English trade east of the Cape. Its Court of Directors will meet in Leadenhall Street for 274 years, and borrow like a state.
events.source: Chaudhuri, The Trading World of Asia and the English East India Company (1978)

events.title: The VOC sells shares to the public
events.text: The Dutch East India Company's charter: capital from anyone, shares transferable on the Amsterdam exchange. The joint-stock company exists.

events.title: The Amsterdam Wisselbank
events.text: A civic bank of deposit on the Venetian model, guaranteed by the burgomasters. Bank money at a premium to coin; every bill over 600 guilders must settle through it. Amsterdam is the centre.

events.title: Coen founds Batavia
events.text: Jan Pieterszoon Coen burns Jayakarta and builds the VOC's Asian headquarters on its ruins. From here the Company runs the spice islands by force and the inter-Asian trade by bill.

events.title: The VOC issues obligaties
events.text: The Company borrows short in Amsterdam against its returning fleets: bonds the Heeren XVII will roll over for 180 years. Safe as the States General, the burghers say.
events.source: Gelderblom, de Jong & Jonker, 'The Formative Years of the Modern Corporation' (2013)

events.title: Tulip mania breaks
events.text: February 1637: contracts for bulbs that changed hands ten times a day find no buyer. The damage is to speculators, not banks — but your speculating depositors are your depositors.

events.title: The goldsmiths of Lombard Street become bankers
events.text: Their receipts pass hand to hand; they lend the deposits; they lend to the Crown against next year's revenue. Notes you can print are the cheapest money there is.

events.title: Charles II wants an advance on the taxes
events.text: The Exchequer sells orders on the next two years' revenue to the goldsmiths. Backwell and Vyner hold most of it. The interest is good and the King is the King.

events.title: The Stop of the Exchequer
events.text: Charles II suspends payment on £1.2 million of orders. Backwell and Vyner, the greatest goldsmith-bankers in London, are ruined; their depositors with them. It will take twenty-two years and a revolution to make the Crown's debt safe.
events.source: Winter, Goldsmith Banking; Roseveare, The Financial Revolution

events.title: The Rampjaar
events.text: France, England, Münster and Cologne attack the Republic at once. The Amsterdam exchange falls by half in a month; the dykes are cut to save the city. The people are 'redeloos', the government 'radeloos', the country 'reddeloos'.

events.title: The Bank of England is founded
events.text: Paterson's scheme, on the Wisselbank's model: £1.2 million lent to the Crown at 8%, in exchange for a charter and the right to issue notes. The state's debt now has a bank of its own. The usury cap holds everyone else to 6%.

events.title: The East India Company lends the state two million
events.text: The New Company buys its charter with a £2m loan to the Crown, and pays for it by selling its own bonds in the City. East India bonds will be the money market's favourite paper for a century.
events.source: Bowen, The Business of Empire (2006)

events.title: Usury capped at 5%
events.text: Parliament lowers the legal maximum to 5%. It will stand until 1854. Bills, which carry no stated interest, do not count.

events.title: The South Sea Bubble
events.text: The Company's stock goes from £128 to £1,000 and back in a year on a scheme to take over the national debt. Parliament's answer is the Bubble Act: no joint-stock company without a charter, for a hundred years.

events.title: The Bubble Act
events.text: Joint-stock is a privilege of the chartered few. Banks in England are partnerships of six, until 1826.

events.title: The Jacobites march on Derby
events.text: A run on the Bank of England; it pays out in sixpences to slow the queue. The Pretender turns back.

events.title: Lisbon is destroyed
events.text: All Saints' Day, 1755: the earthquake, the fire and the tsunami. Most of the city and its warehouses are gone, and the merchants' ledgers with them.

events.title: Plassey
events.text: Clive defeats the Nawab of Bengal. The Company becomes the ruler of the richest province in India, and collects its land revenue. Calcutta's counting-houses fill.

events.title: The Amsterdam crisis of 1763
events.text: De Neufville Brothers, overextended on acceptance credit after the Seven Years' War, fail in July. Hamburg's and Berlin's houses go with them. The first crisis of the acceptance market.
events.source: Schnabel & Shin, 'Liquidity and Contagion: The Crisis of 1763' (2004)

events.title: The Bengal famine
events.text: A third of Bengal's people die and the Company's land revenue collapses. The dividend it has promised its shareholders it can no longer earn.

events.title: The Company cannot pay its bills
events.text: East India stock begins to slide on the news from Bengal; Alexander Fordyce, who has gambled on it with other people's money, flees in June 1772 and takes the Ayr Bank's London correspondents with him. In July the Company asks the Bank of England for a million and the government for more. The Regulating Act of 1773 lends it £1.4m and puts it under Parliament.
events.source: Kosmetatos (2018); Bowen, Revenue and Reform (1991)

events.title: The Ayr Bank fails
events.text: Douglas, Heron & Co. lent before its partners had paid in their capital; its notes were two-thirds of Scotland's currency. It stops in June 1772 and takes twenty London houses with it. The partners are liable for everything, and lose it.
events.source: Kosmetatos, The 1772–73 British Credit Crisis (2018)

events.title: The Fourth Anglo-Dutch War
events.text: The Royal Navy takes the VOC's fleets at sea. The Company cannot ship its goods home and borrows to pay its dividends. It never recovers.

events.title: War with Revolutionary France
events.text: A crisis of confidence; a hundred country banks stop. The Exchequer issues bills to the merchants to keep them going. The war will last twenty-two years and cost more than every war before it.

events.title: The Bank suspends gold payments
events.text: A French landing in Wales and a drain of gold: the Bank of England stops paying its notes in coin. Paper pounds for twenty-four years. Country-bank notes, now unconvertible too, multiply.

events.title: The VOC is dissolved
events.text: Nationalised in 1796, wound up on the last day of 1799. Its debts pass to the Batavian Republic and its creditors are paid in the state's paper, late and at a discount. Batavia becomes a colony of the Dutch state.
events.source: Gaastra, The Dutch East India Company (2003)

events.title: Louisiana for sale
events.text: Napoleon sells the territory to the United States for $15 million and wants cash now. Barings and Hope take the American bonds at a discount and pay him $8.8 million. Britain is at war with France. The deal goes through.

events.title: Waterloo
events.text: The war ends. The houses that financed it — Barings, and now Rothschild — float the peace: the French indemnity loans of 1817–18 are the largest issues the world has seen. Sovereign bonds, sold to the public, are the business now.

events.title: Resumption of cash payments
events.text: The pound is gold again at the old parity. Prices fall; debtors suffer; the City is the world's safe harbour.

events.title: Buenos Aires wants a million
events.text: Barings floats a £1m loan for the province of Buenos Aires at 85. The new republics of South America are the fashion of the London market.

events.title: The panic of 1825
events.text: Latin American mining shares and the bonds of a country that did not exist (Poyais) collapse together. Seventy banks stop; a tenth of England's country banks never reopen. The Bank of England lends 'by every possible means' and the Bubble Act is repealed.

events.title: The Country Bankers Act
events.text: Joint-stock banks with more than six partners, allowed — outside sixty-five miles of London. Joint-stock without limited liability, which is a different thing.

events.title: Buenos Aires stops paying
events.text: War with Brazil and a blockade of the Plate: the province suspends its dividends. The bondholders will wait thirty years for a settlement.
events.source: Marichal, A Century of Debt Crises in Latin America (1989)

events.title: The Calcutta agency houses fail
events.text: Palmer & Co., 'the princes of merchants', stop in 1830; Alexander & Co., Mackintosh & Co. and the rest follow by 1834. They had lent their depositors' money to indigo planters, and indigo fell.
events.source: Webster, The Twilight of the East India Company (2009)

events.title: The Company loses the China trade
events.text: The Charter Act ends the East India Company's monopoly of the tea trade. Jardine Matheson and the private houses take it over, and with it the opium that pays for it.

events.title: The Opium War
events.text: Lin Zexu destroys the opium at Humen; the Royal Navy answers. Canton's trade stops for three years. At Nanking in 1842 China cedes Hong Kong and opens five ports.

events.title: The Bank Charter Act
events.text: Peel's Act: the Bank of England's note issue is tied to its gold, and no new bank may issue notes. Yours, if you have them, will run off. In every crisis for the next forty years the Act will have to be suspended.

events.title: The railway mania breaks
events.text: Calls on railway shares drain the money market; the Act is suspended for the first time. Bills on the corn trade go bad with the harvest.

events.title: Gold in New South Wales
events.text: Bathurst in February, Ballarat by August. The colonies' population triples in a decade and the banks buy gold dust over the counter.

events.title: The Sultan borrows abroad
events.text: The Crimean War: the Ottoman Empire's first foreign loan, floated in London and Paris. Twenty years of borrowing follow.

events.title: The panic of 1857
events.text: From Ohio to Glasgow to Hamburg: the first crisis to cross the Atlantic by telegraph. The Act is suspended again. The Western Bank of Scotland fails.

events.title: The Indian Rebellion
events.text: Meerut in May, Delhi by June, Cawnpore and Lucknow besieged. The Company's rule survives the year and not the reckoning.

events.title: Limited liability for banks
events.text: The Joint Stock Banks Act of 1858, consolidated in 1862: a bank may register with limited liability. Most do not, at first. Shareholders who have not read the deed will learn what unlimited means in 1878.

events.title: The Crown takes India
events.text: The Government of India Act: the Company's territories, army and debts pass to the Crown. Its stock will be redeemed in 1874 and the Court of Directors will meet no more.

events.title: Overend Gurney stops
events.text: The greatest discount house in the world asks the Bank of England for help on 9 May and is refused: it is insolvent, not illiquid. At 3.30 on 10 May it suspends. Black Friday. The Chancellor suspends the Act and the Bank lends to everyone solvent, without limit, at a high rate. The lender of last resort exists from this afternoon.
events.source: Bank of England Quarterly Bulletin 2016 Q4; Bank Underground, 21 Dec 2016

events.title: The Suez Canal opens
events.text: 17 November 1869. London to Bombay is thousands of miles shorter, and the steamer, which could not carry coal enough to round the Cape at a profit, now owns the Eastern trade. Alexandria comes back to life.

events.title: Bagehot publishes Lombard Street
events.text: Lend freely, at a penalty rate, on good collateral. The Bank's duty in a panic, written down so that it cannot be forgotten. It is forgotten anyway, in 2007.

events.title: The Sultan stops paying
events.text: October 1875: the Ottoman government halves its coupons; Egypt follows in 1876. The Ottoman Public Debt Administration will run the Empire's revenues for its creditors from 1881.
events.source: Pamuk, The Ottoman Economy and Its Institutions (2009)

events.title: The City of Glasgow Bank fails
events.text: £6 million of losses hidden by false accounts; the directors go to prison. The bank is unlimited, and 1,819 shareholders are called for £2,750 a share. 1,565 of them are ruined. Every unlimited bank in Britain registers as limited within four years.
events.source: Turner, Banking in Crisis (2014)

events.title: Argentina wants a water company financed
events.text: Buenos Aires Water Supply and Drainage: Barings underwrites it and cannot place it. The Argentine boom is the emerging market of its day. Everyone is in.

events.title: The Baring crisis
events.text: Argentina defaults and Barings, holding £21 million of its paper, is insolvent. The Governor organises a guarantee fund from every bank in the City in a weekend; Barings is liquidated and refounded as a limited company. No depositor loses. The first orderly resolution.
events.source: Ziegler, The Sixth Great Power

events.title: The Australian bank crash
events.text: The land boom breaks: thirteen of Australia's trading banks suspend in April and May. Most reopen after 'reconstruction', with their depositors' money frozen for years.
events.source: Merrett, 'The Australian bank crashes of the 1890s revisited' (2013)

events.title: China borrows to pay Japan
events.text: The indemnity after the Sino-Japanese war: large loans in 1896 and 1898, floated by the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank and the Deutsch-Asiatische Bank against the Maritime Customs.

events.title: The Tsar's great loan
events.text: After the war with Japan and the revolution of 1905, Russia floats the largest foreign loan the world has seen, mostly in Paris, partly in London. French savers hold Russian bonds the way their grandchildren will hold houses.

events.title: The panic of 1907
events.text: The Knickerbocker Trust fails in October; J.P. Morgan locks the bankers in his library until they agree to lend. Six years later Congress creates the Federal Reserve so that it need never happen again.

events.title: August 1914
events.text: The Stock Exchange shuts on 31 July and stays shut for five months. Every accepting house in London is insolvent on paper: the German bills they have accepted will not be paid. A moratorium, and the Bank buys the bills. The Bank rate goes to 10%.
events.source: Roberts, Saving the City (2013)

events.title: The Bolsheviks repudiate the Tsar's debts
events.text: Every Russian bond ever sold in London and Paris is worth nothing. The French rentier takes most of it.

events.title: The Great Kantō earthquake
events.text: 1 September 1923: Tokyo and Yokohama burn. The Bank of Japan rediscounts 'earthquake bills' that are still unpaid in 1927, when the Shōwa bank panic finishes what the earthquake began.

events.title: The Wall Street crash
events.text: October 1929. New York first; the world follows in 1931 when the Creditanstalt fails in Vienna and the contagion reaches Berlin and London.

events.title: Sterling leaves gold
events.text: 21 September 1931. The pound floats and falls a quarter. The gold standard, as the City knew it, is over.

events.title: Glass–Steagall and deposit insurance in America
events.text: Commercial and investment banking separated; the FDIC guarantees deposits. Britain does neither for forty-six years. Your New York branch now has to choose what it is.

events.title: War again
events.text: Exchange control, a Treasury that borrows everything, and a City that is a utility for six years.

events.title: China suspends its foreign debt
events.text: With Japan holding the coast and the Customs, the Nationalist government stops paying. The bondholders will wait decades.

events.title: Bretton Woods
events.text: Fixed exchange rates against a dollar fixed to gold, and capital controls to defend them. The dollar is the world's money; New York is where it lives.

events.title: The Eurodollar market
events.text: Sterling crisis; the Bank restricts sterling trade credit; the merchant banks lend dollars instead, from London, where no one regulates them. The City has found its way back.
events.source: Schenk (1998)

events.title: Competition and Credit Control
events.text: The Bank abolishes the clearers' cartel and the lending ceilings. Credit grows 50% a year; property prices double. Nixon closes the gold window the same summer. Bretton Woods is over.

events.title: The secondary banking crisis
events.text: The property market turns and the fringe banks — London and County, Cedar Holdings, thirty more — cannot roll their wholesale deposits. The Bank and the clearers launch the Lifeboat: £1.2 billion, 40% of the clearers' capital, lent to keep the fringe from sinking the system.
events.source: Reid, The Secondary Banking Crisis 1973–75

events.title: The Banking Act 1979
events.text: Deposits are protected, to a limit, for the first time in Britain, and banks must be authorised. Exchange controls are abolished the same year.

events.title: Mexico wants a syndicated loan
events.text: OPEC's surpluses are on deposit in London and New York, and the banks lend them on to Latin America at floating rates. Countries do not go bust, Walter Wriston says.

events.title: Mexico cannot pay
events.text: August 1982: the petrodollars recycled through London to Latin America stop coming back. Every syndicated loan to the region is restructured; the big banks' capital is wiped on paper and the regulators let them pretend otherwise for seven years.

events.title: Big Bang
events.text: 27 October 1986: fixed commissions abolished, jobbers and brokers merged, foreign ownership allowed, the floor replaced by screens. Every merchant bank buys a broker; most will be bought by an American or a Swiss within a decade.

events.title: Basel I
events.text: The Basel Committee's accord: 8% of risk-weighted assets, with four risk buckets, for every internationally active bank. The first capital rule a British bank has ever had.

events.title: Tokyo's bubble bursts
events.text: The Nikkei, near 39,000 at the end of 1989, falls by more than a third within the year; land follows. Japanese banks, the largest in the world, will spend a decade not admitting their losses.

events.title: BCCI is closed
events.text: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International, supervised by no one in particular, is shut by the Bank of England on 5 July 1991 with $10 billion missing. The Bingham report rewrites supervision.

events.title: Argentina's Brady bonds
events.text: The peso is pegged one-for-one to the dollar and Argentina is the IMF's model pupil. Its new bonds are in every emerging-markets fund.

events.title: Barings fails
events.text: Nick Leeson, 28, in Singapore, loses £827 million in unauthorised futures positions hidden in error account 88888. The oldest merchant bank in London is sold to ING for £1. Your Singapore desk's controls are now a question.
events.source: Board of Banking Supervision report (1995)

events.title: The Asian crisis
events.text: Thailand floats the baht in July; Korea, Indonesia and Malaysia follow it down. Dollar loans to Asian corporates double in local terms overnight.

events.title: The dot-com crash
events.text: The NASDAQ loses three quarters of its value in two years. Investment banking fees halve.

events.title: Argentina defaults
events.text: December 2001: about $90 billion, then the largest sovereign default in history. The 2005 exchange offers some thirty cents on the dollar.
events.source: Sturzenegger & Zettelmeyer, Debt Defaults and Lessons from a Decade of Crises (2006)

events.title: Dubai World wants a syndicated loan
events.text: Ports, islands shaped like palm trees, and a tower half a mile high, financed in London. The emirate is good for it, everyone says.

events.title: Basel II comes into force in the UK
events.text: Internal models for credit risk, with permission. Capital falls. Northern Rock, funded 75% in the wholesale market, is the first British run in 140 years, in September.

events.title: Lehman
events.text: 15 September 2008. The interbank market closes. RBS and HBOS are hours from failing; the Treasury takes £37 billion of their equity in October. A wholesale-funded bank with a mortgage book is a run waiting to happen, as Overend Gurney could have told them.

events.title: Dubai World asks for a standstill
events.text: November 2009: some $26 billion of debt rescheduled. Abu Dhabi lends Dubai $10 billion and the creditors are paid in full — later.

events.title: The FSB publishes the first G-SIB list
events.text: Twenty-nine banks whose failure would matter everywhere, scored on size, interconnectedness, substitutability, complexity and cross-border activity, and charged extra capital for it. Being on this list is what this game is for.

events.title: Basel III / CRD IV
events.text: CET1 of 4.5%, a conservation buffer of 2.5%, a countercyclical buffer, a G-SIB surcharge, a leverage ratio and an LCR. The Bank of England runs its first concurrent stress test.

events.title: Ring-fencing
events.text: Banks with more than £25 billion of core deposits must put retail behind a fence the investment bank cannot reach across. Capital and liquidity are trapped on each side.

events.title: The pandemic
events.text: Markets seize in March; central banks buy everything. The stress test the banks had been running for six years turns out to have been worth it.

events.title: Basel 3.1
events.text: 1 January 2027. The revised standardised approach, FRTB, the output floor phasing to 72.5% by 2030. The last turn. The FSB's list is published in November.

deck.title: An Eastern state bank parks its dollars in London
deck.text: A Soviet-owned bank with a London address would rather not keep its dollars in New York, where a Senate committee might freeze them. It asks to place them with you for thirty and ninety days and lend them on. The Bank of England, sterling being short, looks the other way.

advice.growth: Dollars nobody else will take at a rate nobody else offers. Lend them to Italian industry by Friday.
advice.prudence: Short dollar deposits lent long are a maturity gap in a currency the Bank cannot print for us.
advice.court: The Governor wants London to be a dollar centre and has not asked whose dollars they are.
advice.conscience: A deposit is not a sin. Know the customer, keep the ledgers straight, and the Cold War is not our affair.

deck.precedent: Moscow Narodny Bank in London and the Banque Commerciale pour l'Europe du Nord in Paris placed Soviet dollar balances in Europe in the 1950s, and Midland took swapped dollar deposits in 1955, seeding the Eurodollar market
deck.source: Schenk, 'The origins of the Eurodollar market in London: 1955–1963', Explorations in Economic History (1998)

deck.title: A run on the pound
deck.text: The reserves are bleeding, the Chancellor swears there will be no devaluation, and Bank Rate goes up on a Thursday. Gilts fall, the forward discount widens and customers with dollar contracts want cover at any price. By the weekend the parity may not exist.

rumour.text: They say the Treasury's knocking on the Fed's door again and the Governor has cancelled his holiday.

advice.growth: Sell sterling forward for the clients and take the spread; a crisis is a dealing room's harvest.
advice.prudence: Square the book and shorten the gilts. A devaluation marks down whatever we hold in pounds.
advice.court: Do not be seen speculating against the pound; the Bank keeps a list, and it is not a short one.
advice.conscience: Advise customers honestly on cover. Telling them all is well when we are hedged ourselves is a lie.

deck.precedent: Sterling devalued from $2.80 to $2.40 on 18 November 1967; forced out of the ERM on Black Wednesday, 16 September 1992
deck.source: Cairncross & Eichengreen, Sterling in Decline (1983)

deck.title: The oil producers turn off the tap
deck.text: A war in the Middle East and an embargo: the posted price of crude quadruples in three months. Petrol queues, a three-day week, and every borrower whose margins depended on cheap fuel—shipping, airlines, chemicals—comes to see you about his covenants.

rumour.text: The tanker men say the Gulf states have met in Kuwait and nobody is chartering for next month.

advice.growth: The producers will drown in dollars and they must bank them somewhere. Be that somewhere.
advice.prudence: Inflation at twenty per cent eats fixed-rate loans alive. Reprice what we can and reserve the rest.
advice.court: Government will want the banks to carry industry through the winter. Showing willing costs little now.
advice.conscience: Do not call loans on firms that were sound a month ago merely because we can.

deck.precedent: The October 1973 Arab–Israeli war and the OAPEC embargo, with OPEC's posted-price rises of October and December 1973, quadrupled the price of oil by January 1974; the Iranian revolution roughly doubled it again in 1979–80
deck.source: Yergin, The Prize (1991)

deck.title: A Gulf central bank places its surplus with you
deck.text: The oil money has to go somewhere, and the producers prefer London's banks to Washington's Treasury. A monetary agency places a block of call and seven-day dollars with your money desk. Short, cheap, enormous, and every penny of it will want to be lent.

advice.growth: Fifty million at call: the most profitable telephone call this house has ever taken.
advice.prudence: Hot money from one depositor at seven days. If they pull it, what do we sell?
advice.court: The Treasury wants the surpluses recycled through London. They will be glad it came to a British name.
advice.conscience: Take the deposit, but do not let its size bully our credit committee into lending it badly.

deck.precedent: OPEC current-account surpluses of some $60bn in 1974 were placed largely as short deposits with Eurobanks in London and New York
deck.source: Spiro, The Hidden Hand of American Hegemony: Petrodollar Recycling (1999)

deck.title: {court} wants a jumbo syndicated loan
deck.text: A finance minister and his advisers are in town for a jumbo: seven years, floating at a spread over six-month LIBOR, cross-default to everything. The lead managers have the petrodollars; they need participants. Your share would be a large one, and the fee is paid up front.

advice.growth: Countries do not go bust; they have assets, oil and a central bank. Take the biggest ticket offered.
advice.prudence: Floating rate means they carry the rate risk, and they cannot carry it. Their risk becomes our credit risk.
advice.court: The Bank of England is relaxed about country lending; it has said so in every speech this year.
advice.conscience: A loan the borrower can only repay by borrowing again is not prudent lending, however handsome the fee.

deck.precedent: Bank syndicates lent heavily to Mexico, Brazil and Argentina at floating rates in 1974–81, Citicorp's chairman declaring that countries don't go bust
deck.source: Devlin, Debt and Crisis in Latin America: The Supply Side of the Story (1989)

deck.title: A counterparty is closed in the middle of the day
deck.text: At half past four a foreign regulator withdraws a bank's licence. You paid your marks to it this morning in Frankfurt; the dollars it owed you were due in New York this afternoon and will never come. Every dealer in town is now refusing to pay first.

advice.growth: Keep dealing; spreads have tripled and we have lines to the names that are still standing.
advice.prudence: Cut settlement limits to every second-tier bank now. Principal risk on an FX leg is the whole amount.
advice.court: The central bank governors will meet in Basel about this. Give them our numbers before they ask.
advice.conscience: Honour every payment we owe on time, even as others hold back. Our word is the settlement system.

deck.precedent: Bankhaus Herstatt was closed by the German authorities on 26 June 1974 after receiving Deutsche Mark legs but before paying dollars, prompting the founding of the Basel Committee
deck.source: Goodhart, The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision: A History of the Early Years 1974–1997 (2011)

deck.title: {court} cannot pay
deck.text: The finance minister flies to Washington and announces he cannot meet principal on the syndicated loans. Every other borrower in the region follows within months. The loans will be rescheduled, rolled and re-rolled; your auditors will be asked, politely, not to look too hard at what they are worth.

rumour.text: The rate on the next rollover is four hundred over, and the central bank's reserves report is late again.

advice.growth: Join the advisory committee and lend the new money; walking away crystallises the loss we can still defer.
advice.prudence: Provision now, honestly. A loss deferred for seven years is still a loss, and the capital is not there.
advice.court: Washington and the IMF want concerted lending. The supervisors will be lenient with banks who cooperate.
advice.conscience: A people should not starve to pay our interest; yet depositors trusted us not to gamble their money.

deck.precedent: Mexico's moratorium of 20 August 1982 began the Latin American debt crisis, resolved only by the Brady Plan from 1989
deck.source: Boughton, Silent Revolution: The International Monetary Fund 1979–1989 (2001)

deck.title: A wire story says the house is in trouble
deck.text: A newswire in Tokyo runs a story that a foreign bank is seeking a buyer; by the London open it has your name in it. The money brokers' screens show your certificates of deposit at a quarter over everyone else, then unquotable. Wholesale money does not queue outside; it simply fails to roll.

rumour.text: A broker on the eurodollar desk says a big Japanese bank has quietly cut its line to someone in London.

advice.growth: Deny it loudly and pay up for term money. Rumours die when a bank is seen borrowing confidently.
advice.prudence: We fund a third of the book overnight. Sell liquid assets now, before the market prices our distress.
advice.court: Call the central bank this morning; a quiet line of liquidity is worth more than any press release.
advice.conscience: Say nothing that is untrue. A denial later contradicted would finish us faster than the rumour.

deck.precedent: Continental Illinois lost billions of wholesale deposits in days after rumours on Japanese and Reuters newswires in May 1984, and was rescued by the FDIC
deck.source: FDIC, History of the Eighties—Lessons for the Future (1997)

deck.title: Queues outside the Chinese banks of {city}
deck.text: Two small banks have shut their doors and the queues have moved to the biggest local bank in the colony, which has lent long on property and cannot pay out at the counter. Its family owners come to you after dark: buy control, or lend against the deeds, or watch them close.

choice.label: Buy a controlling stake
choice.result: Its depositors become yours and the run stops, but you inherit a management you do not yet control.

choice.label: Lend against the title deeds
choice.result: You earn a fat margin on secured money and the bank survives, still its owners'.

choice.label: Stand aside
choice.result: The bank closes, the run spreads, and the colony remembers who kept its doors shut.

rumour.text: The tea-house talk is that a bank in Wanchai has been paying out in small notes only.

advice.growth: A franchise like this comes up once a generation. Buy it at panic prices and own the colony's savings.
advice.prudence: Its loans are concrete on a hillside. We would be buying a run, not ending one—stay out entirely.
advice.court: Government House wants the run stopped by a sound bank, and will remember which one did it.
advice.conscience: Ordinary families queue for their savings. Whatever we choose, do not profit by prolonging their fear.

deck.precedent: After runs on Ming Tak and Canton Trust in February 1965, Hang Seng Bank suffered a run in April and sold 51% to the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank
deck.source: King, The History of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, vol. IV (1991)

deck.title: The central bank passes the hat
deck.text: A bullion-dealing bank has lent recklessly through its banking arm and will not open on Monday. The Governor summons the senior bankers on Sunday evening: the bank will take it over, but wants an indemnity shared among the houses at the table. Nobody is obliged. Everybody will remember.

choice.label: Subscribe your share of the indemnity
choice.result: Money tied up at a poor return, and a seat at the table when the rules are next written.

choice.label: Decline politely
choice.result: Capital preserved; the Governor's eyebrows noted in every supervisory meeting for a decade.

choice.label: Offer to buy its sound book instead
choice.result: A modest bargain and some goodwill, with clients and staff of uncertain quality.

advice.growth: Buy the good loans cheap. Rescues are where franchises change hands at a discount.
advice.prudence: An open-ended indemnity on a book nobody has audited. Cap our share or decline.
advice.court: Say yes before he finishes the sentence. The Bank's favour is the cheapest capital we will ever raise.
advice.conscience: Our depositors did not consent to underwrite another bank's folly—but a collapse would harm them more.

deck.precedent: The Bank of England rescued Johnson Matthey Bankers on 1 October 1984, buying it for £1 with an indemnity shared by the clearers and others
deck.source: Bank of England, Report and Accounts 1985; Moran, The Politics of Banking (1986)

deck.title: A nationalised utility is to be sold to the public
deck.text: The government is selling a state telephone company to anybody with a few hundred pounds and a coupon from the newspaper. The issue needs receiving banks, underwriters and sub-underwriters, and the fees are fixed in advance. Every branch counter will be busy for a month.

advice.growth: Underwrite as much as they will give us; the issue is priced to go to a premium.
advice.prudence: Fine, but remember underwriting is a put sold to the Treasury. Ask what happens in a crash week.
advice.court: Ministers want the sale to succeed visibly. Being on the tombstone is worth more than the fee.
advice.conscience: Do not tell small savers that shares cannot fall. Explain the risk at the counter, even if it slows the queue.

deck.precedent: British Telecom was floated in November 1984 and British Gas in December 1986, with the clearing banks as receiving banks and underwriters
deck.source: Florio, The Great Divestiture: Evaluating the Welfare Impact of the British Privatizations 1979–1997 (2004)

deck.title: The market falls a fifth in a single day
deck.text: No war, no default: just portfolio insurance selling into a falling market, specialists who will not make prices and a futures pit in Chicago that runs ahead of New York. By the close the index is down more than a fifth. Your market-making arm has positions it could not get out of.

advice.growth: Buy tomorrow morning. Nothing has changed in the economy but prices, and prices come back.
advice.prudence: Count the margin calls our clients cannot meet before counting bargains. That is where the loss is.
advice.court: The central banks will flood the market with liquidity by breakfast. Be ready to say we need none.
advice.conscience: Brokers who forget to execute client sell orders while dumping our own are committing fraud, not making markets.

deck.precedent: Black Monday, 19 October 1987: the Dow Jones fell 22.6% in one session, with London and Tokyo following
deck.source: Report of the Presidential Task Force on Market Mechanisms (Brady Commission, 1988)

deck.title: A commodity buffer stock runs out of money
deck.text: An intergovernmental council that props up a metal price has been buying forward on the exchange with borrowed money. Its manager tells the ring he can no longer pay. Trading is suspended; brokers and their banks hold contracts with a body owned by two dozen states, none of whom admit they must pay.

rumour.text: The ring dealers say the buffer stock manager's cheques are clearing slower than his warrants.

advice.growth: Lending to a body backed by twenty governments is as safe as lending to the governments.
advice.prudence: Read the constitution: a separate legal person. Our claim is against it, not against its members.
advice.court: Ministers will not let the exchange fail. Wait for the settlement they are bound to arrange.
advice.conscience: Brokers ruined by this are our customers. Do not squeeze them harder than the default already has.

deck.precedent: The International Tin Council's buffer stock stopped paying on 24 October 1985; the House of Lords held member states not liable (J.H. Rayner v DTI, 1989)
deck.source: J.H. Rayner (Mincing Lane) Ltd v Department of Trade and Industry [1990] 2 AC 418

deck.title: The Lords say councils could never write swaps
deck.text: A London borough ran an interest-rate swap book larger than its budget, and rates moved against it. The auditor went to court; the House of Lords holds that local authorities had no power to enter swaps at all. Every swap your desk wrote with a council is void ab initio, and the restitution claims begin.

rumour.text: The District Auditor has been asking a borough treasurer why his swap book is ten times his capital programme.

advice.growth: A council is as good as the Treasury. Write them all the swaps they want—local government cannot default.
advice.prudence: Capacity is the first question on any counterparty. Where is the statutory power? Nobody on the desk knows.
advice.court: The Bank of England will press for legislation to validate the trades. Lobby, and hope.
advice.conscience: We sold speculation to ratepayers dressed as hedging. The courts are telling us what our lawyers should have.

deck.precedent: Hazell v Hammersmith and Fulham LBC, decided 24 January 1991, held council swaps ultra vires, leading to years of restitution claims (Westdeutsche v Islington, 1996)
deck.source: Hazell v Hammersmith and Fulham LBC [1992] 2 AC 1

deck.title: Washington freezes a client's dollars—in your London branch
deck.text: A presidential order freezes all property of a foreign state's bank held by American persons, overseas branches included. That state's bank keeps a large call account in dollars at your London office, governed by English law, and demands payment today—in cash if need be. New York is telling you not to pay.

choice.label: Pay out in London as English law requires
choice.result: The client is satisfied and London's name as a deposit centre with it, but Washington is not amused.

choice.label: Honour the freeze worldwide
choice.result: You keep the Americans sweet and get sued in the Commercial Court for the whole deposit.

choice.label: Hold the funds and let a judge decide
choice.result: A year of litigation and interest accruing, but nobody can say you chose a side.

advice.growth: This client keeps a hundred million with us. Lose it and every Gulf depositor reads the lesson.
advice.prudence: Whichever way we go we are sued somewhere. Choose the court whose judgment we can actually satisfy.
advice.court: An American order binds a branch wherever it sits. Freeze it all—London law has no say over dollars.
advice.conscience: We promised to repay on demand in London. A foreign executive order does not unwrite our contract.

deck.precedent: The US froze Iranian assets on 14 November 1979 and Libyan assets on 8 January 1986; in Libyan Arab Foreign Bank v Bankers Trust an English court held the London dollar deposit payable
deck.source: Libyan Arab Foreign Bank v Bankers Trust Co [1989] QB 728

deck.title: The land bubble in {city} bursts
deck.text: The stock index peaked at the year-end party; by summer it is down a third, and the land in the city centre is no longer worth more than whole foreign countries. Developers stop paying, and the local banks, holding shares in each other and land as collateral, begin a decade of not admitting it.

rumour.text: The ministry has told the banks to cap property lending, and the golf-club memberships are not selling.

advice.growth: Land here has not fallen since the war. The banks are the biggest in the world; lend alongside them.
advice.prudence: Collateral valued at the peak, loans sized to the collateral. Cut the book before the valuations are redone.
advice.court: The Finance Ministry will not let its banks fail, but it will not protect foreign lenders either.
advice.conscience: If we roll loans we know are bad to avoid booking losses, we are lying in our accounts.

deck.precedent: The Nikkei peaked at 38,915 on 29 December 1989 and fell some 39% in 1990, with land prices following; Hong Kong property fell by two-thirds 1997–2003
deck.source: Wood, The Bubble Economy: Japan's Extraordinary Speculative Boom of the '80s (1992)

deck.title: {court} issues new bonds, a model reformer
deck.text: The old bank loans have been swapped for collateralised bonds, the currency is pegged one-for-one to the dollar by law, and the IMF holds the country up as its best pupil. The new bonds trade in every emerging-markets fund and yield three times Treasuries. The lead manager has an allocation for you.

advice.growth: A currency board cannot devalue; it is written into law. This is dollar risk at peso spreads.
advice.prudence: A peg that needs a law to hold it is a peg that will break the day the law is changed.
advice.court: The Treasury and the Fund both endorse the programme. Declining would look like disloyalty to the plan.
advice.conscience: We should tell the clients we sell these to that a yield of ten per cent is paying them for something.

deck.precedent: Argentina completed its Brady exchange in April 1993 under the 1991 Convertibility Law pegging the peso to the dollar
deck.source: Cline, International Debt Reexamined (1995)

deck.title: A surprise rise in rates routs the bond market
deck.text: The central bank moves a quarter point when nobody expected it, then keeps going. Long yields rise by two and a half points in months; mortgage-backed hedgers sell into the fall, a county treasurer's leveraged fund implodes, and every bond desk on the Street marks down its carry trades.

rumour.text: The Fed chairman's testimony is next week and he is said to be worried about inflation he can't see yet.

advice.growth: Yields at these levels are a gift. Add duration and carry while others are being stopped out.
advice.prudence: Measure the convexity in the mortgage book. Duration that lengthens as rates rise is a short option.
advice.court: The supervisors will want our interest-rate risk numbers by the end of the month. Have them ready.
advice.conscience: We sold leveraged notes to public treasurers as safe. Their losses will be our lawsuits.

deck.precedent: The Fed's surprise tightening from 4 February 1994 drove the 'great bond massacre' and Orange County's bankruptcy in December 1994; echoed in the UK gilt crisis of September 2022
deck.source: Borio & McCauley, 'The economics of recent bond yield volatility', BIS Economic Papers 45 (1996)

deck.title: A currency peg breaks and the region follows
deck.text: One central bank spends its reserves defending the peg, then floats. Its neighbours go down with it. Companies that borrowed in dollars to build towers and factories now owe twice as much in local money, and the short interbank lines that funded them are not rolled.

rumour.text: Forward points on the baht are flashing, and they say the central bank has sold most of its reserves forward defending the peg.

advice.growth: Tigers grow at eight per cent a year. A dip is a chance to take market share from timid lenders.
advice.prudence: Dollar loans to borrowers with local revenues are FX options we wrote for free. Reduce them.
advice.court: The IMF will defend these pegs with whatever it takes. No floating rate regime will be allowed here.
advice.conscience: When we cut lines, real firms and their workers fail. Cut where the risk is, not where it is easiest.

deck.precedent: Thailand floated the baht on 2 July 1997, followed by Indonesia, Malaysia and Korea; Mexico's peso crisis of December 1994 had the same shape
deck.source: Radelet & Sachs, 'The East Asian Financial Crisis', Brookings Papers on Economic Activity (1998)

deck.title: A trader in {city} has been hiding losses
deck.text: A bond trader who also runs his own back office has been booking fictitious trades for years to cover a loss that started small. The reconciliations were his to do. He confesses in a letter to the chairman; the regulators learn of it from the newspapers, which is worse.

advice.growth: He was our best earner for three years. One bad trade should not shake confidence in the desk.
advice.prudence: No one who books trades may confirm or settle them. Segregate the back office today, everywhere.
advice.court: Tell the regulator before the press does. Concealment of a loss is now a second, larger problem.
advice.conscience: His managers rewarded profits nobody understood. The fraud is his; the blindness was ours.

deck.precedent: Daiwa Bank's New York bond trader concealed $1.1bn over eleven years, disclosed September 1995; Société Générale €4.9bn (January 2008); UBS $2.3bn (September 2011)
deck.source: Société Générale, General Inspection Department, Mission Green: Summary Report (2008)

deck.title: The new-economy shares collapse
deck.text: Companies with no profits and a website were worth more than steel mills. Then the index peaks, the IPO window shuts, and in two years three-quarters of the technology board's value is gone. Your advisory fees halve and the loans to telecom carriers that bought spectrum at auction look very different.

rumour.text: Analysts are marking their own IPOs 'strong buy' and the shoeshine boy is asking about options.

advice.growth: The internet has abolished the business cycle. Valuations reflect a new economy; old metrics no longer apply.
advice.prudence: We hold lockup stock and telecom loans whose only collateral is spectrum. Hedge both, now.
advice.court: Regulators are asking about research conflicts. Separate analysts from bankers before they insist.
advice.conscience: Our analysts privately call these stocks junk while publicly rating them buys. That is fraud on investors.

deck.precedent: The NASDAQ peaked at 5,048 on 10 March 2000 and fell 78% by October 2002; the 2003 Global Research Analyst Settlement followed
deck.source: Shiller, Irrational Exuberance (2000)

deck.title: {court} defaults and freezes the banks
deck.text: Four presidents in a fortnight, deposits frozen, pots and pans banged in the streets. The peg is gone and the government stops paying on its bonds—the largest sovereign default yet recorded. There will be an exchange offer, in some years, at a fraction of par; holdouts will sue in New York for a decade.

rumour.text: The IMF's mission has left early and there are queues at the cash machines in the capital.

advice.growth: Buy the defaulted bonds at twenty cents. The exchange offer will pay thirty; the courts may pay par.
advice.prudence: Write it down to what the market pays today, not what a judge in New York might award a decade from now.
advice.court: The G7 will not finance another bailout. Expect no help from any official sector this time.
advice.conscience: Suing a bankrupt nation for par while its pensioners lose savings is lawful. Whether it is right is another question.

deck.precedent: Argentina defaulted on about $90bn in December 2001, settling at around 30 cents in 2005; Russia's GKO default of 17 August 1998 had the same shape
deck.source: Sturzenegger & Zettelmeyer, Debt Defaults and Lessons from a Decade of Crises (2006)

deck.title: The mainland opens across the border
deck.text: A special economic zone is declared across the river: factories, joint ventures and letters of credit for everything from toys to televisions. Exporters need trade finance, the colony's banks are the only door, and the volume of documentary credits passing through {city} doubles in a few years.

advice.growth: A billion customers and the cheapest factories on earth. Open branches before the Americans arrive.
advice.prudence: Joint-venture accounts are not audited to any standard we know. Lend against the letters of credit, not the balance sheets.
advice.court: Beijing rewards early friends. Be patient, polite and present at every trade fair in Canton.
advice.conscience: Know which factories we finance and how their workers are treated; one day the press will ask.

deck.precedent: The Shenzhen Special Economic Zone was established in August 1980; China acceded to the WTO on 11 December 2001
deck.source: Vogel, Deng Xiaoping and the Transformation of China (2011)

deck.title: A state developer of {court} wants a syndicated loan
deck.text: Ports, islands shaped like palm trees, a tower half a mile high. The state-owned holding company wants a large syndicated loan, unsecured, priced as if the ruler's guarantee were written down. It is not. Everyone says the emirate is good for it; the arrangers say the book is already oversubscribed.

advice.growth: Ruling families do not let flagship companies fail. Implied sovereign support at a corporate spread.
advice.prudence: Implied is not express. Read the documents: no guarantee, no security, and assets that are sand.
advice.court: Turning down the emirate's flagship would close the door to every future mandate in the Gulf.
advice.conscience: Ask who built the tower and on what terms. Financing a project is not neutral about how it is built.

deck.precedent: Dubai World and its property arm Nakheel borrowed heavily from international bank syndicates in 2005–08 without an express sovereign guarantee
deck.source: IMF, United Arab Emirates: 2009 Article IV Consultation, IMF Country Report No. 10/42 (2010)

deck.title: {court}'s flagship company asks for a standstill
deck.text: On the eve of a holiday the state holding company asks creditors to stand still on its debt for six months. The government says it never guaranteed anything. Then a richer neighbour lends ten billion, and the creditors are paid in full—eventually, after a rescheduling that stretches maturities by years.

rumour.text: Contractors on the islands haven't been paid since spring and the CDS on the emirate has doubled.

advice.growth: Sign the standstill fast. Banks that cooperate will be first in line for the next decade's mandates.
advice.prudence: Mark the loan to where it trades, then wait. Rescheduled at par is not the same as paid at par.
advice.court: The federal neighbour will not let the name fall. Quiet patience will be rewarded.
advice.conscience: Do not sell our stake to retail funds as 'temporarily delayed' when we privately expect losses.

deck.precedent: Dubai World requested a standstill on some $26bn on 25 November 2009; Abu Dhabi lent Dubai $10bn on 14 December 2009 and creditors were repaid in full over extended maturities
deck.source: IMF, United Arab Emirates: 2009 Article IV Consultation, IMF Country Report No. 10/42 (2010)

deck.title: A trophy bank is for sale in a bidding war
deck.text: An activist investor has put a large continental bank in play. A rival is bidding in shares; you could bid mostly in cash, with a consortium to break it up afterwards. Due diligence would be a few weeks of public documents and no data room. The Board likes the idea of becoming the largest in Europe.

choice.label: Win it, in cash, at the top of the market
choice.result: You are vast overnight, with a balance sheet you cannot see into and capital stretched thin.

choice.label: Bid only for the division you understand
choice.result: A modest, digestible acquisition; the press calls you timid.

choice.label: Walk away
