choice.result: The rival wins and grows; your shareholders grumble at the AGM.

advice.growth: Scale is the game. The winner will be among the top five banks in the world; the loser a target.
advice.prudence: No data room, cash consideration, at peak valuations, funded short. Every one of those is a red flag.
advice.court: The supervisor will ask how our core capital looks after paying cash. Have a good answer ready.
advice.conscience: Ambition is not a strategy. A Board that cannot say why it wants this should not buy it.

deck.precedent: The RBS-led consortium won ABN AMRO in October 2007 for some €71bn, largely in cash; RBS required state rescue in October 2008
deck.source: FSA, The Failure of the Royal Bank of Scotland (2011)

deck.title: A corporate treasurer wants to 'cut his funding cost'
deck.text: A consumer-goods company's treasurer wants to beat his budget. Your structurers have a swap that pays him a lower rate if rates stay put—and a leveraged spread that ruins him if they rise. He cannot price it himself and will rely on your marks. The margin hidden in it would fund the desk's bonuses.

choice.label: Sell him the leveraged swap
choice.result: A fat day-one profit; if rates rise, a lawsuit, taped calls and a regulator's order.

choice.label: Offer a plain vanilla hedge instead
choice.result: A modest fee and a client who stays a client.

choice.label: Decline and tell him why
choice.result: He takes the trade to a competitor who will sell it to him.

advice.growth: He is a sophisticated counterparty dealing at arm's length. Caveat emptor; it is his budget, not ours.
advice.prudence: If he loses big, he sues and we hold an uncollateralised receivable from a hostile client.
advice.court: Regulators are starting to treat 'reliance on our marks' as an advisory duty. Do not create one.
advice.conscience: If our desk would be embarrassed hearing its own telephone tapes read in court, the trade is wrong.

deck.precedent: Procter & Gamble and Gibson Greetings lost heavily on Bankers Trust leveraged swaps in 1994; taped calls led to an SEC/CFTC settlement in December 1994
deck.source: SEC, In the Matter of BT Securities Corporation, Release No. 33-7124 (22 December 1994)

deck.title: The derivatives desk wants the fixing nudged
deck.text: Every morning a junior in treasury submits the rate at which the house thinks it could borrow. The swaps desk, sitting near enough to shout, would like it a basis point lower on certain days. In a panic, a high submission tells the world you are in trouble. No statute governs the fixing.

choice.label: Let the desks lean on the submitters
choice.result: Steady trading profits for years, then fines, prosecutions and a chief executive's resignation.

choice.label: Wall off the submitters and submit honestly
choice.result: Your high honest fixes in a panic are read as weakness by the press.

choice.label: Submit low only during the panic
choice.result: You avoid looking weak in the crisis, and later find your excuse in the regulator's final notice.

advice.growth: Everyone does it, and a basis point on a trillion notional is real money. Keep up.
advice.prudence: Write down who may speak to submitters, and keep the e-mails. Chat logs last forever.
advice.court: The central bank wants rates low in a crisis. A word from Threadneedle Street means no one will mind.
advice.conscience: The fixing settles mortgages and swaps worldwide. Moving it for profit is market manipulation.

deck.precedent: Barclays was fined £290m by UK and US authorities on 27 June 2012 for LIBOR misconduct, including lowballing in 2007–08; UBS was fined $1.5bn in December 2012
deck.source: FSA, Final Notice to Barclays Bank plc (27 June 2012)

deck.title: A sanctioned client wants dollar clearing in {city}
deck.text: A long-standing commodity client sells crude from a country under American sanctions. Your branch could clear the dollars through New York if the payment messages omitted the client's name—'stripping', as the operations manual quietly calls it. Elsewhere it is lawful; in New York it is a felony.

choice.label: Clear it with the messages stripped
choice.result: Good fees for years, then a guilty plea, a multi-billion-dollar penalty and a ban on dollar clearing.

choice.label: Exit the client
choice.result: Revenue and a relationship lost; a clean file when the investigators come.

choice.label: Clear transparently only under a licence
choice.result: Slow, expensive and mostly refused; the client takes most of its business elsewhere.

advice.growth: These sanctions are American, not ours. Our branch is not in America, and the client is not ours to judge.
advice.prudence: Every dollar payment touches New York. If America can reach it, America can fine us for it.
advice.court: Our own regulator will not protect us from the Department of Justice. Assume extraterritorial reach.
advice.conscience: Altering payment messages to deceive a correspondent is dishonest whatever jurisdiction one stands in.

deck.precedent: BNP Paribas pleaded guilty on 30 June 2014 to processing dollar payments for sanctioned countries and paid about $8.9bn
deck.source: US Department of Justice, press release 'BNP Paribas Agrees to Plead Guilty' (30 June 2014)

deck.title: The regulator orders redress for mis-sold insurance
deck.text: For years branch staff sold payment protection insurance with every loan, on commission, often to borrowers who could never claim. The industry challenged the regulator in judicial review and lost. Now every sale must be reviewed, and the claims-management firms are cold-calling your customers.

rumour.text: The ombudsman's complaint numbers have trebled and a consumer magazine is running a campaign.

advice.growth: Fight every claim. Most customers knew what they were buying and the commission was disclosed.
advice.prudence: Provision generously and early. Every half-year we under-reserve, the market punishes us twice.
advice.court: The regulator wants visible contrition. Pay fast, apologise, and the enforcement team will be gentler.
advice.conscience: We paid staff to sell cover to people who could not claim on it. Repaying them is not generosity.

deck.precedent: The British Bankers' Association lost its judicial review of PPI rules in April 2011; UK banks paid some £38bn in PPI redress before the August 2019 deadline
deck.source: R (British Bankers Association) v Financial Services Authority [2011] EWHC 999 (Admin)

deck.title: A systems upgrade leaves customers locked out
deck.text: A software update to the overnight batch fails; nobody can roll it back. For days salaries are not credited, mortgages not paid, and customers see other people's accounts on their phones. Parliament calls the chief executive; the regulator calls the auditors.

advice.growth: Waive fees, offer compensation and move on; customers forget faster than the papers.
advice.prudence: We outsourced the batch to a firm that outsourced it again. Know who touches the ledger.
advice.court: Operational resilience is now a supervisory priority. Expect a skilled person's review.
advice.conscience: Tell customers the truth about what went wrong and how long it will take. Do not over-promise.

deck.precedent: A failed batch-software update locked RBS and NatWest customers out in June 2012 (fined £56m in 2014); TSB's migration failed in April 2018
deck.source: Slaughter and May, Independent Review of the TSB IT Migration (2019)

deck.title: A phone-app bank takes your young customers
deck.text: A new bank with a banking licence, a coral-coloured card and no branches signs up a million customers in a year. Open banking rules let it read your customers' accounts, with their consent. It pays them nothing much, but it sends a notification every time they spend.

advice.growth: Buy one. A licence and a million users are cheaper than building the app ourselves.
advice.prudence: These banks lose money on every account and will never be granted a full licence. Ignore them.
advice.court: Competition is the regulator's priority. Do not be seen to obstruct open banking data access.
advice.conscience: Our overdraft charges are why customers leave. Fix those before blaming the app.

deck.precedent: The CMA's retail banking market investigation (final report August 2016) and its Retail Banking Market Investigation Order 2017 mandated open banking from January 2018; Monzo obtained a full banking licence in April 2017
deck.source: Competition and Markets Authority, Retail Banking Market Investigation: Final Report (2016)

deck.title: A pandemic closes the world
deck.text: Cities lock down. In March the markets seize—even government bonds cannot be sold—and the central banks buy almost everything. Governments guarantee loans to firms through the banks. The stress test the house has run for years against a deep recession turns out to have been worth running.

advice.growth: Volatility is volume. Trading revenues will be the best in a decade once the dust settles.
advice.prudence: Draw on nothing, hoard liquidity, and assume the credit losses arrive late.
advice.court: The supervisor will ask us to cancel dividends and lend under the state schemes. Volunteer both.
advice.conscience: State-guaranteed lending invites fraud. Check borrowers properly even when Whitehall says speed matters.

deck.precedent: COVID-19: the 'dash for cash' of March 2020 disrupted even US Treasury and gilt markets, met by central bank asset purchases
deck.source: BIS, Annual Economic Report 2020

deck.title: A trading bonanza after the panic
deck.text: Competitors have pulled out, spreads are wide, and the central bank's purchases lift everything you own. The fixed-income desks have their best year on record. Shareholders ask why bonuses are rising; politicians ask louder.

advice.growth: Pay the traders well; they will be poached otherwise, and next year can be bigger still.
advice.prudence: Bank the profit as capital. Windfalls from a rate rally reverse when rates normalise.
advice.court: Public opinion is volatile. A restrained bonus round now saves a bank levy later.
advice.conscience: Profits earned on public money should not be distributed as if they were earned by genius.

deck.precedent: Wall Street's record trading revenues in 2009, after the 2008 crisis and the Fed's asset purchases; repeated in 2020
deck.source: Goldman Sachs, Annual Report 2009

deck.title: A rival's depositors walk in
deck.text: A smaller lender has queues on the evening news and its savers want somewhere that looks too big to fail. They arrive at your branches with building-society passbooks and cheques for the deposit-insurance limit and a bit over. Your staff open accounts until midnight.

advice.growth: Take them all and cross-sell mortgages. This is a decade's marketing in a week.
advice.prudence: Deposits that arrive in a panic leave in a panic. Keep them in gilts until they settle.
advice.court: Don't be seen gloating or advertising against a failing rival—the authorities hate it.
advice.conscience: Be honest about deposit insurance limits; do not let customers believe we are a sovereign.

deck.precedent: The run on Northern Rock from 14 September 2007 sent retail deposits to the largest banks
deck.source: House of Commons Treasury Committee, The Run on the Rock (2008)

deck.title: The rebels are said to be on the North Road
deck.text: An army is marching south, or the French have landed. Either way, every depositor in town wants coin today. The great Bank pays out in sixpences, counted slowly, to buy a week. The country banks have no sixpences to spare.

rumour.text: Dragoons riding hard through Derby, they say, and the Highlanders not far behind.

advice.growth: Rebels never reach London. Lend on, and let the hoarders lose their interest while they sit on coin.
advice.prudence: Fetch coin from our correspondents tonight and pay every note promptly. Slow paying is how a run starts.
advice.court: Stand firm beside the great Bank. The Ministry will remember which houses kept their doors open.
advice.conscience: The depositors' coin is theirs, not ours. Give it back without tricks or excuses.

deck.precedent: Run on the Bank of England as the Jacobites reached Derby, paid in sixpences, Dec 1745; country bank stoppages and £5m Exchequer bills lent to merchants on the outbreak of war with France, 1793
deck.source: Clapham, The Bank of England: A History (1944)

deck.title: The ground opens under {city}
deck.text: All Saints' morning: the churches are full of candles when the earth heaves. The fire follows, and then the river comes up over the quays. The English Factory's warehouses are gone, and so are the ledgers that said who owed what to whom.

advice.growth: Lisbon will be rebuilt in stone and on English credit. Lend to the rebuilders before the Dutch do.
advice.prudence: Write down every Lisbon debt today. The ledgers that proved them are ash, and so are half the debtors.
advice.court: Parliament will vote relief. Stand with the English Factory and be seen to stand with it.
advice.conscience: Preachers call it judgment on a sinful trade. Whatever it is, call in no widow's debt this winter.

deck.precedent: The Lisbon earthquake, fire and tsunami, 1 November 1755
deck.source: Kendrick, The Lisbon Earthquake (1956)

deck.title: Protested acceptances on the {city} Exchange
deck.text: A great house accepted bills for half the Exchange, against grain bought for the armies at war prices. Peace has halved the price of grain. The house cannot meet its acceptances, and they are coming back protested to every drawer from Hamburg to Berlin.

rumour.text: A certain house on the Dam has asked its friends to renew rather than pay.

advice.growth: Acceptance is the cleanest business on the Exchange: a signature, a fee, and no coin leaves the till.
advice.prudence: Find out whose names stand behind our acceptances. If two of them are the same grain contractor, cut one.
advice.court: Keep the burgomasters sweet. They decide which houses get help and which are left to fall.
advice.conscience: Accepting a bill is giving our word. We honour ours, even at a loss.

deck.precedent: Failure of De Neufville Brothers and the Amsterdam acceptance crisis, July–Aug 1763; the Hamburg crisis of autumn 1799
deck.source: Schnabel & Shin, 'Liquidity and Contagion: The Crisis of 1763', JEEA (2004)

deck.title: Famine in the Company's province
deck.text: Last year the rains failed, and this year the rice failed too. In the districts the Company now governs, a third of the cultivators are dead or fled, yet the collectors squeeze the land revenue out of the survivors all the same. Somehow the Company's servants are still sending home fortunes.

advice.growth: The revenue will come back with the rains. Buy Company stock while it is cheap.
advice.prudence: Revenue squeezed from a dying province cannot last. Cut our Calcutta drafts to what we hold in hand.
advice.court: Parliament will inquire into the Company. Better to be its creditor than its partner when that happens.
advice.conscience: Men are dying while the Company's servants corner rice. We touch none of that trade.

deck.precedent: The Bengal famine of 1769–70: revenue was wrung from the survivors regardless, but the Company's finances buckled into the crisis of 1772
deck.source: Marshall, Bengal: The British Bridgehead, 1740–1828 (1987)

deck.title: {court} cannot meet its bills
deck.text: Its revenue has fallen short and its paper is sliding. A speculator who bet on it has fled abroad, owing half of Lombard Street. {court} asks the house for a bridging loan until the next fleet, or the next tax, comes in, and it promises that Parliament will see it right.

advice.growth: Seven per cent from a borrower that Parliament dare not let fail is the best paper on offer.
advice.prudence: If it cannot pay its bills now, it cannot pay ours later. Lend only against goods in a warehouse.
advice.court: Whoever lends the bridge gets a seat at the table when Parliament takes it in hand.
advice.conscience: Lend if you will, but not so that it can pay dividends it has not earned.

deck.precedent: Alexander Fordyce flees, June 1772; the cash-starved East India Company seeks emergency loans from the Bank of England that summer; the Loan Act of 1773 lends it £1.4m
deck.source: Bowen, Revenue and Reform: The Indian Problem in British Politics 1757–1773 (1991)

deck.title: The gentlemen's bank stops payment
deck.text: A new bank of landed gentlemen lent before its partners had paid in their capital. It kept its London drafts afloat by drawing and redrawing on the same few names. Its notes are half the paper in the country, and this morning its doors stayed shut.

rumour.text: Their London agent is said to have refused a draft on Saturday.

advice.growth: Their notes are dead, and every farmer still needs paper. Ours can fill the country.
advice.prudence: Our London drafts pass through the same correspondents as theirs. Find out which ones, today.
advice.court: The public banks will sit on their hands. We had better look after ourselves.
advice.conscience: Their partners are liable to their last acre. Press for the small noteholders to be paid before the lawyers.

deck.precedent: Douglas, Heron & Co. (the Ayr Bank) stops, June 1772, a fortnight after the failure of Neal, James, Fordyce & Downe broke its London drafting and redrafting chain
deck.source: Kosmetatos, The 1772–73 British Credit Crisis (2018)

deck.title: The homeward fleet is taken at sea
deck.text: It is war at sea, and the enemy's frigates are waiting off the Cape. The Company's homeward fleet has been taken and its pepper and cloth sold as prize. In {city} the Company is borrowing on next year's ships to pay this year's dividend.

advice.growth: Prize goods sell cheap in London. Buy the pepper at the auction and sell it to Amsterdam after the peace.
advice.prudence: A company that pays dividends with borrowed money is already broke. Sell its paper.
advice.court: Our cargoes sail under a neutral flag, and the Navy respects neutrals. We have nothing to fear.
advice.conscience: Profit on prizes is lawful in war. Trading in a ruined company's secrets is not.

deck.precedent: The Fourth Anglo-Dutch War: the Royal Navy takes VOC shipping and the Company never recovers, 1780–84
deck.source: Gaastra, The Dutch East India Company: Expansion and Decline (2003)

deck.title: {court} will pay in its own new paper
deck.text: {court} has taken over its old debts, or consolidated them, which comes to the same thing. Creditors will be paid in new state paper. It is at par on its face, at a heavy discount in the street, and late.

rumour.text: The deputies are debating a 'reorganisation' of the public debt, behind closed doors.

advice.growth: State paper bought at a discount rises when peace comes. Hold it, and buy more.
advice.prudence: Sell the paper for coin now and book the loss. The discount will only get deeper.
advice.court: Accept it with good grace. The creditor who complains is the one paid last.
advice.conscience: A debtor who pays in paper worth less than its face has defaulted, whatever the decree calls it.

deck.precedent: VOC nationalised 1796 and wound up 31 Dec 1799, its debts passing to the Batavian Republic; the French 'tiers consolidé' writes off two-thirds of the rentes, Sept 1797
deck.source: Gaastra, The Dutch East India Company (2003); Sargent & Velde, 'Macroeconomic Features of the French Revolution', JPE (1995)

deck.title: {court} wants cash now and bonds later
deck.text: {court} needs money at once and will pay for it in bonds. The house is asked to take the whole issue at a fixed price, carry it, and sell it on to the public in London and Amsterdam before the market turns. The commission is handsome. The risk in between is all ours.

advice.growth: Take the whole issue. The commission and the turn on resale will make our year.
advice.prudence: Take a share and pass the rest to Amsterdam. Never carry a whole loan through a war.
advice.court: Lending to a government at war with ours needs a nod from the Ministry first.
advice.conscience: Bonds sold to widows at a premium must be good bonds. Read the security yourself.

deck.precedent: Barings and Hope take the US stock that paid for Louisiana, 1803; the French indemnity loans contracted by Barings and Hope, 1817–18
deck.source: Ziegler, The Sixth Great Power: Barings 1762–1929 (1988)

deck.title: {court} wants a million at eighty-five
deck.text: {court} proposes six per cent bonds, issued at eighty-five, with two years' dividends kept back out of the proceeds. The prospectus has a map, a mint and a cathedral. The coffee-houses are full of new republics, and every one of them wants London's money.

advice.growth: Two years' coupons held back means the bonds pay themselves until the mines come in. Safe as Consols.
advice.prudence: Interest paid out of the loan proves nothing. Nobody knows whether they can pay in the third year.
advice.court: The Foreign Office favours these republics, and our merchants want their markets.
advice.conscience: Read what the prospectus says about the mines, and ask whether anyone has visited the country.

deck.precedent: Barings' £1m 6% loan for the province of Buenos Aires, issued at 85, 1824, at the height of the Latin American loan boom (Poyais included), 1822–25
deck.source: Dawson, The First Latin American Debt Crisis (1990)

deck.title: The mining shares break
deck.text: For a year every subscription list in the coffee-houses has filled within the hour: Andean silver, pearl fisheries, a steam company to drain a lake. Now the calls are due, the ships bring no silver, and the country banks that lent on the scrip are sending to London for gold.

rumour.text: A West Country bank is said to have sent a chaise to London for sovereigns, twice this week.

advice.growth: The calls are a passing squeeze. The Andes are full of silver, and steam will bring it up.
advice.prudence: Stop lending on scrip and send to London for gold before the country banks take it all.
advice.court: The great Bank will lend freely this time. The Ministry has told it to.
advice.conscience: Many of these companies were formed to be sold, not to dig. We sold some of them.

deck.precedent: The panic of December 1825 after the Latin American mining boom; some seventy banks stop
deck.source: Neal, 'The Financial Crisis of 1825 and the Restructuring of the British Financial System', Fed. Reserve Bank of St Louis Review (1998)

deck.title: {court} suspends its dividends
deck.text: There is war with a neighbour, a blockade of the river, and the customs house that was meant to pay the dividends is empty. {court} suspends payment on its foreign bonds. It sends the bondholders' committee a polite letter promising better days.

rumour.text: The half-year's remittance has not come on the packet, and the agents say nothing.

advice.growth: Buy the defaulted bonds at thirty. One day they will settle at sixty.
advice.prudence: Write them down by half now, and stop counting the coupons as income.
advice.court: The Foreign Office will not send gunboats for bondholders. Do not wait for them.
advice.conscience: We sold these bonds to customers. We owe them the truth about the price.

deck.precedent: Buenos Aires suspends dividends during the war with Brazil, 1827; nearly every Latin American loan of 1822–25 is in default by 1828
deck.source: Marichal, A Century of Debt Crises in Latin America (1989)

deck.title: The agency houses of {city} stop
deck.text: The great agency houses took the savings of Company officers at eight and ten per cent and lent them to indigo planters up-country. Indigo has fallen by half. One house has stopped, and its depositors are running on all the rest.

advice.growth: Indigo always comes back. Lend to the planters now, at the bottom.
advice.prudence: Our Calcutta deposits are lent long to the same planters. Shorten them.
advice.court: The Company will never let the agency houses fall. Its own servants' savings are in them.
advice.conscience: These houses took widows' savings at ten per cent. We will not buy their remains at a discount.

deck.precedent: Palmer & Co. stops in 1830; Alexander & Co., Mackintosh & Co. and the other Calcutta agency houses follow by 1834
deck.source: Webster, The Twilight of the East India Company (2009)

deck.title: The factories at {city} are shut
deck.text: An imperial commissioner has seized the foreigners' chests of a forbidden drug, and the warships are on their way. The factories on the river are shut. The hong merchants will not settle what they owe, and the tea season is lost.

advice.growth: When this war ends, five ports will open instead of one. Lend now for the trade that comes after.
advice.prudence: Every bill on Canton is now a bill on a closed port. Mark them down.
advice.court: The Ministry backs the merchants, and the fleet is ours.
advice.conscience: The goods seized are a drug the Emperor forbids. Do not plead for that trade.

deck.precedent: Opium destroyed at Humen, June 1839; the Opium War stops the Canton trade until the Treaty of Nanking, 1842
deck.source: Lovell, The Opium War (2011)

deck.title: Railway calls drain the money market
deck.text: Parliament has passed railway bills by the hundred, and every scrip-holder must now pay his calls. Money that sat at call with the bill-brokers is going into embankments. A poor harvest has left the corn merchants holding bills on grain that is falling.

rumour.text: The brokers say Lombard Street will not take corn bills at any rate this week.

advice.growth: The lines will carry the kingdom. Lend to the brokers on railway scrip, and calls be damned.
advice.prudence: Call money is going into embankments. Keep our reserve in Exchequer bills, not scrip.
advice.court: If the Bank runs dry, the Treasury will write a letter. Do not count on it coming early.
advice.conscience: Directors who pay dividends out of capital deserve no credit from us.

deck.precedent: The railway mania of 1845–47 breaks; the corn-bill failures and the first suspension of the Bank Charter Act, 25 Oct 1847
deck.source: Lewin, The Railway Mania and its Aftermath, 1845–1852 (1936)

deck.title: Fire in the warehouses of {city}
deck.text: Fire broke out in a warehouse in the night, and the wind did the rest. Whole streets of merchants' stores and counting-houses are ash. The insurers cannot pay it all, and neither can the merchants who owed you.

advice.growth: Rebuilding needs credit. Open a book with the builders.
advice.prudence: Find out which insurers can still pay before we count on any of their policies.
advice.court: The city fathers will borrow to rebuild. Offer to take their bonds.
advice.conscience: Pay the clerks who lost their homes their wages in advance.

deck.precedent: The Great Fire of New York bankrupts most of the city's fire insurers, Dec 1835; the Great Fire of Hamburg, May 1842
deck.source: Burrows & Wallace, Gotham: A History of New York City to 1898 (1999)

deck.title: A wet summer and a dear loaf
deck.text: The wheat is thin and blighted and bread is dear. Gold is going to the Baltic to pay for foreign corn. The farmers' bills are coming back to the country banks, and there is a crowd in the market-place.

advice.growth: Dear corn makes rich corn-factors. Discount their bills while prices are high and the bills are good.
advice.prudence: Bullion is leaving for the Baltic. Keep coin in the till for when the farmers come for theirs.
advice.court: Parliament will pay bounties on imported corn. Finance the importers.
advice.conscience: Lend nothing to the forestallers who hoard grain while the poor riot.

deck.precedent: The harvest failures of 1795 and 1799–1800, with grain imports draining bullion before and during the Restriction
deck.source: Wells, Wretched Faces: Famine in Wartime England 1793–1801 (1988)

deck.title: A partner has been forging powers of attorney
deck.text: To cover his losses on building speculations, one of the partners forged customers' powers of attorney and sold their Consols. The forgeries ran for nine years. The customers want their stock back, and the hangman wants the partner.

advice.growth: Keep it quiet and restore the stock from our own capital. The clients need never know.
advice.prudence: Go through every power of attorney he signed, and make good each sale he made.
advice.court: The great Bank prosecutes every forgery. There will be a trial, and it will be public.
advice.conscience: The clients have been robbed. Pay them first, and ask mercy for him afterwards.

deck.precedent: Henry Fauntleroy of Marsh, Sibbald & Co. hanged for forging powers of attorney to sell clients' stock, Nov 1824
deck.source: Bleackley (ed.), Trial of Henry Fauntleroy and Other Famous Trials for Forgery (Notable British Trials, 1924)

deck.title: Our agent in {city} trades on his own account
deck.text: Our agent has been trading on his own account with the house's credit: salt, opium, piece-goods. He has also lent to the local governor in his own name. The profits are his. The bad debts, it now appears, are ours, and his letters take eight months to answer.

advice.growth: His private trade made money. Take it into the house and make him a partner.
advice.prudence: Recall him by the next ship, and send a man who reports every month.
advice.court: The governor he lent to is a useful friend. Do not embarrass him.
advice.conscience: A servant trading on his master's credit is a thief who has not yet lost.

deck.precedent: Private trade by East India Company servants in Bengal; William Bolts deported for it, 1768
deck.source: Marshall, East Indian Fortunes: The British in Bengal in the Eighteenth Century (1976)

deck.title: Eight per cent, if we call three of it commission
deck.text: Money is tight, and a good name will pay eight per cent for three months. The law allows five. His broker proposes the usual arrangement: five per cent interest, a commission for 'trouble', and a little play in the rate of exchange.

choice.label: Take the commission
choice.result: The bill is discounted at eight in all but name, and an attorney's clerk takes a note of the terms.

choice.label: Lend at five and no more
choice.result: He takes the money gratefully and tells the Exchange the house is straight.

choice.label: Decline the business
choice.result: He goes to a less careful house, and so do two of his friends.

advice.growth: Every house charges commission. Five per cent is a law for country squires, not merchants.
advice.prudence: If he offers eight, he cannot borrow at five anywhere else. Ask why.
advice.court: Judges see through a commission, and a common informer can sue us for treble the sum.
advice.conscience: The law says five. Usury does not stop being usury because we call it commission.

deck.precedent: Evasion of the 5% usury ceiling of 1714 by commissions and exchange devices, until bills of under three months were exempted by the Bank Charter Act of 1833
deck.source: Homer & Sylla, A History of Interest Rates (4th ed., 2005)

deck.title: A great foreign house moves to London
deck.text: The armies of a revolution are on the frontier. The greatest house of a neighbouring city has packed up its partners, its plate and its pictures and left for London. Its correspondents need a new house to accept their bills, and some of them have chosen yours.

advice.growth: Take every client they bring, and the clerks who came with them.
advice.prudence: Their clients come with their bad debts. Take the correspondents, but check every acceptance.
advice.court: Their friends at the exiled court may be useful later. Be polite.
advice.conscience: They are refugees. Do not use their misfortune to blacken their name.

deck.precedent: The Hopes leave Amsterdam for London ahead of the French, 1794–95, working closely with Barings, which gains much of their London business
deck.source: Buist, At Spes Non Fracta: Hope & Co. 1770–1815 (1974)

deck.title: A convention pays the debts the war forgot
deck.text: A war ago, the house's correspondents across the ocean owed it money that the peace forgot. Now two governments have signed a convention. One of them pays a lump sum, a commission divides it among the creditors, and a debt long written off comes back to life.

advice.growth: Spend it on a branch in New York while the Americans are friendly.
advice.prudence: Put it in the reserve. It is money we had already lost once.
advice.court: The Ministry made this treaty. Thank them, in writing.
advice.conscience: Some of the debtors were ruined by the war. Do not pursue them for the balance.

deck.precedent: Anglo-American convention of Jan 1802: the United States pays £600,000 to settle pre-Revolutionary debts owed to British creditors
deck.source: Perkins, The First Rapprochement: England and the United States 1795–1805 (1955)

deck.title: Decrees, Orders and an embargo
deck.text: One emperor declares the islands of his enemy blockaded and forbids his allies their goods. The enemy's navy answers by stopping every neutral that has not called first at its own ports. The neutral republic keeps its ships at home. Coffee rots on the quays at {city}.

rumour.text: The packet from the Elbe says French douaniers are searching every warehouse.

advice.growth: Running goods through Heligoland pays thirty per cent. Lend to the smugglers.
advice.prudence: A neutral cargo is now any navy's prize. Stop accepting bills against them.
advice.court: The Orders in Council are law. Finance only licensed trade.
advice.conscience: Licences are sold and forged every day. Do not lend on paper we know is false.

deck.precedent: The Berlin Decree, Nov 1806; the British Orders in Council, 1807; the US Embargo Act, Dec 1807
deck.source: Crouzet, L'économie britannique et le blocus continental (1958)

deck.title: The American houses are refused at the Bank
deck.text: Three London houses have accepted bills for half the cotton and dry-goods trade of the American seaboard, on the strength of American banks' paper. The great Bank now refuses to discount their bills. Cotton has broken, and the American banks have stopped paying in specie.

rumour.text: The Bank's Court met late, and the American houses' bills were not taken on Thursday.

advice.growth: American banks are chartered by the states and backed by land. Their paper is as good as ours.
advice.prudence: Our acceptances for American houses are twice our capital. Cut them now.
advice.court: When the great Bank stops discounting a name, it is warning everyone. Heed it.
advice.conscience: We pressed this credit on them. Give the honest ones time to pay.

deck.precedent: Failure of the 'three Ws' (Wildes, Wiggin, Wilson) in Anglo-American acceptance credit, 1836–37, and the US suspension of specie payments, May 1837
deck.source: Hidy, The House of Baring in American Trade and Finance (1949)

deck.title: Pestilence in {city}
deck.text: A ship from the Levant brought it past the lazaretto, or a coal brig brought the new blue sickness. In {city} the market is closed by a cordon and the rich have left. The debtors who stayed are in the burial lists.

advice.growth: The merchants who flee leave the trade to those who stay.
advice.prudence: Move the coin and the ledgers out, and make no new loans there until the cordon lifts.
advice.court: The magistrates will quarantine the port. Obey the cordon to the letter.
advice.conscience: Pay double to the clerks who stay, and pensions to their widows if they die.

deck.precedent: Plague of Marseille brought by the Grand Saint-Antoine, 1720–22; cholera reaches Sunderland in Oct 1831, and London and Paris in 1832
deck.source: Durey, The Return of the Plague: British Society and the Cholera 1831–2 (1979)

deck.title: The money of {city} is worth a tenth
deck.text: The treasury pays its armies in paper secured on confiscated land, or in coin with less silver in it every year. Prices double by the season. Debts payable in the local money are repaid, to the letter of the contract, in money worth a fraction of what was lent.

advice.growth: Buy confiscated land with their paper at a discount. That is where the bargains are.
advice.prudence: Write our contracts in sterling or in silver by weight, never in their money.
advice.court: Their minister has promised to redeem the paper at par. We can take him at his word.
advice.conscience: Repaying gold with paper is lawful there. Here it would be called theft.

deck.precedent: French assignats, 1790–96; the Austrian Finanzpatent cuts the Bancozettel to a fifth, 1811; Ottoman debasements under Mahmud II, 1808–39
deck.source: Sargent & Velde, JPE (1995); Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire (2000)

deck.title: Peace, cheap wheat and shut banks
deck.text: Two good harvests and the end of the war have halved the price of wheat. Farmers who borrowed at war prices to enclose and drain cannot pay their rents, and their landlords cannot pay the bank. Up and down the county, shutters are going up on banks that lent their own notes on land.

advice.growth: Land is cheap now. Lend to the buyers at the bottom.
advice.prudence: Our notes were lent on land. Collect what we can, and keep coin for the run.
advice.court: The landed interest sits in Parliament. It will raise the corn duties.
advice.conscience: Do not foreclose on tenants whose landlords have failed them.

deck.precedent: The post-war collapse of agricultural prices and the wave of English country bank failures, 1814–16
deck.source: Pressnell, Country Banking in the Industrial Revolution (1956)

deck.title: The Treasury needs gold beyond the blockade
deck.text: The Treasury has promised its allies millions in subsidy and must get coin to armies on the far side of a blockaded continent. The house is asked to remit it by bills on Hamburg and Frankfurt, buying gold quietly wherever it can, for a commission.

advice.growth: Take the commission and the bullion dealing that comes with it. Nobody else can move this much.
advice.prudence: Insure every shipment, and never let one convoy carry more than we can lose.
advice.court: Serve the Treasury well now, and the next loan will be ours.
advice.conscience: War money is honest money if the accounts are honest.

deck.precedent: Rothschild remittances for Wellington's army and the allied subsidies, arranged with the Commissary-in-Chief, 1814–15
deck.source: Ferguson, The World's Banker: The History of the House of Rothschild (1998)

deck.title: A treaty of commerce opens {city}
deck.text: Two old enemies have signed a treaty of commerce: lower duties on cloth and pottery one way, on wine and brandy the other. The merchants on the Exchange say the trade will double. The weavers who lose their market say they will starve.

advice.growth: Open a book with the wine merchants and the potters both.
advice.prudence: Treaties are torn up at the next war. Lend for one season at a time.
advice.court: The Ministry made this treaty. Finance it, and be seen to.
advice.conscience: The weavers will lose their work. Give to the parish relief.

deck.precedent: The Methuen Treaty with Portugal, 1703; the Eden Treaty with France, Sept 1786
deck.source: Browning, 'The Treaty of Commerce between England and France in 1786', TRHS (1885)

deck.title: The senior partner dies away from home
deck.text: The senior partner has died suddenly, abroad. His will is clear that his capital must stay in the house. His widow's advisers say a will cannot bind what she does with her share, and the younger partners are already quarrelling over his chair.

choice.label: Buy out the heirs
choice.result: The heirs leave rich. The house is smaller, but it is wholly ours.

choice.label: Keep the heirs in as sleeping partners
choice.result: The capital stays, and so do the heirs' opinions on how it should be lent.

advice.growth: Keep his capital in at any cost. The house is its capital.
advice.prudence: Heirs who do not understand the business ask for their money at the worst moment.
advice.court: His connections at Court die with him unless his sons keep them up.
advice.conscience: Honour his will, and his widow's needs as well.

deck.precedent: Nathan Rothschild dies at Frankfurt, July 1836, his will binding his sons to the partnership
deck.source: Ferguson, The World's Banker (1998)

deck.title: {court} decrees a loan from the rich
deck.text: {court} has decreed a loan from the rich, assessed by a committee on what it believes you have, and payable within the month. The receipt is a certificate that may one day buy confiscated land.

rumour.text: The section committee has been asking the porters which houses keep coin.

advice.growth: Pay, and use the receipts to buy national land cheap.
advice.prudence: Move what we can abroad before the assessors come.
advice.court: Refusing now is treason. Pay with good grace.
advice.conscience: We are bound to obey lawful authority, even when it robs us.

deck.precedent: France's emprunt forcé on the rich, decreed May 1793, and the forced loan of Dec 1795
deck.source: Bosher, French Finances 1770–1795 (1970)

deck.title: A rival's clerk arrives with a bag of our notes
deck.text: A rival bank has been quietly collecting our notes for months. This morning its clerk stands at our counter with a bag of them and demands gold for the lot, and another bag is said to be on its way. Our notes carry the option clause: payment may be deferred six months, with interest.

choice.label: Pay every note in gold
choice.result: The till is scraped bare, but the town sees that our notes are as good as coin.

choice.label: Invoke the option clause
choice.result: The gold stays in the vault, and every tavern says our notes are not worth the paper.

choice.label: Raid them back
choice.result: Both banks spend the winter presenting each other's notes, and the merchants grow tired of both.

advice.growth: We hold as many of their notes as they hold of ours. Raid them back.
advice.prudence: Pay every note in gold today. The option clause is a confession of weakness.
advice.court: The public bank's governors are friends of the Ministry. Do not quarrel with them.
advice.conscience: The note promises payment on demand. The small print is not the promise.

deck.precedent: Note raids between the Edinburgh public banks and their rivals, and the Bank of Scotland's option clause, 1730–65; option clauses banned by Act of 1765
deck.source: Checkland, Scottish Banking: A History, 1695–1973 (1975)

deck.title: Preliminaries of peace, and the funds jump
deck.text: The preliminaries of peace are signed. The funds rise several points in a day, and the house's stock of government annuities is worth more than the partners paid for it. The bill-brokers are cheerful. The army contractors are not.

advice.growth: Sell the funds into the rally, and buy them back at the next war scare.
advice.prudence: Take the profit on half, and keep the rest as reserve.
advice.court: Peace means fewer Treasury loans. Look for new business.
advice.conscience: Rejoice that fewer men will die, not that our stock has risen.

deck.precedent: Consols rally on the preliminaries of the Peace of Amiens, Oct 1801
deck.source: Neal, The Rise of Financial Capitalism (1990)

deck.title: A Liverpool house asks us to accept its bills
deck.text: A Liverpool house asks us to accept bills drawn at long sight by its captains in the islands, against the sale of enslaved Africans there. The trade is legal, the drawer is sound, and the commission is the best in England. The abolitionists' petitions are in every parish this year.

choice.label: Accept the bills
choice.result: The commission comes in every season, and so do the pamphlets that name the houses behind the trade.

choice.label: Decline
choice.result: The West India interest finds another acceptor and remembers which house said no.

advice.growth: The paper is good, the trade is legal, and Liverpool pays the best commission in England.
advice.prudence: Long-sight bills on island sales depend on sugar, the war and the fever. Cap them.
advice.court: Parliament debates abolition every session. The Ministry may yet change sides.
advice.conscience: These are bills on the sale of men and women. No commission makes that clean.

deck.precedent: London and Liverpool houses accept and guarantee the long-dated remittance bills of the slave trade until the Abolition Act of 1807
deck.source: Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002)

deck.title: The heir of {court} owes a fortune
deck.text: The heir of {court} owes more than a quarter of a million to jewellers, builders and his own servants. His secretary proposes that the house take up the debts on his bond, payable when he comes to the throne or when Parliament takes pity on him.

choice.label: Take up the bond
choice.result: The heir is grateful, and the capital is locked up until Parliament feels generous.

choice.label: Lend a part against his jewels
choice.result: The diamonds go into our vault and he remembers the insult, though not for long.

choice.label: Refuse politely
choice.result: The secretary bows and goes to another house, and the heir does not forget.

advice.growth: The heir will be king, and a king's banker is never short of clients.
advice.prudence: Royal bonds are paid when Parliament pleases, which may be never.
advice.court: Refuse him now, and you refuse the next reign.
advice.conscience: Lend nothing for jewels and gaming while his tradesmen go unpaid.

deck.precedent: The Prince of Wales's debts, settled by Parliament in 1787 and again on his marriage in 1795
deck.source: Smith, George IV (Yale English Monarchs, 1999)

deck.title: A neighbour asks for a subscription
deck.text: A larger house, London agent to forty country banks, is losing deposits by the hour. Its partners ask us to join a subscription to see it through the week, and the great Bank will lend too, on good security. If it stops, its country banks will need a new London house by Monday.

choice.label: Subscribe
choice.result: Our money goes in. Whether it is enough is something the week will tell.

choice.label: Refuse and court its clients
choice.result: It stops on Saturday, and its correspondents come to us, eyeing us with suspicion.

advice.growth: Let it fail. Its forty country banks will need a new London agent, and that agent is us.
advice.prudence: If it falls, its correspondents run on us next. Better to stop the fire at its door.
advice.court: The great Bank is lending. Join it, and be seen to join it.
advice.conscience: We drank their port for twenty years. We owe them a hand.

deck.precedent: Pole, Thornton & Co., supported by the Bank of England, stops anyway and brings down its country correspondents, Dec 1825
deck.source: Clapham, The Bank of England: A History (1944)

deck.title: {court} floats a war loan in London and Paris
deck.text: Its armies are in the field and its revenues are already pledged to the tax-farmers. {court}'s envoy wants a gold loan issued at a deep discount, coupons payable in London, and a house of name to sign the prospectus. The subscription lists open next week, with or without you.

advice.growth: Seven per cent, issued at a discount, with a fat underwriting commission: the year's profit in one signature.
advice.prudence: War loans are serviced by the side that wins, and we do not yet know which side that is.
advice.court: Sign, and the envoy will remember us when the railway and tobacco concessions are handed out.
advice.conscience: We are lending for powder; at the least, make the prospectus state honestly which revenues are already pledged.

deck.precedent: The Ottoman Empire's first foreign loan, floated in London during the Crimean War, 1854; Russia's great post-war loan in Paris and London, 1906
deck.source: Clay, Gold for the Sultan (2000); Siegel, For Peace and Money (2014)

deck.title: {court} borrows against its customs house
deck.text: An indemnity is owed to a victorious neighbour, and the treasury cannot pay it. {court} offers a gold loan secured on its maritime customs, which are collected by foreign inspectors and paid into a foreign bank. The rival national syndicates are already quarrelling over the shares.

advice.growth: Five per cent on a pledge collected by our own countrymen is as near a certainty as the East offers.
advice.prudence: A pledge is only as good as whoever holds the customs house ten years from now.
advice.court: Our government wants this loan in friendly hands; refuse, and we hand it to a rival power's bank.
advice.conscience: We profit from a beaten people's tribute; price the loan fairly and do not puff it to small investors.

deck.precedent: Indemnity loans to China after the Sino-Japanese War, secured on the Maritime Customs, 1895–98 (Anglo-German loans of 1896 and 1898)
deck.source: King, The History of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, vol. 2 (1988)

deck.title: {court} wants its waterworks financed
deck.text: Land values double each season, immigrants arrive by the shipload, and every house in the City holds a slice of {court}'s paper. Now its capital wants drains and water mains, and a firm underwriting of the whole issue. The public's appetite has been bottomless. So far.

advice.growth: Eight per cent from a booming republic; the whole City is in, and we cannot be the house that missed it.
advice.prudence: Underwriting is a promise to buy whatever the public refuses. Ask what happens if they refuse.
advice.court: Their minister dines with ours every week; a refusal will be noticed on both sides.
advice.conscience: If we cannot place the issue we must not pretend we have; the market should know what we hold.

deck.precedent: Barings underwrote the Buenos Aires Water Supply and Drainage Company issue and could not place it, 1888–89
deck.source: Marichal, A Century of Debt Crises in Latin America (1989)

deck.title: A panic comes in by the mail steamer
deck.text: A western trust company has stopped, railroad paper is unsaleable, and the steamer brings word that the American banks have suspended specie payments. Glasgow and Hamburg houses that drew on New York are suddenly holding bills nobody will discount. Bank Rate goes to ten.

rumour.text: The New York packet is overdue and the American houses here have stopped discounting.

advice.growth: Good bills are going cheap; buy the paper of sound American houses at a fat discount.
advice.prudence: Fill the till, shorten the bill case, and accept nothing drawn on New York this month.
advice.court: The Government will suspend the Act if it must; stay close to Threadneedle Street this week.
advice.conscience: Our clerks must tell depositors plainly what we hold; rumour feeds on silence.

deck.precedent: The panic of 1857: Ohio Life failed in August, US banks suspended, the Western Bank of Scotland and Hamburg houses failed; Bank Charter Act suspended 12 November 1857
deck.source: Calomiris and Schweikart, 'The Panic of 1857: Origins, Transmission, and Containment', Journal of Economic History (1991)

deck.title: A trust company runs dry on Broadway
deck.text: New York's trust companies take deposits like banks, keep reserves like nobody, and sit outside the clearing house. One of them has lent on a failed copper corner, and by noon the queue runs round the block. There is no central bank: the city's great private bankers will decide who is saved.

rumour.text: They say the trust companies have been lending on copper shares at call.

advice.growth: Call money will touch a hundred per cent while others panic; there has never been a better day to lend.
advice.prudence: Our New York balances sit with trust companies; draw them home today and ask questions after.
advice.court: The senior private banker downtown will organise a pool; be seen to subscribe to it.
advice.conscience: Do not repeat the tale about that trust; our name should not be the match that lights it.

deck.precedent: The panic of 1907: the Knickerbocker Trust failed in October after the United Copper corner collapsed
deck.source: Bruner and Carr, The Panic of 1907 (2007)

deck.title: The sepoys rise in the presidencies
deck.text: A regiment refuses its cartridges, shoots its officers and marches on the old capital. Up-country agencies go silent, indigo and opium consignments are lost, and the Calcutta agency houses draw hard on London for specie. The rising will be put down; the season's trade will not recover.

rumour.text: Chapatis are passing from village to village, and nobody can say why.

advice.growth: When the rising is crushed, indigo land will go for nothing; keep the agency open and buy.
advice.prudence: Call in the up-country advances and hold nothing but bills on the Treasury.
advice.court: The Company will be blamed and the Crown will step in; lend to the Crown, not the Company.
advice.conscience: Our agents must not buy looted goods sold cheap at the coast, whatever the margin.

deck.precedent: The Indian Rebellion of 1857: Meerut on 10 May, Delhi taken, Cawnpore and Lucknow besieged
deck.source: Metcalf, The Aftermath of Revolt: India 1857–1870 (1964)

deck.title: {court} halves its coupons
deck.text: {court} has borrowed abroad for twenty years to pay the interest on what it borrowed before. A decree announces that half of each coupon will be paid in cash and half in new bonds of doubtful worth. Bondholders' committees convene in London and Paris; the ambassadors begin to talk of administering the revenues.

rumour.text: Their treasury is said to be meeting the coupon with a fresh advance from its own bankers.

advice.growth: Their customs and tobacco revenues are pledged; a government with pledged revenues does not default. Buy the dip.
advice.prudence: Sell into any rally; a borrower paying interest out of new loans has already failed.
advice.court: The Powers will impose a debt administration; get our man onto its council early.
advice.conscience: We sold these bonds to widows and parsons; we owe them a seat at the bondholders' committee.

deck.precedent: The Ottoman government halved its coupons, October 1875; Egypt suspended, April 1876; Ottoman Public Debt Administration, 1881
deck.source: Pamuk, The Ottoman Economy and Its Institutions (2009); Landes, Bankers and Pashas (1958)

deck.title: Revolution in {court}: the old debts are void
deck.text: The new government declares every loan of the old regime a contract between tyrants and usurers, annulled without compensation. Coupons go unpaid, the bonds become curiosities for collectors, and the bondholders' associations begin a wait that will outlast most of their members.

rumour.text: The capital is full of strikes, and the soldiers are said to be electing their own officers.

advice.growth: Bonds at sixty are cheap if the regime survives the winter; add to the position.
advice.prudence: No price is cheap for paper whose next master may not recognise it.
advice.court: The ambassador assures us the dynasty is secure and these disturbances are mere bread riots.
advice.conscience: We lent a despot money to shoot strikers; we may be about to learn what that costs.

deck.precedent: Soviet decree repudiating all Tsarist foreign debts, January/February 1918
deck.source: Oosterlinck, Hope Springs Eternal: French Bondholders and the Repudiation of Russian Sovereign Debt (2016)

deck.title: {court} suspends its foreign debt under invasion
deck.text: An invading army holds the treaty ports, and with them the customs revenues pledged to the foreign loans. {court}, fighting from the interior, announces that service on its external debt is suspended for the duration. The bonds trade at a fraction; the bondholders will still be negotiating long after the war.

rumour.text: The customs receipts at the coast are said to be lodged in an enemy bank now.

advice.growth: Defaulted bonds at fifteen are a lottery ticket on peace; buy a few.
advice.prudence: Write it down now; a pledge held in enemy hands is no pledge at all.
advice.court: The occupying power has promised to respect the customs pledge, and the Foreign Office believes it.
advice.conscience: Press our claim honestly, but do not lobby for gunboats to collect it.

deck.precedent: Nationalist China suspended service on its customs-secured foreign loans, January 1939, after Japan seized the coastal customs
deck.source: Goetzmann, Ukhov and Zhu, 'China and the World Financial Markets 1870–1939', Economic History Review (2007)

deck.title: {court} cannot meet its gold coupons
deck.text: The boom has turned. Paper money has collapsed against gold, the provincial banks have stopped paying on their cédulas, and {court} cannot remit gold for its next coupon. The paper nobody in London could get enough of last year is unsaleable at any price, and one great house is holding far too much of it.

rumour.text: The gold premium in their capital is said to be over a hundred and fifty.

advice.growth: A temporary embarrassment; the pampas still grow wheat, and at this price the bonds are a gift.
advice.prudence: One house holds millions of this paper; if it falls, its acceptances fall on us.
advice.court: The Governor has been very quiet this week, which is how he behaves when he is worried.
advice.conscience: If we sell our holding to clients today, we must tell them what we know.

deck.precedent: Argentina's default and the Baring crisis, 1890–91
deck.source: Ziegler, The Sixth Great Power: Barings 1762–1929 (1988)

deck.title: The Governor passes the hat
deck.text: A great house has accepted more of a foreign government's paper than it can carry, and the Governor has summoned the City to his parlour on a Saturday. He wants a guarantee fund to wind the house down in good order, every bank subscribing by its size, and he is writing down the names of those who decline.

choice.label: Subscribe generously, near the top of the list
choice.result: Your name stands beside the great joint-stock banks, and the calls on the guarantee may turn out to be real money.

choice.label: Subscribe the minimum your size demands
choice.result: You are on the list, and nobody remembers for how much.

choice.label: Decline and let the house fall
choice.result: You keep your money, the fund fills without you, and the parlour remembers.

advice.growth: Our money would back a rival's bad underwriting; subscribe the least that looks decent.
advice.prudence: If that house stops, its acceptances hit every bill case in London, ours included; subscribe.
advice.court: The Governor is keeping a list; be on the first page of it.
advice.conscience: The guarantee protects depositors who did nothing wrong; it is a fair use of our strength.

deck.precedent: The Bank of England's guarantee fund for Baring Brothers, November 1890
deck.source: Ziegler, The Sixth Great Power: Barings 1762–1929 (1988)

deck.title: A great Scottish bank stops: the books were false
deck.text: A bank with branches in every burgh has closed its doors. The investigators find bad debts carried as assets, gold reserves overstated and directors' friends lending to themselves. The bank is unlimited: every shareholder is liable to his last spoon, and the call letters are going out. Depositors everywhere are asking who else is unlimited.

rumour.text: The bank is said to have been buying its own shares to hold up the price.

advice.growth: Frightened Scottish depositors want somewhere safe; open an Edinburgh office and take them.
advice.prudence: Register as limited under the Act before our own shareholders take fright and sell.
advice.court: The Treasury will want audited accounts soon; volunteer ours before Parliament asks.
advice.conscience: Unlimited liability is the honest form of banking; a house that limits its liability limits its honour.

deck.precedent: Failure of the City of Glasgow Bank, October 1878; directors imprisoned, unlimited shareholders ruined; Companies Act 1879 introduces reserved liability
deck.source: Turner, Banking in Crisis: The Rise and Fall of British Banking Stability (2014)

deck.title: The land boom breaks in {city}
deck.text: Suburban allotments sold on instalments, building societies lending on paper valuations, and banks lending to the building societies. Now the buyers have vanished, the societies are suspending and the depositors are queueing. Banks that pledged to stand by one another discover how few of them meant it.

rumour.text: Land in the outer townships is changing hands for half last year's price.

advice.growth: Land in a young country never falls for long; the immigrants keep coming. Lend on.
advice.prudence: Stop every new advance on land and bring the London deposits home.
advice.court: The colonial government may proclaim bank holidays; be ready to reconstruct rather than fail.
advice.conscience: Do not freeze the small depositors' money while the directors' overdrafts run on.

deck.precedent: The Australian bank crash of April–May 1893 after the Melbourne land boom; thirteen trading banks suspended
deck.source: Merrett, 'The Australian bank crashes of the 1890s revisited', Business History Review (2013)

deck.title: Earthquake and fire level {city}
deck.text: At noon the ground moved, and by evening the wooden city was burning from end to end. Warehouses, their contents and the bills drawn against them are ashes together. The central bank will rediscount 'earthquake bills' to keep the merchants alive, and some of those bills will still be unpaid years from now.

advice.growth: Rebuilding needs credit; the first foreign bank to lend will own the reconstruction.
advice.prudence: Take no earthquake bills at face value; mark them down and expect years of renewals.
advice.court: The government will remember the banks that rediscounted freely; be counted among them.
advice.conscience: Forbear on the debts of the ruined; foreclosing on ashes buys nothing but hatred.

deck.precedent: The Great Kantō earthquake, 1 September 1923; the unpaid earthquake bills fed the Shōwa bank panic of 1927
deck.source: Tamaki, Japanese Banking: A History, 1859–1959 (1995)

deck.title: War again: the Treasury takes the deposits
deck.text: Exchange control is clamped on at once, foreign securities are requisitioned, and within the year the Treasury tells the banks what they will lend it. Each week a slice of your deposits goes into Treasury Deposit Receipts at a little over one per cent: unsaleable, and not to be refused.

advice.growth: Lending to the Treasury is dull, but it will be the only business for six years; take it cheerfully.
advice.prudence: No default risk, but we will be locked into one per cent if rates rise after the war.
advice.court: Volunteer before we are directed; the Treasury remembers who made it ask twice.
advice.conscience: The country is fighting for its life; this is no moment to haggle over an eighth.

deck.precedent: Second World War finance: exchange control from September 1939, Treasury Deposit Receipts from July 1940
deck.source: Sayers, Financial Policy 1939–45 (1956)

deck.title: A great railroad's bonds stop selling
deck.text: A transcontinental line has been building into the wilderness on the proceeds of bonds sold to clergymen and schoolteachers. The bond sales stall, the banking house behind them closes its doors, and the stock exchange in {city} shuts for days. Every railroad security in your strongroom is now priced by rumour.

rumour.text: Its banker has been carrying the construction on overdraft since the spring.

advice.growth: The bonds are secured on millions of acres of land grants, and land does not run away.
advice.prudence: Railroad bonds are only as good as traffic that does not yet exist; reduce them.
advice.court: Do not expect help from the government; it has only just finished paying for the last war.
advice.conscience: We sold these bonds as safe; our clients are owed a straight account of the line.

deck.precedent: Jay Cooke & Co. failed over Northern Pacific bonds, 18 September 1873, and the NYSE closed for ten days; Vienna had crashed that May
deck.source: Lubetkin, Jay Cooke's Gamble: The Northern Pacific Railroad, the Sioux, and the Panic of 1873 (2006)

deck.title: The cable to {city} has gone silent
deck.text: The submarine cable to {city} carried one garbled message yesterday and nothing today. Until it is grappled up and spliced, instructions go by steamer, prices are a fortnight old, and your agent there is once again his own master. Some agents enjoy that more than others.

advice.growth: Our rivals are equally blind; our agent's judgement is an advantage this week, not a risk.
advice.prudence: Write by every steamer: no new commitments above his limit until the cable speaks again.
advice.court: The Admiralty wants that cable mended too; offer to help finance the repair company.
advice.conscience: Trust him, but have his books brought home by the next mail.

deck.precedent: The first Atlantic cable failed after about three weeks, September 1858; no lasting link until 1866
deck.source: Gordon, A Thread Across the Ocean (2002)

deck.title: The cotton boom in {city} ends overnight
deck.text: While war cut off American cotton, the city sold the only bales in the world and spent the proceeds on reclamation companies, new banks and shares bought on time bargains. Now the steamer brings news of peace. Cotton halves, the share premiums vanish, and settlement day approaches with nobody able to pay.

rumour.text: The Liverpool letters say the Southern armies are finished.

advice.growth: Cotton is king and the American war has years to run; Back Bay shares will double again.
advice.prudence: Close every time bargain before settlement; we cannot know which counterparties will pay.
advice.court: The Presidency bank is lending on shares itself; do not expect it to save anyone.
advice.conscience: Brokers' clerks are wagering their wages on premiums; we should not be lending to them.

deck.precedent: The Bombay share mania collapsed at the end of the American Civil War, 1865; the Bank of Bombay failed in 1868
deck.source: Wacha, A Financial Chapter in the History of Bombay City (1910)

deck.title: A new goldfield sends bullion through {city}
deck.text: Prospectors have struck a reef that runs for miles, and the mining companies need everything: assays, advances on crushings, insurance on shipments, and a bank that will buy their gold and draw bills on London against it. The first consignments are already at the coast.

advice.growth: Buy the gold, finance the crushings, float the companies: this is the century's harvest.
advice.prudence: Finance shipments, not shafts; reefs peter out and promoters lie.
advice.court: The colonial government will want the gold kept within the Empire; be its banker for that.
advice.conscience: Mining shares are being sold to clerks on tips; do not lend our name to the promoters.

deck.precedent: Discovery of the Witwatersrand gold reef, 1886
deck.source: Kubicek, Economic Imperialism in Theory and Practice: The Case of South African Gold Mining Finance 1886–1914 (1979)

deck.title: {city} opens to foreign trade
deck.text: A treaty signed under the guns of a foreign squadron obliges the government to open a port, admit foreign merchants and permit the exchange of coin. Its ratio of gold to silver is wildly out of line with the rest of the world, and the first houses to arrive will make fortunes before the gap closes.

advice.growth: Open an agency at once; the bullion arbitrage alone will pay for the building.
advice.prudence: Trade with a closed island kingdom is a curiosity; it will never be worth a branch.
advice.court: Our minister there wants one of our banks on the Bund and will help with the licence.
advice.conscience: Draining their gold by arbitrage is lawful, but it ruins the country; do not boast of it.

deck.precedent: Yokohama opened to foreign trade under the treaties of 1858, July 1859; the gold–silver arbitrage drained Japanese gold
deck.source: Sugiyama, Japan's Industrialization in the World Economy 1859–1899 (1988)

deck.title: Forged bills discovered in {city}
deck.text: A charming foreign customer opened an account with letters of introduction, discounted some excellent first-class bills, and then discounted several thousand pounds more. On the due date the acceptors deny ever having seen them. The signatures and stamps were perfect; the customer has sailed.

advice.growth: One loss on a clever forgery is the price of new customers; do not stop discounting.
advice.prudence: No bill from a new name without a word from the acceptor's own banker.
advice.court: Let the police chase him across the Atlantic; a public prosecution shows we are not soft.
advice.conscience: Our clerk was deceived, not dishonest; do not sack him merely to look stern.

deck.precedent: The great Bank of England forgery: American fraudsters discounted forged bills at the Western branch, discovered March 1873
deck.source: Booth, The Thieves of Threadneedle Street (2015)

deck.title: The manager in {city} lent beyond his powers
deck.text: Head office believed the branch was financing exports against shipping documents. It was in fact lending to planters on the security of their estates, renewing the advances every season, and blight has now taken the crop. The inspector's report runs to forty pages; the overdrafts will not be repaid this decade.

rumour.text: Planters' paper from that coast is being renewed rather than paid.

advice.growth: Plantation lending pays twelve per cent, and the manager knows his district better than London does.
advice.prudence: Send an inspector by the next mail and take away his discretion over renewals.
advice.court: The governor relies on the planters; a hard line will cost us his goodwill.
advice.conscience: Whatever his reasons, the manager deceived us; he cannot stay.

deck.precedent: The Oriental Bank Corporation suspended in May 1884 after branch lending to Ceylon coffee planters ruined by leaf blight
deck.source: Baster, The Imperial Banks (1929)

deck.title: A copper corner collapses in {city}
deck.text: A metals syndicate has spent a year buying every ton of copper and contracting forward for the mines' output, financed by a great deposit bank. Now the mines are producing more than anyone can store, the price breaks, and the bank's director is found dead in his office. Its depositors are already at the counters.

rumour.text: The syndicate is said to be warehousing copper it cannot sell.

advice.growth: The syndicate needs fresh money to hold the price; we can name a ruinous rate.
advice.prudence: Call in every advance against metal warrants before the price is reported.
advice.court: The central bank will save the deposit bank and let the syndicate burn; position for that.
advice.conscience: Do not lend a dying syndicate money it can only lose for its other creditors.

deck.precedent: Collapse of the Société des Métaux copper corner and the Banque de France's rescue of the Comptoir d'Escompte, March 1889
deck.source: Hautcoeur, Riva and White, 'Floating a lifeboat: The Banque de France and the crisis of 1889', Journal of Monetary Economics (2014)

deck.title: A rival's collapse sends its clients to you
deck.text: A brash new bank that promised to beat the old houses at their own game has failed, after its own shares were pushed to absurd premiums with its own money. Its depositors, and the provincial notaries who advised them, now want somewhere dull. Your door is open and your name is old.

advice.growth: Take every account and lend it out; new deposits are the cheapest money we will ever see.
advice.prudence: Frightened money leaves as fast as it arrives; keep a good share of it in the till.
advice.court: The central bank lent to the brokers so the Bourse could settle; thank it publicly.
advice.conscience: No gloating in the newspapers; a rival's ruin includes thousands of small savers.

deck.precedent: The crash of the Union Générale, January 1882; deposits fled to the established Paris houses
deck.source: White, 'The Crash of 1882 and the Bailout of the Paris Bourse', Cliometrica (2007)

deck.title: Silver falls, and the East pays in cheaper coin
deck.text: One after another the gold countries stop coining silver, and the white metal slides month by month. Every rupee and tael remitted home buys fewer pounds, and houses with capital in silver in the East and sterling liabilities at home are quietly insolvent unless they have sold forward.

advice.growth: Borrow in silver in the East, hold gold at home: the fall is a trade, not a threat.
advice.prudence: Fifteen and a half to one has held for seventy years; this is a passing fright.
advice.court: The India Office may close the mints; keep close to whoever is drafting the minute.
advice.conscience: Our silver depositors cannot hedge as we can; warn them before we protect ourselves.

deck.precedent: Silver's depreciation after German and American demonetisation, 1871–73, and the closing of the Indian mints to silver, June 1893
deck.source: Flandreau, The Glitter of Gold: France, Bimetallism, and the Emergence of the International Gold Standard (2004)

deck.title: Central Europe stops: your credits are frozen
deck.text: The largest bank of a small, broke republic has published losses greater than its capital. Panic spreads to its neighbours, gold leaves, and governments impose exchange control. Your acceptance credits to their banks cannot be repaid in sterling, and a standstill agreement will keep them frozen for years.

rumour.text: The German banks are drawing every London credit line at once.

advice.growth: Their banks pay well over Bank Rate for our acceptances; renew the lines and collect the commission.
advice.prudence: Short credits to a country short of gold become long credits in a crisis; cut them now.
advice.court: The Governor wants the City to stand by the Germans; he fears worse if it does not.
advice.conscience: Renewing credits we never expect to see repaid, merely to look loyal, is not honest banking.

deck.precedent: Collapse of the Creditanstalt, May 1931; the German Standstill Agreement froze short-term foreign credits, September 1931
deck.source: Accominotti, 'London Merchant Banks, the Central European Panic, and the Sterling Crisis of 1931', Journal of Economic History (2012)

deck.title: Cholera in {city}: the port is quarantined
deck.text: A city that never got round to filtering its drinking water is paying for it. Hundreds die each day, ships from the port are turned away everywhere else, and the exchange stands deserted. Bills are falling due on merchants who are sick, dead or fled.

advice.growth: Extend the bills of sound merchants by a month, and they will remember who did.
advice.prudence: Quarantine stops trade; expect protested bills and keep coin at hand.
advice.court: The city fathers will need a loan for filter beds; we should be the first to offer.
advice.conscience: No clerk is to be ordered into the stricken quarters to collect a debt.

deck.precedent: The Hamburg cholera epidemic, August–October 1892, about 8,600 dead
deck.source: Evans, Death in Hamburg: Society and Politics in the Cholera Years 1830–1910 (1987)

deck.title: The harvest rots in the fields
deck.text: The wettest summer in memory: the corn sprouts in the stook, the sheep die of liver rot, and cheap American grain arrives regardless. Farm rents are cut, land values fall, and the country banks discover what their mortgage books were really worth.

advice.growth: Land at depressed prices is a bargain for our richer clients; finance their purchases.
advice.prudence: Mark the farm mortgages down now; with American wheat, rents are not coming back.
advice.court: Parliament will be asked for relief, and the landed interest remembers its friends.
advice.conscience: Do not foreclose on tenants who paid for thirty years; give them a season.

deck.precedent: The disastrous British harvest of 1879, opening the agricultural depression
deck.source: Perren, Agriculture in Depression, 1870–1940 (1995)

deck.title: A distant republic wants its railway floated
deck.text: A small Central American republic wants a railway from ocean to ocean and a London loan to build it. Its revenues would barely pay the coupon on a tenth of the sum, but the promoters offer a handsome commission and will support the price with the loan's own proceeds until it is sold. Your name would sell it.

choice.label: Bring it out and sell it to the public
choice.result: The commission is splendid; when the coupons stop, a select committee will want to read your letters.

choice.label: Take a small share of the underwriting behind another house
choice.result: A quieter fee and a smaller stain, with some of the bonds left on your own books.

choice.label: Decline politely
choice.result: Another house brings it out at a premium, and your partners grumble until the coupons stop.

advice.growth: Ten per cent commission for a signature; if the public wishes to buy, that is the public's affair.
advice.prudence: A coupon paid out of the loan's own proceeds is a fraud with a timetable.
advice.court: Members are already asking questions about foreign loans; this is the wrong year for it.
advice.conscience: To sell bonds we believe will default is to rob our clients by prospectus.

deck.precedent: The Honduras railway loans of 1867–70, propped up by market rigging and exposed by the Select Committee on Loans to Foreign States, 1875
deck.source: Report from the Select Committee on Loans to Foreign States (House of Commons, 1875)

deck.title: The legislature investigates the money power
deck.text: A committee of the legislature, egged on by the newspapers and the farmers' leagues, wants to know who sits on whose boards, who allots whose issues, and how much of the nation's credit a few houses control. Its counsel has subpoenaed your partners and asked for your syndicate books.

choice.label: Open the books and send the senior partner to testify
choice.result: He is grilled for two days and the newspapers dislike him; the committee finds little it did not already know.

choice.label: Fight the subpoena with the best counsel money can buy
choice.result: You win on the law and lose in the press, and the eventual statute is written with you in mind.

choice.label: Resign the interlocking directorships before the hearings
choice.result: You give up a dozen boards and the business that came with them; the committee praises you as the exception.

advice.growth: We have nothing to apologise for; our syndicates built the railways these congressmen ride on.
advice.prudence: Hand over the books; a contempt finding would do more harm than anything inside them.
advice.court: Cooperate fully; the next banking law will be drafted by these same men.
advice.conscience: If our directorships cannot bear daylight, we should not be holding them.

deck.precedent: The Pujo Committee's 'Money Trust' investigation, 1912–13; the Senate's Pecora hearings, 1932–34
deck.source: Report of the Committee Appointed to Investigate the Concentration of Control of Money and Credit (Pujo Report, 1913)

deck.title: Bank Rate at seven: the bill brokers want call money
deck.text: Gold is leaving for New York, the Bank has raised its rate to the highest in a generation, and the discount houses are scrambling to renew the call money that carries their bill portfolios. They offer a full rate for a week's loan against good bills. Your cashier wants every sovereign in the vault.

choice.label: Lend to the brokers freely against good bills
choice.result: You earn a fat week's interest, and the market remembers who stayed in.

choice.label: Call in your loans to the market and hold coin
choice.result: Your till is full and the brokers are driven into the Bank at a penalty rate; they will not forget it.

choice.label: Lend only against Treasury bills and the finest acceptances
choice.result: Less interest, no bad paper, and nobody calls you a deserter.
