advice.growth: Seven per cent for a week against first-class bills is the best money we will see this year.
advice.prudence: Call in everything; the Bank will let the brokers drown before it lends to them.
advice.court: The Governor wants the market supplied; call our money and the Bank must do it for us.
advice.conscience: The brokers have dealt fairly with us for decades; abandoning them now is a poor return.

deck.precedent: Bank Rate raised to 7 per cent in November 1907 to draw gold from America; the London money market held
deck.source: Sayers, The Bank of England 1891–1944 (1976)

deck.title: {court} asks you to buy its munitions abroad
deck.text: {court} is at war and needs shells, horses and wheat from a neutral country, paid for in that country's currency. It wants your house as sole purchasing agent and as manager of a great loan placed with neutral investors. The commission on purchases is a small percentage and an enormous sum.

choice.label: Take the agency and manage the loan
choice.result: Fees roll in, the court is grateful, and the enemy's sympathisers call you a war profiteer.

choice.label: Take the agency but not the loan
choice.result: A steady commission with no balance-sheet risk, and the court notices the half-heartedness.

choice.label: Stay neutral
choice.result: Your neutral clients approve; the court will remember who would not help.

advice.growth: The largest commission in history; whoever wins, the munition makers must be paid through someone.
advice.prudence: If the court loses, its loan becomes our loss; take the agency, not the bonds.
advice.court: This is the court's hour of need; there will never be a better chance to earn its gratitude.
advice.conscience: Financing one side of a slaughter for a commission deserves a long hour of thought.

deck.precedent: J.P. Morgan & Co. as British purchasing agent in America from January 1915, and manager of the Anglo-French loan, October 1915
deck.source: Burk, Britain, America and the Sinews of War, 1914–1918 (1985)

deck.title: A rebel government offers bonds payable in cotton
deck.text: A breakaway republic, blockaded and unrecognised, offers bonds convertible into its cotton at a fixed price, deliverable after the war or at its own ports. With cotton at famine prices the conversion right looks golden, and the London subscription will be oversubscribed the day the lists open. Its agent offers you a share of the underwriting.

choice.label: Underwrite and sell your allotment at once
choice.result: The bonds open at a premium and you are out with a fat commission before the price-support operations begin to fail.

choice.label: Subscribe for your own book
choice.result: You hold a right to cotton that will never be delivered, and the victors will write the debt's nullity into their constitution.

choice.label: Refuse
choice.result: You miss the premium and keep clear of a cause your Lancashire clients pity and your conscience does not.

advice.growth: At famine prices the cotton option is worth more than the bond; take all they will give us.
advice.prudence: Cotton that cannot be shipped is not collateral; sell any allotment on the first day.
advice.court: The Government will not recognise the rebels; a London house too close to them invites trouble.
advice.conscience: This republic was founded to keep men in chains, and its cotton is picked by slaves.

deck.precedent: The Confederate Erlanger cotton loan, March 1863, oversubscribed in London; Confederate debt voided by the Fourteenth Amendment, 1868
deck.source: Gentry, 'A Confederate Success in Europe: The Erlanger Loan', Journal of Southern History (1970)

deck.title: The Cabinet needs millions by Monday
deck.text: A bankrupt foreign ruler is selling his shares in a strategic canal, Parliament is not sitting, and the Prime Minister cannot borrow without it. {court} asks your house to advance the purchase money at once, against nothing but its word, for a commission.

advice.growth: Two and a half per cent for three months' credit to the safest borrower alive.
advice.prudence: Make sure the coin is genuinely spare; millions out of the till makes for a long weekend.
advice.court: Say yes before he finishes the sentence; this is how a house becomes the Government's banker.
advice.conscience: Parliament has not voted the money; lend, but insist the Commons be told at once.

deck.precedent: N M Rothschild & Sons advanced £4 million for the British purchase of the Khedive's Suez Canal shares, November 1875
deck.source: Ferguson, The House of Rothschild, vol. 2: The World's Banker 1849–1999 (1998)

deck.title: {court} settles with the bondholders
deck.text: After years of arrears, and a bondholders' council that never stopped writing letters, {court} offers terms: arrears capitalised, coupons reduced, and creditors handed railways, guano rights or a share of the customs in exchange for the old bonds. It is less than par, and more than anyone expected.

advice.growth: Take the new paper and the railways; a defaulter that has settled is a borrower again.
advice.prudence: Take the cash portion and sell the rest before the next revolution.
advice.court: Accept quickly; the Foreign Office wants this matter closed and will note who obliged.
advice.conscience: The small holders must get the same terms as the syndicate; insist on it at the council.

deck.precedent: The Grace Contract, 1889: Peru's bondholders took its railways and guano through the Peruvian Corporation, 1890; the Corporation of Foreign Bondholders, founded 1868
deck.source: Marichal, A Century of Debt Crises in Latin America (1989)

deck.title: {court} seeks a depositary
deck.text: The treasurer of {court} wants one house to hold its receipts and advance against revenues not yet collected: tithes, annates, a tax farm falling due next year. The account brings prestige, a float of coin and every prelate's remittance business. It also brings a debtor no court in Christendom will let you sue.

advice.growth: Every bishop's remittance will pass through our counter; the advance is the price of the door.
advice.prudence: Advance against next year's tithes only what this year's tithes have already paid in.
advice.court: Refuse, and the account goes to a rival who will dine with the treasurer every week.
advice.conscience: Holding the Church's money is honourable; charging it disguised interest on advances is another matter.

deck.precedent: The Medici as depositaries of the Apostolic Chamber under Martin V and Eugenius IV, advancing against papal revenues; the Curia's account was kept in Florence during Eugenius's residence, 1434–36 and 1439–43
deck.source: G. Holmes, 'How the Medici Became the Pope's Bankers', in Rubinstein (ed.), Florentine Studies (1968); R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963), ch. 9

deck.title: A duke at war wants the branch's money
deck.text: {court} is raising an army, and its treasurer calls on your branch manager with a courtier's smile: an advance, unsecured, against aides voted by estates that have not yet met. The manager writes that refusal would cost the branch its licence to export and its best customers at court.

advice.growth: Twenty in the hundred from a sovereign prince beats anything the wool trade will pay this decade.
advice.prudence: This sum is twice the branch's capital; if he loses one battle, the branch is his.
advice.court: A duke who owes you is a duke who must protect you; his debt is your safe-conduct.
advice.conscience: Lending a prince money for a war of conquest is not commerce, and the confessor will say so.

deck.precedent: After the Medici lifted their ban on lending to princes (1471), Tommaso Portinari's Bruges branch lent Charles the Bold sums far beyond its capital, 1471–77
deck.source: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963), ch. 13

deck.title: {court}'s prince falls in battle
deck.text: A courier brings the news: the prince was found days after the battle, stripped, frozen into a pond. His heir acknowledges the debts in principle and pays nothing in fact, and the revenues assigned to you turn out to be pledged twice over to others.

rumour.text: A courier from the camp says the Swiss are coming down from the hills in greater numbers than anyone counted.

advice.growth: The heir needs bankers more than his father did; he will honour the debt to keep the credit.
advice.prudence: Write it down now, sell the claims at whatever a Genoese will pay, and stop lending.
advice.court: Send condolences and a partner to the new court before the other houses' partners arrive.
advice.conscience: We lent for a war and the war has collected its debt; let the house learn humility.

deck.precedent: Charles the Bold killed at Nancy, 5 January 1477; the Medici Bruges branch, crippled by his debts, was wound up in 1478–80
deck.source: R. Vaughan, Charles the Bold (1973); R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963), ch. 13

deck.title: {court} pays in licences, not coin
deck.text: The king acknowledges every penny and offers to repay through licences to export wool free of custom, once the war, the parliament and the harvest allow. The branch takes the licences, buys the wool and ships it, and finds it has become a wool merchant whose capital is a king's debt.

advice.growth: Custom-free wool sells dear in Flanders; we may come out ahead of a cash repayment.
advice.prudence: Licences are a promise to let us pay ourselves; book the debt at what the wool will fetch.
advice.court: Take whatever form of payment the king offers, and thank him for it in writing.
advice.conscience: Better slow payment honestly offered than a lawsuit against an anointed king.

deck.precedent: The Medici London branch's loans to Edward IV during the Wars of the Roses, part-repaid through wool-export licences; the branch was wound up with heavy losses, 1478–80
deck.source: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963), ch. 13

deck.title: The regime falls in {city}; its bankers are hunted
deck.text: A foreign king on the march demands passage, and the ruling family's heir surrenders fortresses without consulting the councils. Within the week the city expels him, and a crowd goes looking for his friends' strongboxes. Anyone with money at a house thought close to the old regime wants it back today.

rumour.text: They say the foreign king's harbingers are already chalking doors for billets in the next valley.

advice.growth: Princes come and go; merchants still need bills of exchange the morning after a revolution.
advice.prudence: Get coin into the till and the ledgers out of the building before the bells ring.
advice.court: We were too close to the old regime; send gifts to the new councillors today.
advice.conscience: Return what depositors ask for without haggling, and the crowd may spare the house.

deck.precedent: Charles VIII's march through Tuscany and the expulsion of Piero de' Medici, November 1494, after which Medici property was seized; also Cosimo de' Medici's exile by the Albizzi faction, 1433
deck.source: F. Guicciardini, Storia d'Italia (1537–40), bk I; R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963), ch. 15

deck.title: A roar on the square: a run in {city}
deck.text: One bench stops payment, then another. The state has borrowed from all of them to pay for the fleet, and the fleet has just been beaten. When the next banker opens his shutters a crowd is already waiting, and they want coin, not a transfer in the book.

rumour.text: On the square they say a great bench has been sending its silver to the mint by night.

advice.growth: A run is noise; open late, look calm, and tell them the books are sound.
advice.prudence: Pay everyone who asks, at once and in coin, and let the crowd watch the sacks open.
advice.court: Ask the councils to guarantee the benches; they owe the benches their fleet.
advice.conscience: These are widows' and guildsmen's savings; we must not shut the shutters on them.

deck.precedent: The Venetian banking crisis of 1499: the Garzoni and Lippomano banks failed early in the year and a crowd ran on the Pisani bank, as the Republic prepared for the Turkish war that brought defeat at Zonchio that August
deck.source: R. C. Mueller, The Venetian Money Market: Banks, Panics, and the Public Debt, 1200–1500 (1997); M. Sanudo, Diarii

deck.title: The pestilence returns to {city}
deck.text: The death lists lengthen. Shops shut, the courts adjourn, and debtors die before they can be dunned. The partners who can leave for their villas in the hills, taking their deposits with them, and the books stay with a junior clerk and the cashier.

advice.growth: Heirs will need loans to settle estates; this is the season to be open when others shut.
advice.prudence: Collect what is due now, before debtors and their witnesses are in the ground.
advice.court: Lend the commune what it needs for the pest-houses; it will remember who stayed.
advice.conscience: Forgive the debts of the dead poor; the house will not miss them, and God sees.

deck.precedent: Recurrent plague in Florence, notably 1400, 1417, 1424, 1430 and 1478–79, each emptying the city of its wealthier citizens
deck.source: A. G. Carmichael, Plague and the Poor in Renaissance Florence (1986)

deck.title: {court} levies another forced loan
deck.text: The war goes badly and the councils vote another forced loan, assessed on every household's estimated wealth. Bankers are rated at the top of the scale, and the credits go onto the Monte at five per cent nominal, trading well below par. Refuse, and your name goes on the list of defaulters, barred from office.

rumour.text: The war officers are said to have asked the Monte officials how much more the city can bear.

advice.growth: Pay it and buy more Monte credits cheap from smaller men who cannot carry theirs.
advice.prudence: Keep a fifth of deposits in coin precisely so that this does not empty the till.
advice.court: Pay early and visibly; the assessors remember who argued about the rate.
advice.conscience: Interest on forced loans is compensation for compulsion; the canonists allow it.

deck.precedent: Florentine prestanze levied repeatedly during the wars with Milan (1423–28) and Lucca (1429–33), and credited to the Monte Comune
deck.source: A. Molho, Florentine Public Finances in the Early Renaissance, 1400–1433 (1971)

deck.title: Monte credits slide on the exchange
deck.text: Interest on the state's funded debt is being paid late and partly, and the market in credits has taken note. Partners who bought them as a safe home for idle coin now hold paper quoted at a fraction of par. Those who took them as collateral want more.

advice.growth: Credits at a deep discount are a bargain; the Republic has never repudiated its Monte.
advice.prudence: Mark the credits at what they fetch on the Rialto, and stop taking them as collateral at par.
advice.court: Selling now is read at the palace as a vote against the war; hold.
advice.conscience: Buying credits from ruined widows at a third of par is not a sin, but it is close.

deck.precedent: The steep fall in Venetian Monte Vecchio quotations and arrears of interest through the wars with Milan and the Turk, 1420s–1470s
deck.source: G. Luzzatto, Il debito pubblico della Repubblica di Venezia (1963); R. C. Mueller, The Venetian Money Market: Banks, Panics, and the Public Debt, 1200–1500 (1997)

deck.title: The {city} manager has been hiding bad debts
deck.text: A visiting partner audits the books and finds debtors carried at full value who have not paid in years, with the hole covered by borrowing from other houses at exchange. The manager's letters were cheerful to the last; his balance sheets were annual, and late.

rumour.text: A Lucchese at the fair says your man borrows from other houses at ten in the hundred.

advice.growth: Every branch carries a few slow debtors; recalling a manager who brings volume is folly.
advice.prudence: Send an auditor with authority to open every chest and read every private letter.
advice.court: Settle quietly; a trial would tell the fair the house cannot govern its own.
advice.conscience: A man who lies in the ledger lies in confession too; remove him.

deck.precedent: Lionetto de' Rossi, Medici manager at Lyon, concealed bad debts and borrowed to mask losses; recalled and imprisoned for debt in Florence, 1485
deck.source: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963)

deck.title: A privateer takes the galley out of {city}
deck.text: The galley sailed under a neutral prince's flag, with bales of cloth and a painted altarpiece for a partner's chapel. A privateer of the German towns took her in the Channel, and his masters say she carried enemy goods. The insurers in Florence and Bruges are already arguing over the wording of the policy.

advice.growth: Insure the next voyage heavier and ship again; the Flanders route still pays.
advice.prudence: Never again put a season's goods in one hull; split cargoes across sailings.
advice.court: We flew a neutral flag; the German towns will return the cargo once the Duke protests.
advice.conscience: Pray for the crew, many of whom will be held for ransom.

deck.precedent: Danzig privateer Paul Beneke seized the Burgundian-flagged galley San Matteo, operated by the Medici Bruges branch, in the Channel in April 1473; Memling's Last Judgment, aboard for Angelo Tani, is still in Gdańsk
deck.source: P. Dollinger, The German Hansa (1970); R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963)

deck.title: The mint of {city} cuts the coin
deck.text: A prince short of money orders the mint to strike more pieces from the mark and cries down the old coin. Debts written in money of account are now paid in worse metal, bills drawn on the city fetch fewer florins, and foreign merchants hold back their goods until they see what the money is worth.

advice.growth: More coins mean more trade and higher prices for our goods; this will lift the market.
advice.prudence: Shorten every bill on the city and hold balances in gold, not the local money.
advice.court: Do not complain at the mint; the prince takes protests about his coin personally.
advice.conscience: A prince who debases his coin steals from his people; we must not profit by it.

deck.precedent: Maximilian's debasements of the Flemish coinage during his war with the Flemish towns, 1485–92; also the debasements of Henry IV of Castile, 1460s
deck.source: P. Spufford, Monetary Problems and Policies in the Burgundian Netherlands, 1433–1496 (1970); A. MacKay, Money, Prices and Politics in Fifteenth-Century Castile (1981)

deck.title: {city} gets a sound common coin
deck.text: The Duke orders one coinage for all his provinces, struck to a fixed standard and current in every town he rules. Exchange between Flemish groats and Brabant money stops being a guessing game. The money-changers grumble; everyone else draws bills with more confidence.

advice.growth: A sound coin draws the English and the Germans; lend more to Flemish cloth men now.
advice.prudence: Good news, but reforms are undone at the next war; keep the bills short anyway.
advice.court: Write to the Duke's treasurer with congratulations and an offer to supply the mint.
advice.conscience: Honest money is a moral good; it ends a hundred small frauds at the changers' tables.

deck.precedent: Philip the Good's monetary unification of the Burgundian Low Countries, 1433–34
deck.source: P. Spufford, Monetary Problems and Policies in the Burgundian Netherlands, 1433–1496 (1970)

deck.title: The confessor raises the matter of the exchange
deck.text: Your confessor says that bills drawn to Bruges and back with no goods behind them are dry exchange, usury by another name. A man who dies without restoring ill-gotten gains, he adds, dies badly. The great banker of the age, he reminds you, was told by the Pope to rebuild a convent.

choice.label: Endow a convent and its library
choice.result: The friars pray for the house and the Signoria notes your piety; the gift is drawn from the partners' accounts.

choice.label: Confine the house to real exchange on real trade
choice.result: Your conscience is clear, and the clients who wanted speculative exchange take it to a rival.

choice.label: Thank him and change nothing
choice.result: The house keeps its profits, and a preacher in the square keeps its name in his sermons.

advice.growth: Exchange is a sale of money in another place; no doctor of the Church has ever called it usury.
advice.prudence: Fictitious exchange keeps capital locked in bills with no goods behind them; trim it on business grounds.
advice.court: A visible benefaction buys more goodwill at the palace than any loan we could make.
advice.conscience: Restitution now is cheaper than restitution by your executors, and far cheaper than purgatory.

deck.precedent: Eugenius IV's counsel that Cosimo de' Medici make restitution by rebuilding San Marco, 1437–44; Antoninus of Florence condemns dry exchange in his Summa (c. 1440–59)
deck.source: Vespasiano da Bisticci, Vite (c. 1480s); R. de Roover, San Bernardino of Siena and Sant'Antonino of Florence (1967)

deck.title: The king moves the great fairs to {city}
deck.text: The king forbids his subjects to attend the fairs beyond his frontier and grants {city} four free fairs a year, with foreign coin allowed to circulate and dead merchants' goods safe from the crown. The Italian houses are already pricing removal carts.

advice.growth: Follow the fair: open in Lyon before the Lucchese and the Genoese take the best houses.
advice.prudence: Move the branch, but settle every account at the old fair first.
advice.court: The king has done us a favour; he will expect one in return before long.
advice.conscience: A fair is a fair; make sure the exchange settled there is on real goods.

deck.precedent: Louis XI's ordinances of 1462–63 diverting the Geneva fairs to Lyon; the Medici moved their Geneva branch to Lyon in 1466
deck.source: J.-F. Bergier, Genève et l'économie européenne de la Renaissance (1963)

deck.title: A great house calls in its loans in {city}
deck.text: The patriarch of the city's largest bank is dead. His son, advised by a friend who wishes him ill, calls in loans to see what his father left. Merchants who borrowed on the old man's word must find coin within the week; several shut their shops, and every creditor in town is now looking hard at every debtor.

rumour.text: They say the young master has asked his factors for a list of every sum lent on his father's word.

advice.growth: His failures are our customers; lend to sound men he has abandoned, at a fair rate.
advice.prudence: Our debtors also owe him; expect them to pay him first and us last.
advice.court: The family still rules the city; do not be seen profiting from the son's error.
advice.conscience: Do not press honest debtors into ruin because a frightened rival did.

deck.precedent: Piero de' Medici's recall of loans after Cosimo's death (1464) and the wave of Florentine failures in 1464–65
deck.source: N. Machiavelli, Istorie fiorentine (1532), bk VII; R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963)

deck.title: A merchant prince dies and leaves it all to the poor
deck.text: Your largest correspondent has died, leaving his fortune to a foundation for the poor administered by the commune. His account with you shows a balance in his favour, and your letters show debts of his you never booked. The foundation's notaries are at the door with the will.

choice.label: Pay the balance and forget what he owed
choice.result: The commune and the preachers praise the house, and the cash leaves the till.

choice.label: Set off his debts and pay the difference
choice.result: Lawful and tidy; the notaries grumble, but the merchants' court upholds you.

choice.label: Litigate for every penny
choice.result: You may win in three years; the town will remember who sued the poor.

advice.growth: His letters are evidence; the merchants' court will set off debts, so claim them all.
advice.prudence: Set off and settle; a three-year lawsuit ties up clerks and coin.
advice.court: The commune administers the foundation; suing it is suing the Signoria.
advice.conscience: A man's last gift to the poor should not be eaten by his banker's lawyers.

deck.precedent: Francesco di Marco Datini of Prato died in August 1410, leaving his estate to the Ceppo dei poveri, whose officers spent years settling his accounts with partners and correspondents
deck.source: I. Origo, The Merchant of Prato (1957)

deck.title: {city} shuts its gates on its prince
deck.text: The guilds have taken the market square and the prince's officers are in the town gaol. This time the prince himself is held, in a house on the square. His armies close the roads and the river, and he orders the foreign merchant nations to leave for a loyal town.

rumour.text: The weavers' deans have been meeting by night, and the militia captains with them.

advice.growth: Revolts end; the town will need credit to pay its fine, and we will be there.
advice.prudence: Move ledgers and coin to Antwerp until the gates open and the fine is settled.
advice.court: Stay neutral in word and loyal to the prince in deed; princes win sieges.
advice.conscience: Do not finance either side's soldiers; the poor of the town will pay for both.

deck.precedent: The Bruges revolts of 1436–38 and 1488, when the town held Maximilian captive in the Craenenburg (February–May) and he ordered foreign merchants to Antwerp
deck.source: J. A. Van Houtte, 'The Rise and Decline of the Market of Bruges', Economic History Review 19 (1966)

deck.title: The foreign nations move to {city}
deck.text: The English cloth fleet and the South German silver men already meet at the Brabant fairs. Now the Portuguese and the Italians are taking houses on the Scheldt. A bench here sees English kerseys, German silver and Portuguese sugar and Guinea pepper all in one season.

advice.growth: Open on the Scheldt now; in twenty years this will be the counting-house of Europe.
advice.prudence: Bruges has been the market of the North for two centuries; it will be again.
advice.court: The prince favours the loyal town; being seen there pleases him.
advice.conscience: A new market is a fresh start; let the branch write honest articles from day one.

deck.precedent: The shift of the Low Countries' entrepôt from Bruges to Antwerp, 1480s–1500s, including Maximilian's orders of 1484 and 1488 and the Portuguese crown's move of its factory to Antwerp, c. 1499
deck.source: H. Van der Wee, The Growth of the Antwerp Market and the European Economy (1963)

deck.title: Alum in the hills: a monopoly is offered
deck.text: A prospector has found alum in {court}'s lands, the best since the Turks took the eastern mines. The court offers your house the farm of the mines and the sale of the alum in the West, with a decree threatening anyone who buys the Turkish kind. The margins are princely, and so are the advances the court will expect.

choice.label: Take the farm and the cartel
choice.result: Alum profits flow, and the cloth towns curse your prices.

choice.label: Take a share of the farm, refuse the advances
choice.result: A smaller profit, and a cooler welcome at court.

choice.label: Decline
choice.result: A rival takes the farm, and with it the court's ear.

advice.growth: Every dyer from Florence to Flanders needs alum; a monopoly is the best business in Christendom.
advice.prudence: The farm is fine; the advances are the hook. Take the alum, not the prince's debts.
advice.court: Refusing a gift from {court} is an insult it will not forget.
advice.conscience: A cartel enforced by religious threat raises the poor weaver's costs; think hard before profiting.

deck.precedent: Alum discovered at Tolfa in the Papal States, 1461–62; the Medici held the papal alum contract 1466–76, and the Volterra alum dispute ended in the sack of the town in 1472
deck.source: J. Delumeau, L'alun de Rome, XVe–XIXe siècle (1962); R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963), ch. 7

deck.title: After a failed plot, your goods in {city} are seized
deck.text: A conspiracy against the ruling family of your seat has failed in blood, and the prince who blessed it is furious at its failure. He declares the house's goods in {city} forfeit and its claims void, and he releases its debtors from paying. The rival who replaced you at his court is pleased to help with the inventory.

rumour.text: Couriers are riding between a prelate's palace and a rival bank at all hours.

advice.growth: Hold your ground; no prince can afford to keep the largest bank out of his city.
advice.prudence: Move liquid assets out of every city that prince controls, before the decree is sealed.
advice.court: Make terms through a third prince; confiscations are bargaining chips, not verdicts.
advice.conscience: Murder in a cathedral; we must not be seen bargaining with those who blessed it.

deck.precedent: After the Pazzi conspiracy (26 April 1478), Sixtus IV excommunicated Lorenzo de' Medici and ordered Medici assets in Rome seized; he had already transferred the papal depository to the Pazzi in 1474
deck.source: L. Martines, April Blood (2003); R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963)

deck.title: War with the Turk closes the eastern trade
deck.text: The Republic has lost an island fortress and the fleet that should have relieved it, and the Sultan's horsemen burn villages within sight of the lagoon's bell-towers. Trade with the Black Sea stops, war taxes rise, and the auction of galley voyages finds no bidders.

rumour.text: Pilots back from the islands say the Sultan is building galleys at Gallipoli by the hundred.

advice.growth: War means freight rates, insurance premiums and state loans; a good bank profits from all three.
advice.prudence: Call in loans on eastern voyages and stop insuring hulls bound past Modon.
advice.court: The Republic always makes peace within a season or two; lend to the war and wait.
advice.conscience: A war against the infidel deserves our help, but not at usurious rates.

deck.precedent: The Venetian–Ottoman war of 1463–79: Negroponte lost in 1470, Ottoman raiders in Friuli 1477–78
deck.source: F. C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: The Sultan fixes the price of pepper in {city}
deck.text: The Sultan's agents have made pepper a royal monopoly: Western merchants must buy from his stores at his price, and private sales are punished. The consuls protest, the galley masters threaten to sail home empty, and in the end everyone pays.

advice.growth: Dearer pepper in Alexandria means dearer pepper in Bruges; finance the stock and wait.
advice.prudence: Cut credit to spice buyers until we see whether the galleys sail full.
advice.court: The Republic will negotiate; do nothing that undercuts its consuls.
advice.conscience: Paying an infidel's monopoly price is lawful; smuggling around it is not.

deck.precedent: Mamluk Sultan Barsbay's pepper monopoly imposed on Venetian and other Western merchants at Alexandria, from 1428 into the 1430s
deck.source: E. Ashtor, Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages (1983)

deck.title: Dearth: the harvest fails around {city}
deck.text: Two wet summers running, and the price of wheat has trebled. Weavers spend their wages on bread, cloth sells slowly, and the commune borrows to buy grain from Sicily. Your merchant debtors ask for time, and the grain dealers ask for credit.

advice.growth: Finance the grain ships; the commune pays well and pays first in a famine.
advice.prudence: Give good debtors time, cut new cloth credit, and keep coin for depositors who must buy bread.
advice.court: Lend to the commune's grain office at cost; it is remembered at the next election.
advice.conscience: Speculating in bread while the poor starve is the sin the preachers will name.

deck.precedent: The north-western European dearth of 1437–40, with grain prices in England and the Low Countries at their highest of the century
deck.source: B. M. S. Campbell, The Great Transition (2016)

deck.title: A rival house is exiled; its clients walk in
deck.text: The councils have banished a great banking family for plotting, and its partners scatter to Bologna and Bruges. Their correspondents need a new house to honour their bills, and their clerical clients need someone to remit their dues to the Curia.

advice.growth: Write to every one of their correspondents tonight; the Curia's business is the prize.
advice.prudence: New deposits are welcome, but new borrowers from a fallen house need fresh scrutiny.
advice.court: Their exile is political; be careful not to look like the faction that profited.
advice.conscience: Honour their bills faithfully; the exiled have dependants too.

deck.precedent: The exile of the Alberti from Florence (1401 and after) broke up their papal banking business, which passed largely to the Medici
deck.source: G. Holmes, 'How the Medici Became the Pope's Bankers', in Rubinstein (ed.), Florentine Studies (1968)

deck.title: Guinea gold reaches {city}
deck.text: The Crown's new fortress on the Guinea coast sends home gold dust by the caravel-load, and the King's factors need bankers to turn it into bills on Bruges and Florence. A Florentine already settled in the city has made himself indispensable to the Crown's African trade.

advice.growth: Gold from source, without Moorish middlemen: open in Lisbon and buy bills on the Crown.
advice.prudence: Gold from beyond the desert is a sailor's tale; wait for a second fleet.
advice.court: The Crown of Portugal wants Italian bankers; arrive with a gift for the treasurer.
advice.conscience: Much of this coast trades in people as well as gold; finance the one, not the other.

deck.precedent: São Jorge da Mina founded on the Gold Coast, 1482; Florentine merchant Bartolomeo Marchionni prominent in Lisbon's African trade
deck.source: J. Vogt, Portuguese Rule on the Gold Coast, 1469–1682 (1979)

deck.title: {city}'s public bank shuts its counters
deck.text: The house of the state's creditors, which also kept current accounts, has stopped paying in coin. Interest on its shares will be paid in instalments years late, and those instalments now trade at a discount on the square. Merchants who kept balances there scramble for cash.

rumour.text: In the Banchi they say the protectors of the House have stopped paying out in silver.

advice.growth: Buy the deferred instalments at a discount; the House always pays in the end.
advice.prudence: Expect its depositors to come to us for cash; fill the till before they do.
advice.court: The House is the Republic's other self; do not talk it down in public.
advice.conscience: Buying a widow's interest coupon at half its value is legal; offer her a fair price.

deck.precedent: The Casa di San Giorgio suspended its banking business in 1444–45, while its interest (paghe) was paid years in arrears and traded at a discount
deck.source: J. Heers, Gênes au XVe siècle (1961)

deck.title: {court}'s financier is arrested; his estate is for sale
deck.text: {court}'s great merchant-financier, master of the mint and lender to the king, is in prison on charges of poisoning, fraud and selling arms to the infidel. His debts to the crown are tripled; the crown's debts to him are forgotten. The commissioners are auctioning his galleys and houses at half their worth.

choice.label: Bid for the estate
choice.result: Bargains, and the uneasy knowledge that you bought a man's ruin from a king who could do it again.

choice.label: Help his factors move his goods abroad
choice.result: His family and the merchants will remember; so will the king.

choice.label: Stand aside
choice.result: Nothing gained, but you note carefully how this court settles its debts.

advice.growth: Galleys and warehouses at half price; the estate will never be cheaper.
advice.prudence: A king who ruins his own banker to cancel a debt is a borrower to avoid.
advice.court: Bid, and be seen bidding; the crown needs buyers to make the confiscation respectable.
advice.conscience: The charges are a pretext for erasing a debt; profiting from it makes us party to it.

deck.precedent: Jacques Coeur, Charles VII's argentier, arrested July 1451 and condemned in 1453; his property was confiscated and sold, and the king's debts to him lapsed
deck.source: M. Mollat, Jacques Coeur ou l'esprit d'entreprise au XVe siècle (1988)

deck.title: {court} pledges its silver mines
deck.text: {court} needs coin for a war and offers the output of its silver mines at a fixed price below the mint's, delivered monthly until the loan is paid. Security you can weigh is rare from a prince. But the mines lie in his country, under his judges, and the next prince may not feel bound.

advice.growth: Silver below mint price is repayment you can melt; this is the safest princely loan there is.
advice.prudence: Lend no more than three months of output, and send our own man to the smelter.
advice.court: A prince who pledges his mines to us is binding his own hands; take it.
advice.conscience: Pledged revenues are honest security; just ensure the rate is no usury in disguise.

deck.precedent: Archduke Sigismund of Tyrol pledged the Schwaz silver output to Jakob Fugger and other lenders against loans, 1487–88
deck.source: M. Häberlein, The Fuggers of Augsburg (2012)

deck.title: Free companies on the roads near {city}
deck.text: Discharged soldiers who call themselves companies, and whom the country people call flayers, are living off the land, ransoming abbeys and holding up the mule trains. Carriers want double for the road, couriers go by night, and the fair is thin.

advice.growth: Settle by bill, not by moving coin; the roads' danger is the exchange banker's profit.
advice.prudence: No specie on the roads until the companies move on; let balances wait at the fair.
advice.court: Offer the king's captain a loan to pay them off; he will pass through again.
advice.conscience: Do not buy their loot, however cheap; it is stolen from monasteries and peasants.

deck.precedent: The Écorcheurs who, after the Treaty of Arras (1435), ravaged Burgundy, Champagne, Lorraine and the Rhône valley until 1444
deck.source: P. Contamine, Guerre, état et société à la fin du Moyen Âge (1972)

deck.title: Apprentices riot against the Italians in {city}
deck.text: A quarrel in the street between a mercer's apprentice and a Lombard ended with the apprentice arrested, and the next day the crowd sacked the Italians' houses. The Italian nations talk of moving to Winchester. The city's merchants, who owe them money, say nothing.

advice.growth: Southampton is closer to the galleys anyway; move the warehouse and keep trading.
advice.prudence: Get the books and plate out of the house before the apprentices come back.
advice.court: Petition the king's council for protection; the crown needs our customs duties.
advice.conscience: Do not answer violence by withholding credit from honest English mercers.

deck.precedent: Anti-Italian riots in London, 1456–57, after which Italian merchants withdrew for a time to Winchester and Southampton
deck.source: A. A. Ruddock, Italian Merchants and Shipping in Southampton, 1270–1600 (1951)

deck.title: {court} demands a sworn return of all your wealth
deck.text: A new tax replaces guesswork with arithmetic: every household must file a sworn return of property, investments, debts and dependants, and bankers must list balances owed by and to them. Officials can check returns against other houses' books. Your return will be read by your rivals' cousins.

choice.label: File honestly: every branch and balance
choice.result: You pay the full assessment and gain a name for candour at the palace.

choice.label: Leave the foreign branches out
choice.result: The assessment is light; the officials' cousins at the fairs may notice.

advice.growth: No official can read a Bruges ledger; leave the branches out and keep the capital working.
advice.prudence: Declare it all; bad debts are deductible, and we have plenty to list.
advice.court: The assessors want a model return from a great house; give them one.
advice.conscience: A sworn return is an oath; a false oath is a sin whatever the tax.

deck.precedent: The Florentine catasto of 1427, requiring sworn declarations of assets including business balances; the Medici returns survive
deck.source: D. Herlihy and C. Klapisch-Zuber, Tuscans and Their Families (1985)

deck.title: The {city} manager wants a bigger share
deck.text: Your branch manager writes that he made the branch and the branch makes the house's profits. He wants the new articles to give him a larger share, his name in the firm and a free hand with the court's business. He hints that a rival house has made him an offer.

choice.label: Grant the share and the free hand
choice.result: He stays, grateful and unsupervised.

choice.label: Grant the share, keep the restrictions in the articles
choice.result: He signs, sulks, and writes fewer letters.

choice.label: Refuse and recall him
choice.result: His successor is honest and new; some clients follow the old man to his new house.

advice.growth: He knows the court and the fair; a bigger share keeps the best man we have.
advice.prudence: A share, perhaps; a free hand with princes, never. Put the lending limit in the articles.
advice.court: His friendships at court are the branch; recall him and we lose the duke.
advice.conscience: A man who threatens to leave for a rival is already half gone; keep him on a short rein.

deck.precedent: Tommaso Portinari's 1471 articles with Lorenzo de' Medici, which made him senior partner at Bruges with wide latitude after Angelo Tani withdrew
deck.source: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963), ch. 13

deck.title: Jubilee year: pilgrims pour into {city}
deck.text: A holy year has been proclaimed, and pilgrims crowd the bridges to the great basilicas, paying in every coin of Christendom. Prelates remit offerings by bill, money-changers work by torchlight, and a bank with a counter near the Curia does a year's business in a season.

advice.growth: Send our best changers to Rome and every spare florin with them.
advice.prudence: Count every coin twice; jubilee crowds bring clippers and counterfeiters too.
advice.court: Offer the Chamber a fair rate on offerings; it notices who gouged the pilgrims.
advice.conscience: Change the pilgrims' coin honestly; cheating them in a holy year is a double sin.

deck.precedent: The Jubilee of 1450, from which the Medici Rome branch drew exceptional profits; it also saw the fatal crush on the Ponte Sant'Angelo that December
deck.source: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank (1963)

deck.title: {court} borrows against its returning fleets
deck.text: {court} wants money for six or twelve months at a fixed rate, secured on the returns and duties of the next ships home, and says plainly that it will renew at maturity. The burghers call such paper as good as a house on the canal. Your cashier calls it short paper that will never be short.

advice.growth: Six per cent on paper the whole Exchange will buy back from us tomorrow. It is the till's best friend.
advice.prudence: Short paper rolled for ever is long paper in disguise. Take only a slice we could hold if nobody renews.
advice.court: The men who govern this paper govern the city. To hold it is to sit at their table.
advice.conscience: A fixed rate on a lawful loan to a public body. The ministers' own widows buy it. No sin here.

deck.precedent: The VOC began borrowing on short obligaties in Amsterdam against its returning fleets, rolled over for generations, 1622 onward
deck.source: Gelderblom, de Jong & Jonker, 'The Formative Years of the Modern Corporation: The Dutch East India Company VOC, 1602–1623', Journal of Economic History (2013)

deck.title: {court} sells a charter for a loan
deck.text: The Treasury will grant a monopoly to whoever lends it two millions. Subscribers are borrowing in order to subscribe, and the subscription receipts will trade in Exchange Alley before the new company's first ship sails. You are asked to take a line in the book, at a rate Parliament has blessed above the legal one.

advice.growth: Whoever lends the state its millions owns a trade for twenty years. Our name belongs on the book's first page.
advice.prudence: These subscribers borrowed to subscribe. When the calls come they will sell, and the price will fall in our hands.
advice.court: Ministers remember who filled the book. A refusal now shuts the door on every contract after it.
advice.conscience: The statute sets the rate, so the usury laws are silent. Ask only whether we can bear the loss.

deck.precedent: The New East India Company won its charter through the General Society's £2m loan to the Crown at 8%, raised by public subscription in the City, 1698
deck.source: Dickson, The Financial Revolution in England (1967); Chaudhuri, The Trading World of Asia and the English East India Company, 1660–1760 (1978)

deck.title: The wind trade breaks in {city}
deck.text: For a season the back rooms of the inns of {city} have traded promises to deliver things not yet in the ground or not yet in being, each changing hands ten times between the pipe and the jug. One morning a seller finds no buyer. By the week's end nobody will honour a contract, and your depositors want their money to cover theirs.

rumour.text: In the colleges at the taverns they say prices doubled again this week, and a bulb went for a house.

advice.growth: Our depositors are making fortunes. Lend them more against their contracts and share the gain.
advice.prudence: Nothing changes hands but paper and wine. Call in every loan secured on these contracts before the music stops.
advice.court: The magistrates call it a gamblers' quarrel and the courts won't enforce wind trades, so it cannot touch us.
advice.conscience: Selling what one does not own for a delivery one cannot make is gaming, and gaming debts poison honest ones.

deck.precedent: Tulip mania collapsed in Haarlem and Amsterdam in February 1637; London's joint-stock promotion boom broke in 1696
deck.source: Goldgar, Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age (2007); Scott, The Constitution and Finance of English, Scottish and Irish Joint-Stock Companies to 1720 (1910–12)

deck.title: {court} sells orders on next year's taxes
deck.text: {court}'s treasury is selling numbered orders on two years of voted revenue, to be repaid strictly in course, with interest at the legal rate. The great shops of the street are taking the lion's share and lending their depositors' money to do it. A little extra is paid as a 'gratuity', which nobody writes down.

advice.growth: Ten per cent, numbered, repaid in strict course out of voted taxes. It is the safest paper in the kingdom.
advice.prudence: We would lend money payable on demand to a king who pays when he pleases. Keep it small.
advice.court: The Treasury keeps lists. A goldsmith who declines this year is not asked next year.
advice.conscience: Six is the legal rate and the rest is a 'gratuity'. Call it what it is before a jury does.

deck.precedent: Downing's Treasury Orders under the Additional Aid, bought largely by the Lombard Street goldsmiths, 1665–71
deck.source: Roseveare, The Treasury, 1660–1870 (1973); Richards, The Early History of Banking in England (1929)

deck.title: {court} stops payment on its orders
deck.text: A proclamation suspends repayment of the Crown's orders for a year 'for the urgent occasions of the State'. Interest is promised, though nobody believes it will come. Every depositor in the street knows where his goldsmith put his money, and the street fills by noon.

rumour.text: They say the Council sat past midnight on the revenue, and the Treasury clerks have stopped paying orders in course.

advice.growth: It is a suspension, not a repudiation. The orders will trade at sixty within the year. Buy more.
advice.prudence: Pay every depositor at the counter without a word of complaint. A house that pays outlives a king who doesn't.
advice.court: Petition the Council humbly. Those who rail in print will be the last paid, if they are paid at all.
advice.conscience: We lent poor men's deposits to a prince's pleasures. Whatever we save belongs to them first.

deck.precedent: Charles II's Stop of the Exchequer, January 1672, which ruined the goldsmith-bankers Backwell and Vyner
deck.source: Horsefield, 'The "Stop of the Exchequer" Revisited', Economic History Review (1982); Roseveare, The Financial Revolution 1660–1760 (1991)

deck.title: {court} suspends its asientos
deck.text: A decree suspends payment on the Crown's short contracts. The bankers are told they will be settled 'by a general means': their silver advances become long juros at a lower rate, assigned on revenues already pledged twice. Juros trade at a discount, and you have become an annuitant against your will.

rumour.text: The Council of Finance has asked the bankers to show all their contracts by Saturday. Nobody asks that kindly.

advice.growth: Juros at five per cent are still income. Hold them and wait for the next asiento at fat margins.
advice.prudence: Sell the juros at the discount while there is a buyer, and stop lending this Crown short.
advice.court: The Council rewards bankers who accept the medio quietly with the next contract. Accept it.
advice.conscience: A debtor who rewrites his debts by decree has broken faith. We may lawfully refuse him more credit.

deck.precedent: Spanish Crown decrees suspending asiento payments in 1607, 1627, 1647, 1652 and 1662, each settled by a medio general in juros
deck.source: Álvarez Nogal, El crédito de la Monarquía Hispánica en el reinado de Felipe IV (1997)

deck.title: Invaded on every frontier at once
deck.text: Four enemies cross the borders in a single spring. Company shares fall by half in a month, the dykes are cut to drown the approaches, and crowds outside the town hall look for someone to hang. Holders queue at the exchange bank for coin. It pays every one of them, and its paying is the only good news of the year.

rumour.text: Letters from the Rhine say the enemy's horse has been seen past the forts, and the bourse is quiet as a church.

advice.growth: Shares are at half. When the water saves the Republic again, we will have bought the Company at a gift.
advice.prudence: Pay out every guilder asked for. A bank that pays in a panic is how the panic ends.
advice.court: The burghers are lynching their own rulers. Keep the shutters down and stay out of the politics.
advice.conscience: The mob wants someone to blame. Let nobody say this house sold short against its own country.

deck.precedent: The Dutch Rampjaar of 1672: the exchange halved, and the Amsterdam Wisselbank met a run and paid in full
deck.source: Israel, The Dutch Republic: Its Rise, Greatness and Fall 1477–1806 (1995)

deck.title: Light coin and a crying-down
deck.text: The princes' mints strike small coin with less silver every month, and changers buy up good thalers at the town gates for the melting-pot. Prices run ahead of wages, and the bakers riot. Then the edict comes, crying the small coin down by half, and every debt written in it becomes a fresh quarrel.

rumour.text: The changers at the gate are paying a premium for old thalers, and nobody will say why.

advice.growth: Buy good coin at the gate and pay creditors in the light stuff. Every changer in town is doing it.
advice.prudence: Keep our books in good thalers or bank money. Every debt in small coin is a loss waiting to happen.
advice.court: The prince's mintmaster swears to me the crying-down is years away.
advice.conscience: Paying a creditor in coin you know is false is theft, whatever the edict tolerates.

deck.precedent: The German Kipper- und Wipperzeit debasements of 1619–23, and the halving of Castilian vellón by decree in August 1628
deck.source: Kindleberger, 'The Economic Crisis of 1619 to 1623', Journal of Economic History (1991); Hamilton, American Treasure and the Price Revolution in Spain (1934)

deck.title: The plague returns to {city}
deck.text: The health office has shut the gates and marked the doors. Those who can have fled to their villas, taking their custom and leaving their debts. Two of your clerks are dead and a third is in the lazaretto, along with half the parish you lent to. Nobody will be paid this season.

rumour.text: Sailors off a ship in quarantine are said to be sick with swellings, and the health magistrates are meeting daily.

advice.growth: The rich flee, but they flee with their bills. Follow them to the country and keep the book alive.
advice.prudence: Debtors will die and clerks with them. Hold coin, call short loans and expect nothing paid for a season.
advice.court: The health magistrates want a loan for the lazaretto. Lend it. They decide whose goods are burned.
advice.conscience: Do not foreclose on widows this year. God and the street both keep accounts.

deck.precedent: The Italian plague of 1629–31, which killed about a third of Venice; Seville in 1649; London in 1665
deck.source: Cipolla, Fighting the Plague in Seventeenth-Century Italy (1981); Slack, The Impact of Plague in Tudor and Stuart England (1985)

deck.title: Fire in {city}
deck.text: It began in a baker's yard and ran four days on an east wind. The goldsmiths carted their running cash and ledgers out ahead of it, and the street where they kept shop is ash. Your vaults held, but half your borrowers' warehouses did not, and their leases are now matters for the courts.

advice.growth: Half the town must be rebuilt. Lend to the builders and own the new street.
advice.prudence: Debts survive only if the books do. Get the ledgers and cash out by cart tonight.
advice.court: The authorities promise a special court to settle leases. Our claims will wait their turn.
advice.conscience: Do not raise the rate on the burnt-out. Charity now is credit later.

deck.precedent: The Great Fire of London, 2–6 September 1666, which burned Lombard Street; the great fire of Constantinople, 1660
deck.source: Porter, The Great Fire of London (1996)

deck.title: An Indiaman lost
deck.text: The news comes on a later ship. The outward fleet's largest hull struck an uncharted reef off a desert coast, and her chests of silver, her trade goods and many of her people are gone. The bottomry you wrote on her was lent at the sea's risk, which is to say at yours.

advice.growth: One ship in twenty or thirty never comes home, and the others pay for her. Send the next.
advice.prudence: We lent on bottomry at sea risk. The loss is ours and no court will say otherwise.
advice.court: The Company's governors will want to hear we stood by them. Renew on the next fleet.
advice.conscience: Bottomry is lawful because we bear the sea's risk. Bearing it honestly is the price.

deck.precedent: The VOC ship Batavia wrecked on the Houtman Abrolhos on her maiden voyage, June 1629
deck.source: Drake-Brockman, Voyage to Disaster (1963)

deck.title: The enemy's silver fleet is taken
deck.text: A Company admiral has caught the enemy's treasure fleet aground in a Cuban bay and taken it almost without a fight. The directors promise a dividend of half the capital, and every shareholder on your books is suddenly liquid, generous and looking for somewhere to put the money.

advice.growth: Half the capital back as a dividend! Put it to work before the shareholders drink it.
advice.prudence: A prize is not a trade. Bank it, and do not expect the admiral to do it twice.
advice.court: The losing king is ruined this year. Whoever lends to him next names his own price.
advice.conscience: Booty from a just war is lawful, they tell me. Give a tithe to the poor anyway.

deck.precedent: Piet Heyn took the Spanish silver fleet at Matanzas in 1628, and the WIC paid a 50% dividend
deck.source: Den Heijer, Geschiedenis van de WIC (1994)

deck.title: Your agent at {city} refuses to be recalled
deck.text: You recalled your agent at {city} over his private trade and unpaid debts. He has locked up his successor, kept the books and the strongroom keys, and writes that he holds the place 'for the service of the house' until better instructions come. The letter took nine months to reach you.

advice.growth: He still trades for us, after his fashion. Write him a sharp letter and keep the business running.
advice.prudence: A man who jails his successor will never render accounts. Write off his ledger and send ships.
advice.court: Petition for a royal warrant. Only the king's name will open those gates.
advice.conscience: We sent a man too far with nobody watching. That is our fault before it is his.

deck.precedent: Sir Edward Winter deposed and imprisoned the EIC's appointed agent at Fort St George, Madras, and held it 1665–68
deck.source: Love, Vestiges of Old Madras 1640–1800 (1913)

deck.title: The enemy is in the river
deck.text: Enemy ships have broken the chain, burned the fleet at its moorings and towed away the flagship. Before nightfall the street is full of men with notes and running-cash receipts, all wanting coin, all at once. Clerks are sending their wives into the country with gold in the luggage.

rumour.text: They say the enemy's fleet lies off the river mouth and our ships have no men aboard to fight them.

advice.growth: Panics pass. Ask depositors to give a week's notice and they'll be back by Michaelmas.
advice.prudence: Pay on demand, at once and in plain sight. Stack coin on the counter where the queue can see it.
advice.court: The Council will not let the City break. A word with the Lord Mayor is worth a cartload of coin.
advice.conscience: The people in that queue are not our enemies. They are owed their own money.

deck.precedent: The Dutch raid on the Medway in June 1667 set off a run on the London goldsmiths, recorded by Pepys
deck.source: Pepys, Diary, 12–13 June 1667; Richards, The Early History of Banking in England (1929)

deck.title: Refugee merchants arrive with their capital
deck.text: A neighbouring king has revoked his toleration of his Protestant subjects. His silk-weavers, clockmakers and merchant houses are slipping over the borders with bills drawn on Lyon and jewels sewn into their hems. They need a house that knows their correspondents and asks few questions about how they came.

advice.growth: Merchants with Lyon connections and gold in their hems. Take every account and the bills that come with it.
advice.prudence: Refugee money leaves as fast as it came. Do not lend it long.
advice.court: Our own court will kindly remember who sheltered its co-religionists.
advice.conscience: These are strangers fleeing for their faith. We take them in first and count their money second.

deck.precedent: The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes, October 1685, drove Huguenot merchants and capital to Amsterdam and London
deck.source: Scoville, The Persecution of Huguenots and French Economic Development, 1680–1720 (1960)

deck.title: The pulpit names the lenders
deck.text: The consistory has ruled that keepers of lending tables and takers of interest may not come to the Lord's Supper. The minister preached on it on Sunday, looking at your pew. The magistrates license interest and the preachers forbid it, and your more devout clients are moving their accounts to the house across the canal.

advice.growth: The pulpit thunders, but its deacons bank with us. Ride it out.
advice.prudence: Clients desert a house the minister names. Keep our rates modest and our heads down until it passes.
advice.court: Ask the magistrates to remind the consistory who licenses whom. Burgomasters have little love for preachers.
advice.conscience: The state permits interest and the church forbids it. Better to be modest than right in public.

deck.precedent: Dutch Reformed consistories barred bankers of lending houses from communion until the States of Holland overruled them, 1658
deck.source: De Vries & van der Woude, The First Modern Economy: Success, Failure, and Perseverance of the Dutch Economy, 1500–1815 (1997)

deck.title: The clipped silver is called in
deck.text: The hammered silver has been clipped to half its weight, and a gold guinea fetches thirty shillings of it. Parliament has called in the old money for recoinage. For months there is no coin to pay wages, rents or notes. Even the new bank pays its notes by instalments, and the goldsmiths stop paying their own notes in specie.

rumour.text: The coffee-houses say the guinea will go to thirty-two shillings, and the Commons talk of nothing but clipping.

advice.growth: Guineas at thirty shillings! Pay out in clipped silver and keep the gold.
advice.prudence: There will be no coin for months. Keep every lawful piece and lend nothing we cannot recall.
advice.court: The Treasury's new interest-bearing bills will pass as money. Take them, and the Treasury will remember.
advice.conscience: Take the poor's clipped coin at its tale. The clipping is the Crown's shame, not theirs.

deck.precedent: The English Great Recoinage of 1696–99, during which the Bank of England paid its notes by instalments in 1696
deck.source: Li Ming-Hsun, The Great Recoinage of 1696 to 1699 (1963); Clapham, The Bank of England: A History (1944)

deck.title: A projector's land bank wants your name
deck.text: A projector with friends at court proposes a bank that lends to country gentlemen on mortgage at low rates and issues notes against their acres. It is meant to rival the new bank of the moneyed men, and Parliament has authorised it to lend the Crown millions if the subscription fills. He wants your house on the list of receivers.

choice.label: Subscribe and act as receiver
choice.result: The subscription raises a pittance, the scheme dies within the summer, and the coffee-houses remember whose name was on the list.

choice.label: Decline and stand with the moneyed men
choice.result: The country party at court calls you a Whig usurer, but the City notes which side you took in a hard year.

choice.label: Discount the scheme's promises quietly to the hopeful
choice.result: You buy subscription receipts cheap from nervous squires and sell them to hopeful ones, a small and unlovely profit.

advice.growth: Cheap loans to every squire on the security of his acres: a bank with the land's own credit!
advice.prudence: Land cannot be sold in a week, so a bank built on it cannot pay a note in a week.
advice.court: The court party wants this to beat the rival bank. Backing it buys their favour.
advice.conscience: Do not lend our name to a promise we believe is hollow, however useful the patron.

deck.precedent: The National Land Bank's subscription of 1696 raised barely £2,100 of the £2.56m sought, and collapsed
deck.source: Dickson, The Financial Revolution in England (1967); Horsefield, British Monetary Experiments 1650–1710 (1960)

deck.title: {court} 'borrows' the bullion at the mint
deck.text: Merchants have long lodged their bullion at the royal mint for safekeeping. This morning {court} sealed the strongroom and declared the silver a loan to the Crown, to be repaid when the realm is quieter. Your share is under seal with the rest. Every merchant in the city is now asking whose strongroom is safe.

advice.growth: Bullion at the mint was a fool's deposit. Merchants will bring theirs to our strongroom now.
advice.prudence: Treat what they took as lost and argue about the interest later.
advice.court: Accept with thanks. The merchants who protested are being named in Council.
advice.conscience: A deposit seized is not a loan, whatever the warrant calls it.

deck.precedent: Charles I seized about £130,000 of merchants' bullion at the Tower mint in July 1640, releasing it only for a £40,000 loan
deck.source: Richards, The Early History of Banking in England (1929); Ashton, The Crown and the Money Market 1603–1640 (1960)

deck.title: {court} levies a loan without consent
deck.text: Commissioners have arrived with a list of names and a sum against each. {court} calls it a loan, though no assembly has voted it, no interest is promised and no date is set. Gentlemen who refused last month have been pressed as soldiers or sent to gaol. Yours is the next name on the list.

choice.label: Pay the full sum
choice.result: The commissioners thank you, the money vanishes into the war, and the court counts you among the loyal.

choice.label: Pay half and plead poverty
choice.result: They take the half and write 'reluctant' beside your name.

choice.label: Refuse, standing on the law
choice.result: A partner spends a winter in the Fleet, and the merchants who admire you for it bring you their accounts.

advice.growth: Pay it and book it as the price of doing business in this realm.
advice.prudence: We will never see this money again. Give the least that keeps us out of prison.
advice.court: Refusers are being pressed for soldiers. Pay, and smile while you do it.
advice.conscience: A loan taken without the assembly's consent is against the law of the land. Many good men refuse.

deck.precedent: Charles I's Forced Loan of 1626–27 and the imprisonment of refusers tested in the Five Knights' Case, 1627
deck.source: Cust, The Forced Loan and English Politics 1626–1628 (1987)

deck.title: The harvest fails around {city}
deck.text: A cold spring and a wet summer have left the fields black, and bread has tripled in price. Peasants are eating bran and grass, the tax-farmers bring in half their quota, and the Crown's rentes are paid late. Your borrowers in the cloth trade have no customers, because nobody buys cloth when they cannot buy bread.

rumour.text: Carters say the rye in the river valleys is rotting in the ear, and the grain merchants have stopped quoting.

advice.growth: Grain dealers need bills to buy in the Baltic. Lend at harvest rates and they'll pay double.
advice.prudence: When peasants starve, taxes fail and rentes go unpaid. Shorten everything we lend to this Crown.
advice.court: The intendants want advances to buy grain for the cities. Refuse them and you will be remembered.
advice.conscience: Lending to forestallers who hoard grain is complicity. Lend to the city granaries instead.

deck.precedent: The French famine of 1693–94, in which some 1.3 million died and royal revenues collapsed
deck.source: Lachiver, Les années de misère: la famine au temps du Grand Roi (1991)

deck.title: The pieces of eight are found light
deck.text: Assayers report that silver from one of the great colonial mints has run short of fine for years, with the mint officials pocketing the difference. The mints of Europe cry the suspect pieces down by a quarter, and every chest of reales in your strongroom must now be weighed and assayed coin by coin.

rumour.text: The Genoese changers are said to be refusing reales of one stamp and weighing every other.

advice.growth: The cry-down is a buying chance. Take suspect pieces at a discount and assay them ourselves.
advice.prudence: Weigh every piece of eight that comes in, and count nothing by tale until the assays are known.
advice.court: The Spanish Crown's silver has always been good and it promises an inquiry. Take them at face value.
advice.conscience: If we know a coin is light, passing it on at full value is fraud.

deck.precedent: The Potosí mint fraud, uncovered 1648–49, led to Peruvian reales being cried down across Europe in 1650
deck.source: Lane, Potosí: The Silver City That Changed the World (2019)

deck.title: The exchange fairs split in two
deck.text: The bankers who meet four times a year to settle Europe's bills have quarrelled over who sets the rates. One nation has taken its men to a fair in a town of its own choosing, and the others stay where they were. Each fair clears half the paper it used to, and bills are carried over at rates nobody trusts.

advice.growth: Two fairs mean two sets of spreads. Send factors to both and arbitrage the quarrel.
advice.prudence: A split fair clears half as much. Expect bills carried over and settlements late.
advice.court: The Republic wants its men at its own fair. Send ours where the Senate tells us.
advice.conscience: Exchange is lawful only as a true exchange. Bills merely rolled from fair to fair become dry exchange.

deck.precedent: The schism of the Piacenza exchange fairs in 1622, when the Genoese moved to Novi
deck.source: Da Silva, Banque et crédit en Italie au XVIIe siècle (1969)

deck.title: {court}, at war without end, asks for a loan
deck.text: {court} is in the fifth year of a war it expected to win in one. It has sold admission to its ruling council to rich commoners, sold offices, sold tax farms, and is now asking for you. The rate is generous and secured on the customs. What it cannot offer is a date when the war will end.

advice.growth: A state at war pays well and long. There is no better customer than one who cannot stop.
advice.prudence: Wars last longer than anyone promises. Lend for two years and plan on six.
advice.court: They sell seats in their council for less than we're asked. Lending opens the same doors.
advice.conscience: If the war is just, a loan to wage it is lawful. If not, no rate will make it clean.

deck.precedent: Venice sold admission to the Great Council for 100,000 ducats a family from 1646 to fund the War of Candia
deck.source: Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: The general's banker seeks partners
deck.text: A great military contractor raises whole armies for the Emperor on credit and pays them from 'contributions' levied on occupied towns. His banker wants partners to advance the soldiers' pay against those levies, with good bills on the imperial mint as security. The profits are princely, and so is the risk if the general falls from favour.

choice.label: Join the syndicate in full
choice.result: Fees pour in while the general rides high, and the merchants of the burned towns curse your name.

choice.label: Discount only his best bills, at short date
choice.result: A modest commission and a modest share of the opprobrium.

choice.label: Decline
choice.result: The general's people call you timid. The Emperor's treasury forgets you for a while.

advice.growth: His armies are the largest in the Empire and his levies come in silver. Join.
advice.prudence: His only security is plunder and the general's favour, and both vanish if he falls.
advice.court: The Emperor's favour now runs through the general. Refuse him and we lose the Empire.
advice.conscience: His contributions are wrung from burnt villages. That money is blood.

deck.precedent: Hans de Witte, Wallenstein's banker, financed the imperial armies against contributions; he was ruined and drowned himself in Prague, 1630
deck.source: Ernstberger, Hans de Witte, Finanzmann Wallensteins (1954)

deck.title: A New Christian financier seeks a hiding place
deck.text: A Portuguese New Christian banker who holds the Crown's asientos believes the Holy Office has his name. His agent comes at night and asks you to take his silver on deposit off the books and remit it by bill to his cousins in the north. The fee he offers is handsome. If the tribunal found out, the penalty would be ruinous.

choice.label: Take the silver and remit it north
choice.result: His silver reaches the north and his gratitude reaches you, but the court has long ears.

choice.label: Refuse politely
choice.result: He finds another house, and the nation's merchants mark you as fair-weather friends.

choice.label: Inform the tribunal
choice.result: The Holy Office thanks you, the Crown takes note, and no New Christian merchant will cross your threshold again.

advice.growth: His silver is good and he will pay well to keep it safe. Take it and send it north quietly.
advice.prudence: If the Holy Office finds his money in our books, it will want to see the rest of them too.
advice.court: Sheltering the tribunal's quarry offends the Crown. Report it and we gain a powerful friend.
advice.conscience: He is a man in fear of the fire. Shelter is a work of mercy, whatever the tribunal says.

deck.precedent: The Inquisition's prosecutions of Portuguese New Christian asentistas at the court of Philip IV, 1630s–1650s
deck.source: Boyajian, Portuguese Bankers at the Court of Spain, 1626–1650 (1983)

deck.title: An interloper wants credit for an Indies voyage
deck.text: A captain who has served in the East plans to sail to the Indies without the Company's licence and buy pepper and calico on his own account. He wants your bills on his correspondents and a loan on bottomry. The Company holds a royal charter, has lawyers at the Admiralty and lends to the king.

choice.label: Finance the voyage
choice.result: The ship comes home fat and the margins are glorious, but the Company's governors now know your name.

choice.label: Decline quietly
choice.result: The captain finds money in Hamburg, and nothing more is said.

choice.label: Warn the Company
choice.result: The ship is seized before she clears the Downs, and the Company is grateful while the free traders are not.

advice.growth: The Company makes a hundred per cent and shares none of it. Finance the interloper and take the margin.
advice.prudence: The Company seizes ships and the courts uphold its charter. Our capital could rot in an Admiralty suit.
advice.court: The Company lends to the king and the king protects the Company. Cross neither.
advice.conscience: A monopoly granted by prerogative is no law of God. Trading freely is no sin.

deck.precedent: English interlopers, among them Thomas Pitt, challenged the EIC monopoly, upheld in East India Company v. Sandys, 1683–85
deck.source: Stern, The Company-State: Corporate Sovereignty and the Early Modern Foundations of the British Empire in India (2011)

deck.title: A nation subscribes to its colony
deck.text: The northern kingdom has chartered a company to plant a colony on the isthmus between the two oceans. A great part of its liquid wealth is in the subscription book, and the merchants of {city} have signed to a man. The king, who wears the southern crown as well, has disowned the scheme to please the English Indies company. The Spaniards say the isthmus is theirs.

choice.label: Subscribe heavily
choice.result: Edinburgh calls you a patriot and brings you its accounts, while London marks you as a friend of its rivals.

choice.label: Take a token share
choice.result: Your name is on the book but your capital is not.

choice.label: Stay out
choice.result: Edinburgh's merchants call you an English creature and take their bills elsewhere.

advice.growth: A colony at the hinge of two oceans, with all Scotland behind it. Get in before the book closes.
advice.prudence: A fever coast, no navy, and a company its own king has disowned. Count this money gone.
advice.court: The king has repudiated it to please the English Company. Every subscription will be read in London.
advice.conscience: A nation is pledging its savings to a shipload of hope. Do not urge widows to subscribe.

deck.precedent: The Company of Scotland's Darien scheme, 1695–1700, which absorbed a large share of Scotland's liquid capital and failed
deck.source: Watt, The Price of Scotland: Darien, Union and the Wealth of Nations (2007)

deck.title: The Treasury floats a lottery loan
deck.text: The Treasury is raising a million by selling ten-pound tickets. Every ticket carries an annuity, and the lucky ones carry great prizes. Goldsmiths and booksellers are licensed to sell them, the coffee-houses talk of nothing else, and the distributors keep a fee on every ticket sold.

advice.growth: The public will queue for these, and we take a fee on every one.
advice.prudence: Sell tickets for cash and never on credit. The fever cools once the draw is done.
advice.court: The Treasury rewards its distributors. This is how a goldsmith becomes a Treasury man.
advice.conscience: A lottery is gaming in a public wig. Take the fee, but do not lend anyone money to buy tickets.

deck.precedent: The Million Adventure, the English state lottery loan of 1694
deck.source: Dickson, The Financial Revolution in England (1967)

deck.title: A great return from the Indies
deck.text: The fleet is home with every hull, holds full of pepper, cloves and mace bought for silver at prices the Exchange can hardly credit. The voyage account will pay its adventurers more than double their stake, and every merchant who held a share on your books is suddenly creditworthy beyond question.

advice.growth: Put every penny into the next voyage. Fortune favours the bold, and the bold are buying now.
advice.prudence: A voyage pays like this once in a decade. Bank the gain and raise our reserve.
advice.court: The Company's governors will remember who held their stock through the lean years.
advice.conscience: Spice bought cheap and sold dear is honest trade. Remember the clerks who kept the books.

deck.precedent: The English East India Company's third separate voyage, 1607–10, returned some 234 per cent on its capital
deck.source: Chaudhuri, The English East India Company: The Study of an Early Joint-Stock Company 1600–1640 (1965)

deck.title: A closed empire's silver flows through {city}
deck.text: The island empire has expelled every European nation but one company, and that company is penned on a small artificial island in a single harbour. Through that narrow gate come silver and copper in quantities that remake the whole Asian trade, and the bills now drawn on {city} are the best in the East.

advice.growth: Silver from a closed empire through one counter. Open a correspondent at {city} at once.
advice.prudence: A realm that expelled one nation can expel another. Don't let this trade carry our capital.
advice.court: The Company's directors hand out credit lines to their friends. Make sure we are one of them.
advice.conscience: They say Christians there are made to trample holy images. Profit from such a gate troubles me.

deck.precedent: After the expulsion of the Portuguese in 1639, the VOC was confined to Dejima from 1641 as the only European traders in Japan
deck.source: Israel, Dutch Primacy in World Trade, 1585–1740 (1989)

deck.title: The coast of {city} is cleared by edict
deck.text: To starve a rebel fleet that holds the offshore islands, the new dynasty has ordered the coastal population to move ten miles and more inland. Villages are burned and seaborne trade is forbidden on pain of death. Your correspondents at {city} write that their bills cannot be met until the edict is lifted, and nobody knows when that will be.

advice.growth: The rebels' junks still sail, and the margin on silk has tripled. Lend to the smugglers.
advice.prudence: When an empire burns its own coast, every bill drawn on it is a hope. Shorten our tenors.
advice.court: The new dynasty will win. Whoever waits patiently will be first through the gate when the ports reopen.
advice.conscience: Villages are burning by edict. Let us not profit from contraband with their ruin.

deck.precedent: The Qing coastal evacuation edicts against the Zheng regime, 1661–84
deck.source: Wills, Pepper, Guns and Parleys: The Dutch East India Company and China, 1662–1681 (1974)

deck.title: Enemy ships seized in the ports of {city}
deck.text: The truce has expired and the embargo has fallen. Every ship of the rebel provinces in the harbour of {city} has been seized, with crews gaoled and cargoes inventoried by the admiralty court. Bills drawn against those cargoes are coming back protested, and a new board of inspectors is checking every neutral hull for hidden enemy goods.

rumour.text: Masters in the river are hurrying their lading, and the admiralty's officers have been counting flags on the quay.

advice.growth: Our flag is neutral. Carry their cargoes under ours and charge them double.
advice.prudence: Goods in their ports belong to nobody until the lawyers finish. Value them at nothing.
