advice.court: Their admiralty courts accept petitions with gifts. We could buy back a ship or two.
advice.conscience: Do not swear to a false flag. An oath given falsely before a prize court is perjury.

deck.precedent: Spain's embargo on Dutch shipping when the Twelve Years' Truce expired in 1621, enforced by the Almirantazgo from 1624
deck.source: Israel, The Dutch Republic and the Hispanic World, 1606–1661 (1982)

deck.title: {court} wants silver against the next pepper fleet
deck.text: The crown holds the pepper monopoly but must pay for the spice in Cochin with silver it does not yet have. Its factor proposes an advance repayable from the sale of the next fleet's cargo in Antwerp, with a share of the pepper as security. If the carracks come home, the margin is handsome. If they do not, you own a claim on the sea.

advice.growth: Pepper sells itself in Antwerp; a lien on the fleet is as good as coin in the chest.
advice.prudence: One storm off the Cape and our security lies on the seabed. Take a smaller share.
advice.court: A crown that owes us its spice will remember us when licences are handed out.
advice.conscience: Payment in kind at a fixed price may hide usury; have the contract read as a true purchase.

deck.precedent: Welser, Fugger and Affaitati bought shares in the 1505 India fleet; Portuguese crown pepper contracts were let to German and Italian syndicates, 1505–1590s
deck.source: Hermann Kellenbenz, Die Fugger in Spanien und Portugal bis 1560 (1990)

deck.title: {court} needs silver for wars on two fronts
deck.text: A new conquest has joined two great harbours under one master, and his treasury now pays armies in Persia and on the Danube at once. His agents offer a farm of customs revenues against an advance of silver: high returns, collected by men you have never met, under a law that is not yours.

advice.growth: Whoever holds the customs of the Levant holds the spice road. Bid before the Ragusans do.
advice.prudence: If the Sultan's treasurer changes, so does the farm. Our only remedy would be a petition.
advice.court: The Signoria trades with the Porte but does not love it. Lend, and be discreet about it.
advice.conscience: Lending to the infidel for war on Christians is forbidden outright; no confessor will absolve it.

deck.precedent: Selim I's conquest of Mamluk Egypt, 1516–17; the Porte's revenues were afterwards farmed out (iltizam) against cash advances
deck.source: Halil İnalcık, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age 1300–1600 (1973)

deck.title: A crown is for sale, and {court} must buy it
deck.text: Seven electors will choose the next Emperor, and every one of them has a price. {court} needs a vast sum within weeks, payable to the electors only if the vote goes the right way, and secured on mines, tolls and promises. Win and you are the empire's banker for a generation. That is the opportunity, and it is also the risk.

advice.growth: A house that makes an Emperor is never again a mere lender. Take the whole loan.
advice.prudence: A prince's gratitude is payable at his convenience. This loan is bigger than our capital.
advice.court: Refuse, and his rival's banker will collect the mines, the tolls and the title.
advice.conscience: Bribing electors is simony in all but name. The house's soul is worth more than a mine.

deck.precedent: Charles V's imperial election of 1519, bought with some 850,000 florins, about two-thirds of it lent by Jakob Fugger
deck.source: Mark Häberlein, The Fuggers of Augsburg (2012)

deck.title: {court} stops payment on its asientos
deck.text: A royal decree suspends every short-term contract with the crown's bankers. Arrears are to be converted into perpetual juros at a rate the crown chooses, and the silver already pledged to you is redirected to the army. The bankers will negotiate a settlement because they have no other option. Meanwhile your bills on the crown are worth roughly what a buyer will pay for them.

rumour.text: The treasury has stopped answering letters, and the Genoese are selling juros at the fair below last quarter's price.

advice.growth: Kings never truly default; they reschedule at par. Buy more contracts while the timid sell.
advice.prudence: Every asiento carries a pledge on silver the king can take back. Shorten the book now.
advice.court: Stay at the table. Those who keep lending through the stop are the first paid in the settlement.
advice.conscience: A crown that breaks its word sins; a banker who sold its paper to widows sinned first.

deck.precedent: Philip II's decretos of 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596, converting asientos into juros; France and Portugal also suspended in 1558–60
deck.source: Mauricio Drelichman & Hans-Joachim Voth, Lending to the Borrower from Hell (2014)

deck.title: A Genoese consortium offers a place in {court}'s asiento
deck.text: The Genoese will lend the crown a sum payable in Flanders, repayable in silver from the next fleet at Seville, with interest, exchange and commission all built into the price. They want partners to take a share and spread the risk. The paper settles at the fair, and they have learned to price a stop of payment into the rate. The question is whether you have.

advice.growth: This is the richest business in Christendom, and the Genoese are inviting us in. Nobody will ask twice.
advice.prudence: They keep the safest share and offer us the rest. Ask which silver repays our part.
advice.court: The king remembers who carried his army to Flanders. So do the Genoese, when they hand out shares.
advice.conscience: Interest dressed as exchange is still interest. At least insist the remittance is real.

deck.precedent: Genoese bankers took over Philip II's short-term asientos after the 1557–60 stops, syndicating shares among partners
deck.source: Drelichman & Voth, Lending to the Borrower from Hell (2014)

deck.title: A banco di scritta fails in {city}
deck.text: A giro bank on the piazza had lent depositors' money to the Mint and to its partners' galleys. It closed its doors at noon, and by vespers every depositor in town wanted coin rather than book entries. The magistrates propped the bank once before. They will not do it again, and depositors are now asking the same questions of you.

rumour.text: The banker's cashier was seen at the Mint twice this week, and he has stopped paying out in ducats.

advice.growth: Their depositors need somewhere to go. Open late and take every one of them.
advice.prudence: Fill the till before the bell. A bank that pays in coin all day survives the evening.
advice.court: The Mint will prop any bank on the piazza; it did so last time. We need not hoard.
advice.conscience: Pay small depositors first. The widows' accounts are a debt of honour as well as of law.

deck.precedent: The failure in a run of the Pisani-Tiepolo bank, Venice's last private giro bank, in 1584, after earlier failures such as the Priuli bank's in 1552; the public Banco della Piazza di Rialto followed in 1587
deck.source: Frederic C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: The bankers' fair leaves {city}
deck.text: Politics has turned, and the foreign bankers are no longer welcome where they used to settle their bills four times a year. They will hold their exchange fair in a frontier town under another prince. Bills already drawn on the old city must be rerouted, and the brokers there are already looking for new trades.

advice.growth: The fair matters more than where it sits. Follow the Genoese to Besançon and keep the clearing.
advice.prudence: Settle every open bill on Lyon before the next payment date. Unsettled positions are where we lose money.
advice.court: The French king made this quarrel; side with him and he may give us the fair's privileges.
advice.conscience: A fair held in no place, netting paper against paper, is closer to dry exchange than ever.

deck.precedent: After Genoa joined Charles V in 1528 its bankers lost Lyon, and their exchange fairs reopened at Besançon in 1535
deck.source: Luciano Pezzolo & Giovanni Tattara, 'Una fiera senza luogo', Journal of Economic History (2008)

deck.title: The payments of the fair are postponed
deck.text: The crown, short of silver, orders that the payment days of the great Castilian fair be put off for another season. Every bill payable there is now in limbo. Acceptors will not pay, drawers will not refund, and the notaries are busy protesting bills that nobody can honour.

rumour.text: Letters from Medina say the cambistas have not set the payment day, and nobody will quote on the next fair.

advice.growth: Buy protested bills at a discount. The fair always pays in the end, and we will collect at par.
advice.prudence: Our bills on the fair are not cash. Write them down and keep coin to meet our own acceptances.
advice.court: The crown postponed the fair to pay its soldiers. Complaining will not move the payment day.
advice.conscience: Charging penalty interest on bills delayed by the king's act is damage we did not suffer.

deck.precedent: Castile repeatedly postponed the payments of the Medina del Campo fairs during and after the 1575 suspension, 1575–78
deck.source: Henri Lapeyre, Une famille de marchands: les Ruiz (1955)

deck.title: The coin of {city} is cried down
deck.text: After years of quietly adding copper to the silver, the crown proclaims that its own coin will pass at half its face value from next week. Debtors rush to pay in the old coin before the day, and creditors refuse it. The house's till, half-full of base testoons, has just lost value by royal decree.

rumour.text: The Mint has stopped striking, and the goldsmiths are buying old coin by weight above its tale.

advice.growth: Lend out the base coin before the day; let the borrowers take the loss at repayment.
advice.prudence: Value the till by weight, not tale, and accept nothing at face after this morning.
advice.court: Hold the coin. The crown must honour its own face value or no one will take its money.
advice.conscience: Passing coin you know will be cried down tomorrow is fraud upon your neighbour.

deck.precedent: The English Great Debasement of 1544–51, ended by proclamations crying down the testoon in 1551
deck.source: C. E. Challis, The Tudor Coinage (1978)

deck.title: The treasure fleet is in at {city}
deck.text: The galleons have crossed the bar with a record cargo of registered silver, and the Casa's vaults are full. Merchants are paying debts, bills on Seville are selling at a premium across Europe, and your correspondents' remittances have arrived on time for once.

advice.growth: Silver is cheap and credit is easy. Lend it out before the next fleet makes it cheaper still.
advice.prudence: More silver means higher prices. Our fixed rents and old loans are worth less every year.
advice.court: The king will hear of the fleet too. Expect a request before the silver leaves Seville.
advice.conscience: Give thanks and pay your debts. Riches from the mines of the Indies carry their own reckoning.

deck.precedent: Registered American bullion arriving at Seville peaked in the 1590s, the decade's remittances the highest of the century
deck.source: Earl J. Hamilton, American Treasure and the Price Revolution in Spain, 1501–1650 (1934)

deck.title: The crown sequesters the merchants' silver
deck.text: The fleet came in, but before the silver reached its owners the crown's officers took the private consignments 'by way of loan' for the war. The owners will receive juros at a modest rate, eventually. Your correspondents in Seville cannot cover the bills you drew on them.

rumour.text: The officials of the Casa are counting chests by night, and the asentistas have gone to court.

advice.growth: Buy the juros they hand out at a discount; the crown always pays the interest eventually.
advice.prudence: Never draw on silver still at sea or in the Casa. It belongs to us only once it is in our vault.
advice.court: It is a loan, not a theft; the Emperor gives juros. Protest quietly and be paid first.
advice.conscience: Taking a subject's goods without consent is against natural law, whatever the paper calls it.

deck.precedent: Charles V's seizures of private American bullion at Seville, notably 1523, 1535, 1553 and 1556, repaid in juros
deck.source: Ramón Carande, Carlos V y sus banqueros (1943–67)

deck.title: A prince detains the bankers' pay-ships
deck.text: Ships carrying a syndicate's silver to pay an army sheltered from privateers in a foreign port, and the local queen has decided to 'borrow' the money herself. Embargo and counter-embargo follow, and the wool and cloth trade with the Low Countries stops overnight. The lenders, who meant to finance only one side of the quarrel, now find themselves creditors of both.

rumour.text: Sailors in Southampton say the bullion hulks are being unloaded under the Queen's guard.

advice.growth: England needs the Antwerp trade; she will release the silver within a week. Keep shipping.
advice.prudence: Silver crossing the Channel belongs to whoever controls the harbour. Insure it or route it overland.
advice.court: Approach the Queen's secretary through her own merchants; she may repay us as a lender after all.
advice.conscience: We cannot blame a prince for seizing money sent to pay soldiers in an unjust war.

deck.precedent: Elizabeth I's seizure of Genoese bullion bound for Alba's army, December 1568, and the Anglo-Netherlands embargo of 1569–73
deck.source: G. D. Ramsay, The Queen's Merchants and the Revolt of the Netherlands (1986)

deck.title: The house's governors overseas go their own way
deck.text: The crown granted the house a province beyond the ocean in payment of debts, and the house sent out its own men to run it. They have spent its capital on expeditions in search of a golden city, chained the natives to work, and quarrelled with the crown's officials. Letters take six months to arrive, and the news in them is worse each time.

advice.growth: One find of gold repays everything. Send another ship with more men and more credit.
advice.prudence: We cannot steer from six months away. Cut what they may draw on us and recall the governor.
advice.court: The Council of the Indies wants an excuse to revoke the grant. Do not give it one.
advice.conscience: The friars report enslavement. A house that profits from it shares the sin.

deck.precedent: The Welser company's Venezuela concession, 1528–46, ended in failed El Dorado expeditions and the murder of its governor
deck.source: Jörg Denzer, Die Konquista der Augsburger Welser-Gesellschaft (2005)

deck.title: A syndicate invites you into a corner
deck.text: A great merchant of the city is buying up every flask of quicksilver in Europe and wants your money to hold the stock until the price doubles. The Diet's commissioners are already petitioning against monopolies, and the man's depositors include half the town's servants. Last week he offered them five per cent.

choice.label: Buy into the ring
choice.result: The corner pays for two seasons, and the town knows exactly whose money held up the price.

choice.label: Lend against the stock, with a margin
choice.result: You earn a modest fee and keep a lien on the flasks in case he fails.

choice.label: Decline and say so on the exchange
choice.result: When his credit wobbles, cautious depositors move their money to you.

advice.growth: Corners have made the great Augsburg houses. A share now costs less than regret later.
advice.prudence: A corner needs every flask in Europe. One new mine and he is selling at any price.
advice.court: The Emperor protects the great companies against the Diet. He wants their loans more than their virtue.
advice.conscience: Monopoly that raises the price of necessities is condemned by every doctor of the Church.

deck.precedent: Ambrosius Höchstetter's attempted quicksilver corner collapsed in 1529, after the anti-monopoly agitation at the Nuremberg Diets of 1522–24
deck.source: Mark Häberlein, The Fuggers of Augsburg (2012)

deck.title: The plague returns to {city}
deck.text: The health office has closed the gates and burned the bedding, and the lazaretto is full. Nobles and merchants have fled to the countryside, and their debts went with them. The counting house operates with half its clerks, and nobody dares accept a letter that came from the infected quarter.

rumour.text: The Provveditori alla Sanità have ordered a house in the parish sealed, and the fishermen talk of fever.

advice.growth: Plague is a disease of the poor quarters; trade carries on. Keep the bank open and lending.
advice.prudence: Call in loans to anyone likely to flee, and keep coin for those who stay and need it.
advice.court: The magistrates will need loans for the lazaretto. Be first to offer and they will remember it.
advice.conscience: The dying want their wills drawn and their debts forgiven. Do not press heirs this season.

deck.precedent: The Venetian plague of 1575–77, which killed roughly a third of the city
deck.source: Paolo Preto, Peste e società a Venezia nel 1576 (1978)

deck.title: Famine: {court} asks you to finance northern grain
deck.text: Two harvests have failed, and the poor are eating bread made with chaff. Baltic grain ships could reach the harbour in six weeks if someone pays the Dutch skippers in advance. The government asks the house to advance the money. Hoarders are already being hanged in the square.

choice.label: Lend to the government at cost
choice.result: The grain arrives, the government is grateful, and the money comes back slowly at almost no interest.

choice.label: Charter the ships on your own account
choice.result: You sell the grain at famine prices and profit, and the crowd shouts your name at the bakers' doors.

choice.label: Refuse; the house is not a granary
choice.result: Others find the money, and the government notes who did not.

advice.growth: Grain bought in Danzig for one ducat sells here for four. This is the trade of the decade.
advice.prudence: An advance to skippers we do not know, for grain we have not seen, is a gamble. Lend to the state.
advice.court: Governments remember who fed them in a famine. They also remember who profited from it.
advice.conscience: To profit from a neighbour's hunger is the very sin the canonists name. Lend at cost.

deck.precedent: The Italian famine of 1590–91, relieved by Baltic grain shipped by Dutch and Hanseatic carriers to Livorno, Genoa and Venice
deck.source: Fernand Braudel, The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II (English trans. 1972; French orig. 1949)

deck.title: Rome condemns the dry exchange
deck.text: A papal bull declares that an exchange bill drawn to a fair and redrawn back, with no real remittance, is usury in disguise, and confessors must refuse absolution to those who deal in it. Your ricorsa business, a quarter of the profit, is exactly that. The doctors at Salamanca are already debating which bills still pass.

choice.label: Unwind the ricorsa bills
choice.result: You lose a profitable line of business, and your confessor and the magistrates approve.

choice.label: Keep them, with a friendly theologian's opinion
choice.result: The profits continue, and so do the sermons about you.

choice.label: Route them through a correspondent at the Genoese fair
choice.result: The business moves offshore, and with it some control over who signs in your name.

advice.growth: Every banker in Europe redraws bills. The Pope cannot excommunicate the whole Piazza.
advice.prudence: Ricorsa credit is short money that rolls each fair. Shrinking it lowers our leverage anyway.
advice.court: The Signoria guards its bankers against Rome. Let the state's lawyers answer the bull.
advice.conscience: A bill with no real remittance is a loan at interest. The bull only says what the doctors always said.

deck.precedent: Pius V's bull In eam pro nostro, 28 January 1571, condemning cambium siccum (dry exchange)
deck.source: John T. Noonan, The Scholastic Analysis of Usury (1957)

deck.title: All {city} wants a piece of the king's loan
deck.text: The king's consolidated loan pays four per cent each fair, sixteen a year, and the subscription has become a fashion. Bankers, notaries, widows and servants are queuing to get in. Your depositors ask whether the house will subscribe, sell them shares, or explain why it does neither.

choice.label: Subscribe heavily for the house
choice.result: The crown's paper sits on your books at sixteen per cent, for as long as the crown keeps paying.

choice.label: Broker shares to your depositors
choice.result: You collect the commission, and your name is on paper that small savers will not forget.

choice.label: Stay out
choice.result: You miss the boom, and the king's treasurer crosses you off his list.

advice.growth: A king paying four per cent a fair, with all Lyon behind him, cannot fail. Subscribe the limit.
advice.prudence: When servants are buying a crown's debt, it is time to sell it, not to buy more.
advice.court: The king's treasurer counts who subscribes. Silence costs us the next licence.
advice.conscience: Selling the poor a loan you would not hold yourself is not commerce. It is a snare.

deck.precedent: The Grand Parti de Lyon, 1555, subscribed by bankers and small savers at 16%, suspended by the French crown in 1557–59
deck.source: Roger Doucet, 'Le Grand Parti de Lyon au XVIe siècle', Revue historique (1933)

deck.title: {court}'s agent on the Bourse wants a loan
deck.text: The crown keeps a factor on the Antwerp Bourse who borrows short, rolls the debt each quarter, and nudges the exchange rate in his master's favour. He proposes a year's loan at the going rate on the crown's bond, countersigned by the City of London. He pays on the day, and he will want to see what you know about the exchange.

advice.growth: A punctual crown at twelve per cent is a better borrower than any duke in Flanders. Take it.
advice.prudence: He pays because he can roll the debt. If the Bourse shuts, he pays nobody.
advice.court: This agent has the ear of the Council. Lending to him is cheaper than buying a pension.
advice.conscience: A bond at fixed interest is plain usury, whatever the Bourse calls it. Confess it, at least.

deck.precedent: Thomas Gresham's borrowing on the Antwerp Bourse as royal agent for Edward VI, Mary and Elizabeth, 1551–74
deck.source: Raymond de Roover, Gresham on Foreign Exchange (1949)

deck.title: {court} levies a forced loan for the war
deck.text: The armies are in the field, and the treasury is empty. Every house in the city is assessed on its estimated wealth and must lend to the state at a nominal interest the state will pay when it can. The assessors have a good idea how large your deposits are.

advice.growth: Pay it gracefully; a seat on the war committee is worth the coupon we lose.
advice.prudence: Each forced loan comes with a promise that the next will be smaller. Keep the till full.
advice.court: Pay early and in full. The city remembers who haggled when the enemy was at the gates.
advice.conscience: Interest from the state's own levy is lawful: the loan is compelled, not sought.

deck.precedent: Venice's forced loans after the defeat at Agnadello, 1509; Florence's accatti during the siege of 1529–30
deck.source: Luciano Pezzolo, 'The Venetian government debt, 1350–1650', in Urban Public Debts (2003)

deck.title: Unpaid soldiers sack {city}
deck.text: An army that has gone months without pay has broken discipline and stormed the walls. For a week they hold merchants for ransom, burn ledgers for warmth and torture cashiers for the keys. When the officers regain control, there is little left to lend against and nobody left to lend to.

rumour.text: The landsknechts have not been paid since spring, and their captains no longer answer to the general.

advice.growth: Armies always threaten and never sack. Keep the branch open; panic sells, and we buy.
advice.prudence: Send the coin and the ledgers to the country tonight. Buildings can be rebuilt; accounts cannot.
advice.court: The Emperor's soldiers would never sack a Christian capital. His honour forbids it.
advice.conscience: Pray, and open the chapel to the townsfolk. Mercy now will be remembered after.

deck.precedent: The Sack of Rome by the unpaid imperial army, May 1527
deck.source: Judith Hook, The Sack of Rome, 1527 (1972)

deck.title: A great house in {city} fails; its clients come to you
deck.text: An old rival over-lent to princes and to its own partners, and its balance shows more debts than assets. Its creditors have gone to the magistrates, its factors are looking for employment, and its best merchant clients are standing in your hall with their bills in hand.

advice.growth: Hire their factors, take their clients, and buy their good debts at forty per cent.
advice.prudence: Their clients' bills come with their clients' habits. Check each name before we accept it.
advice.court: The magistrates want an orderly liquidation. Offer to act as receiver; it pays and it pleases.
advice.conscience: Do not exult at a neighbour's ruin. His widow will need someone honest to settle the estate.

deck.precedent: The failures of the Manlich and Haug-Langnauer firms of Augsburg, 1573–74
deck.source: Mark Häberlein, Brüder, Freunde und Betrüger (1998)

deck.title: Riot and image-breaking in {city}
deck.text: After a hedge-preacher's sermon, crowds have stripped the churches bare and smashed altars and statues. The regent's troops are marching, the Calvinist merchants are packing their books, and nobody will discount a bill until they know which faith will rule the city next season.

rumour.text: Field preachers drew thousands outside the walls on Sunday, and the guilds are arming.

advice.growth: Merchants leaving need cash for their goods. Buy their stock at half and be patient.
advice.prudence: Move the deposits of the anxious to a safer correspondent before the regent's army arrives.
advice.court: The regent will punish the city and reward the loyal. Lend him money for his troops.
advice.conscience: Heresy breeds disorder. Yet the men who fled are clients; we owe them honest accounts.

deck.precedent: The Beeldenstorm, which reached Antwerp in August 1566, followed by Alba's repression from 1567
deck.source: Peter Arnade, Beggars, Iconoclasts, and Civic Patriots (2008)

deck.title: The Inquisitors ask about a New Christian's deposits
deck.text: One of your largest depositors, a converso spice merchant, is accused of secretly practising Judaism. The crown's officers demand his balances and his correspondence. His family asks you to remit what is left to a correspondent in Ferrara before the order is served. Both sides will remember what you do.

choice.label: Surrender the balances
choice.result: The crown is satisfied, and every converso merchant in Europe moves his account elsewhere.

choice.label: Remit the funds quietly before the order
choice.result: The family is saved, the network trusts you, and the crown suspects what you did.

choice.label: Plead that the books are in another city
choice.result: You gain a season, at the cost of a little goodwill everywhere.

advice.growth: The converso network carries half the spice trade. Lose their trust and we lose Lisbon.
advice.prudence: Disobeying the crown in its own city puts every partner here in its prisons.
advice.court: Comply fully. The crown rewards obedience and never forgets a banker who hid a heretic.
advice.conscience: A depositor's money is a trust. The officers want his wealth, not his soul.

deck.precedent: Diogo Mendes's arrest in Antwerp on charges of Judaizing, 1532, and the Mendes house's flight with its capital, 1545
deck.source: Cecil Roth, Doña Gracia of the House of Nasi (1948)

deck.title: Silver finds a road to the East
deck.text: A trading post on the China coast now sends a great ship each year to Japan, carrying silk outward and bringing silver back. The Chinese price silver higher than any mint in Europe, and the factors of Goa can buy for less what the Cantonese will pay dearly for.

advice.growth: Silver bought cheap in Japan, sold dear in Canton. Open a correspondent in Macao now.
advice.prudence: A voyage of three years and one carrack a season. One loss would wipe out the margin.
advice.court: The Portuguese crown licenses the voyage. Lend to the captain-major and buy a place.
advice.conscience: The Jesuits are in Japan; a share for the mission would bless the cargo.

deck.precedent: The Portuguese settlement at Macao, 1557, and the Macao–Nagasaki great ship trade from 1571
deck.source: C. R. Boxer, The Great Ship from Amacon (1959)

deck.title: {court} settles with its bankers
deck.text: After two years of empty fairs, the crown and its creditors have signed a general settlement. Arrears are paid partly in juros, partly in licences to export silver, and the bankers resume lending to the crown. It is less than you were owed, but more than you had written off.

advice.growth: The settlement proves the crown pays in the end. Take a full share of the new asiento.
advice.prudence: Sell the juros while the settlement is news; they will be worth less after the next stop.
advice.court: The crown is grateful to those who signed without fuss. Sign and offer a new advance.
advice.conscience: Accept what is fairly offered. Squeezing a king in his weakness is its own sin.

deck.precedent: The medio general of December 1577 ending Philip II's 1575 suspension; similar settlements in 1560 and 1597
deck.source: A. W. Lovett, 'The General Settlement of 1577', Historical Journal (1980)

deck.title: {court} offers a revenue farm in pledge
deck.text: In place of cash, the crown offers a lease on the revenues of the military orders, with the right to work their quicksilver mine as well. You will collect rents from shepherds in three provinces, run a mine worked by forced labour, and repay yourself out of the proceeds. The crown counts this as its debt repaid. You will find the business harder than that.

advice.growth: A pledge we collect ourselves beats a king's promise. Mines and rents do not stop payment.
advice.prudence: We are bankers, not stewards. Collecting from shepherds costs more than the interest.
advice.court: The crown will steer the profit of the farm through its own accountants. Lease it anyway.
advice.conscience: Revenue farming is lawful commerce, not usury. The forced labourers in the mine are another matter.

deck.precedent: The Fugger lease of the maestrazgos, the revenues of the Spanish military orders, with the Almadén mines, from 1525
deck.source: Hermann Kellenbenz, Die Fugger in Spanien und Portugal bis 1560 (1990)

deck.title: {court} seizes the mines pledged to the house
deck.text: Miners rioted over wages paid in debased coin, and the nobles of the diet blamed the foreign bankers. The court has confiscated the mines pledged for its loans, arrested the factors, and declared the house's contract void. The mines can perhaps be bought back, at a price.

advice.growth: The court cannot run the mines without us. Wait; they will beg us back within the year.
advice.prudence: A pledge of land and mines is worth what the lord of that land allows. Lend less there.
advice.court: Ask the Emperor to intercede with his brother-in-law. Royal pressure recovers what lawsuits cannot.
advice.conscience: Wages paid in base coin to miners were wrong. Settle with them and the anger fades.

deck.precedent: The Hungarian diet's confiscation of the Fugger mines at Neusohl (Banská Bystrica) after the miners' revolt, 1525
deck.source: Mark Häberlein, The Fuggers of Augsburg (2012)

deck.title: War with the Sultan closes the Levant
deck.text: An Ottoman fleet has landed on a Venetian island, the Republic has seized Turkish goods on the Rialto, and the Sultan has seized Venetian ones in his ports. Ships in Alexandria are held, factors are imprisoned, and every bill drawn on the Levant comes back protested.

rumour.text: The bailo's letters speak of an arsenal working by night at Galata, and grain buyers have left Alexandria.

advice.growth: War pushes up the price of spice. Our stock in Venice is worth half again what it was.
advice.prudence: Write off the factors' balances in Alexandria today, and hope to be pleasantly surprised.
advice.court: The Republic will keep peace with the Sultan, as always. This is a squall; keep trading.
advice.conscience: Ransom the imprisoned factors before the goods. Christian men come before pepper.

deck.precedent: The Ottoman–Venetian war of 1570–73 and the loss of Cyprus, with Venetian goods seized in Ottoman ports
deck.source: Frederic C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: Pepper returns by the Red Sea
deck.text: Portuguese patrols cannot close the Red Sea, and Gujarati and Acehnese ships are bringing spice to Jeddah again. Caravans to Cairo are full, the bazaars of Alexandria are busy, and the Venetian galleys are loading pepper for the first time in years.

advice.growth: The old spice road is open again. Reopen the Alexandria account with full credit.
advice.prudence: A revival that depends on the Portuguese being weak lasts until the Portuguese grow strong.
advice.court: The Signoria will reward bankers who finance the galleys. Subscribe to the convoy.
advice.conscience: Fair trade with Muslim merchants in pepper is allowed. Selling them arms is not.

deck.precedent: The revival of the Red Sea spice route to Alexandria and Venice in the 1540s–1560s
deck.source: Frederic C. Lane, 'The Mediterranean Spice Trade', American Historical Review (1940)

deck.title: {court} offers a title for a cheap loan
deck.text: The prince offers to make the senior partner a count, with arms, lands and the right to coin money, in return for a large loan at well below the market rate. The house would rank alongside princes. Its merchant clients would wonder whether it still keeps their accounts or the prince's.

choice.label: Accept the title and the cheap loan
choice.result: The house is ennobled and its capital is locked in a prince's debt at four per cent.

choice.label: Lend at the full rate, no title
choice.result: The prince borrows, sulks, and pays market price.

choice.label: Decline politely
choice.result: You remain merchants, and the court notes who refused its honours.

advice.growth: A count's son marries a duke's daughter. That marriage is worth more than any coupon.
advice.prudence: Titles do not pay interest. Four per cent from a prince is a loss with a coat of arms.
advice.court: Ennoblement puts us in the room where loans and licences are decided. Accept with gratitude.
advice.conscience: Honours bought with money tempt pride, but a cheap loan at least is not usurious.

deck.precedent: Jakob Fugger's ennoblement in 1511 and elevation to Imperial Count in 1514, amid lending to Maximilian I
deck.source: Mark Häberlein, The Fuggers of Augsburg (2012)

deck.title: A laden carrack is lost off the Cape
deck.text: News arrives by a later ship. The carrack carrying the house's shipment was overloaded, sailed late in the season, and broke up on a southern African shore. Survivors are walking north through the bush. The underwriters on the Bourse dispute the policy, and the factor's pepper is lost.

advice.growth: One lost carrack makes the survivors' cargo worth more. Our next shipment will sell dear.
advice.prudence: Never put more than a tenth of a factor's goods in one hull. Spread it across three ships.
advice.court: The crown will blame the captain, not the overloading. Do not expect compensation.
advice.conscience: Pay masses for the drowned and settle with the sailors' widows before the underwriters.

deck.precedent: The wreck of the São João on the Natal coast, 1552, on the homeward Carreira da Índia
deck.source: Bernardo Gomes de Brito (comp.), História Trágico-Marítima (1735–36)

deck.title: A royal ransom passes through your hands
deck.text: Two kings have made peace, and one must pay a vast sum in gold to recover his sons, who are hostages. The money must be assembled from across a kingdom, counted, checked for clipping, and handed over at a river crossing. You are hired to collect and assay it, and you charge a commission on every crown.

advice.growth: Fees on a fortune, with no capital at risk. Bid low for the mandate and charge for the assay.
advice.prudence: Counted gold on a frontier road attracts thieves. Insure every chest before it moves.
advice.court: Both crowns will watch who handles this honestly. A good reputation here is worth the fee.
advice.conscience: Fees for honest labour are lawful. Do not shave a single crown, even for weighing.

deck.precedent: The 1.2 million gold écus paid at the Bidassoa in 1530, under the Peace of Cambrai, to ransom Francis I's sons
deck.source: R. J. Knecht, Renaissance Warrior and Patron: The Reign of Francis I (1994)

deck.title: The Genoese offer you a seat at the fair
deck.text: The fair's consuls have voted to admit your house among the bankers who fix the conto, the fair's exchange rates, and net their bills in the fair's balance books. You will clear huge sums with almost no coin and see every flow of the European exchanges as it happens. In return you must honour your bills on the payment day, whatever happens.

advice.growth: Inside the conto we see the rates first. That is worth more than any single asiento.
advice.prudence: Netting looks safe until a member fails. Then every bill we cleared is owed again.
advice.court: The Genoese are the King's bankers. Sitting beside them brings us closer to his business.
advice.conscience: A fair with real bills settled honestly is lawful exchange. Keep it that way.

deck.precedent: The Genoese exchange fairs of Besançon and from 1579 Piacenza, where some sixty banchieri di conto fixed rates and cleared bills
deck.source: Luciano Pezzolo & Giovanni Tattara, 'Una fiera senza luogo', Journal of Economic History (2008)

deck.title: {court} offers the wool customs as security
deck.text: The king's wardrobe clerk calls with a proposal: advance coin now, and the house will collect the customs on wool and hides at every port until repaid. The last Italians to hold this farm grew rich and were then thrown out by the barons. Interest will be paid as 'gifts' and compensation for delay.

advice.growth: The customs are the surest revenue in Christendom, and we collect them ourselves. Take the farm before the Lucchesi do.
advice.prudence: A farm held at a king's pleasure ends at his barons' displeasure. Lend only what the wool repays in two years.
advice.court: Hold the customs and the king needs us; refuse, and another house holds him, and our licences with him.
advice.conscience: Call it gift and damages if you must; a fixed return on a loan is still usury before God.

deck.precedent: The Frescobaldi farmed the English customs for Edward I and Edward II, 1299–1311, and were expelled under the Ordinances of 1311; the Riccardi of Lucca had been seized in 1294
deck.source: R. W. Kaeuper, 'The Frescobaldi of Florence and the English Crown', Studies in Medieval and Renaissance History 10 (1973)

deck.title: A king at war: {court} wants more than ever
deck.text: Heralds have gone out, the host is mustering, and the allies across the sea want their subsidies in advance. {court} asks the house to fund the campaign against future customs and a promise of the realm's wool. The sum is larger than any prince has borrowed, the rate generous, the security a parchment.

rumour.text: Purveyors are buying ships, and the king's envoys dine every night with the Florentines.

advice.growth: The greatest loan in Christendom at a fat rate. Whoever leads it leads the age.
advice.prudence: War loans are repaid by victory, and victories are slow and dear. Lend a slice, never the house.
advice.court: A king who wins pays double, and this king cannot lose; his archers are the terror of every field.
advice.conscience: Lending for Christian blood at interest compounds two sins. At least refuse to fund the foreign subsidies.

deck.precedent: The Bardi and Peruzzi advanced Edward III vast sums against the wool customs to open the Hundred Years' War, 1337–40
deck.source: E. S. Hunt, The Medieval Super-Companies: A Study of the Peruzzi Company of Florence (1994)

deck.title: Benches stop paying in {city}
deck.text: Pepper bought on the bankers' own account has fallen a third since the galleys came in, and copper with it. One bench closes its book; next morning there is a crowd at every other. The Commune will audit the wreck and jail the banker. It will not pay the depositors.

rumour.text: A banker was seen selling his wife's plate at the goldsmiths' this morning.

advice.growth: Their failure is our harvest. Buy their pepper cheap with our depositors' coin and wait for the price to return.
advice.prudence: Fill the till, call in merchant loans as they fall due, and sell our spices before the crowd reaches us.
advice.court: Show the Signori an orderly book. When they audit the fallen, they will remember who was sound.
advice.conscience: A deposit is a trust. Pay every depositor who asks, even at a loss.

deck.precedent: Repeated Rialto bank failures in the 14th century, after bankers lent deposits into commodity ventures on their own account; in 1374 the Senate barred bankers from trading in copper, tin, iron, lead, saffron and honey
deck.source: R. C. Mueller, The Venetian Money Market: Banks, Panics, and the Public Debt, 1200–1500 (1997); F. C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: {court} stops payment
deck.text: The king's receivers no longer honour assignments on the customs; the tallies they hand over are good only at an exchequer with nothing in it. Promises to pay from next year's subsidy are offered instead. The house holds the paper and is learning what it is worth.

rumour.text: The king's treasurer has been replaced, and the new man wants to see the creditors' accounts again.

advice.growth: Kings always pay in the end. Buy the other creditors' claims at a quarter and wait for the peace.
advice.prudence: Write the loan down now, tell no one how far, and keep coin ready for depositors who will hear.
advice.court: Petition humbly for assignments on another revenue. Quarrelling with a king only moves us down the queue.
advice.conscience: The interest we hid as gifts is lost first. Perhaps that is the lesson.

deck.precedent: Edward III's failure to repay ruined the Peruzzi (1343) and the Bardi (1346); Villani's figures of 600,000 and 900,000 florins are thought inflated by Hunt
deck.source: E. S. Hunt, The Medieval Super-Companies (1994); G. Villani, Nuova Cronica, ed. G. Porta (1990–91), bk XIII

deck.title: The greatest company in Christendom stops
deck.text: Its partners sit in the Commune's debtors' prison, and its factors are fleeing creditors from London to Naples. Depositors do not read ledgers; they read faces. By noon every company that keeps a bench, sound or not, has a line at its counter.

rumour.text: A clerk of the great company was seen burning letters in the courtyard.

advice.growth: Their clients need a new house tomorrow. Stay open late and greet them warmly.
advice.prudence: Pay quickly and visibly. Stack coin on the counter where the queue can see it.
advice.court: Lend the Signoria a little now. A commune that owes us keeps its bailiffs off our door.
advice.conscience: Speak no ill of the fallen in the piazza; our own book holds the same kings.

deck.precedent: The Florentine crash of 1342–46: the Acciaiuoli (1345) and the Bardi (1346) followed the Peruzzi (1343) and a string of smaller companies
deck.source: A. Sapori, La crisi delle compagnie mercantili dei Bardi e dei Peruzzi (1926); Hunt (1994)

deck.title: {court} levies a forced loan
deck.text: An enemy fleet is off the coast, and the councils have voted a levy on every estate, assessed on the tax rolls. The house's share is set by men who can count its deposits better than it would like. Payment is in coin by Friday. The claim will be written into the public debt at a rate the Commune chose.

rumour.text: The assessors have had the estimo books open late into the night.

advice.growth: Pay up, then buy public-debt shares cheap from widows who must sell to meet their own levies.
advice.prudence: It is coin out of the till. Call in short loans now, before the levy falls due.
advice.court: Pay early and in full. The house that lends in the Republic's worst hour keeps its bench afterwards.
advice.conscience: A citizen's loan to his city is no usury; most friars allow the Monte's interest.

deck.precedent: The War of Chioggia, 1378–81: repeated Venetian prestiti assessed on the estimo, and a collapse in the price of Monte shares (the fund later called the Monte Vecchio)
deck.source: G. Luzzatto, Il debito pubblico della Repubblica di Venezia (1963); F. C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: The prince's mint debases the coin
deck.text: To pay for war the prince's mints strike more pennies from each mark of silver, and his coin buys a third less than at Easter. Debts owed in it shrink; rents in it vanish. Worse may follow. When the prince returns to strong money, every debtor owes a third more and the city riots.

advice.growth: Weak money is good for debtors. Borrow in the prince's pennies now and repay in lighter ones.
advice.prudence: Keep our books in florins and ducats, and lend nothing in the prince's pennies until his mint settles.
advice.court: The mint-masters pay a premium for bullion. Sell them silver and earn the prince's thanks.
advice.conscience: A prince who debases steals from widows. We need not help him melt their pennies.

deck.precedent: Philip IV's debasements of the French coinage, 1295–1305, and the return to strong money in 1306 that set Paris rioting; the Flemish counts' repeated debasements under Louis of Male, 1350s–1380s
deck.source: P. Spufford, Money and its Use in Medieval Europe (1988)

deck.title: Italians arrested in {city}
deck.text: At dawn the bailiffs seal every Italian counting house in {city}, take the factors to the castle and cart off the ledgers to be searched for usury. Release will come on payment of a fine set at what the crown supposes the house can bear. Debtors in the town have stopped paying until the matter is settled.

rumour.text: The royal bailiffs are asking innkeepers which foreign lodgers keep strongboxes.

advice.growth: Pay the fine quickly. The business here is worth ten fines, and expulsions never last.
advice.prudence: This is why the branch stays thin: little coin there, the accounts here, and a factor told to settle fast.
advice.court: A gift to the queen's household before the fine is set will shrink it. Send it today.
advice.conscience: If the ledgers show interest plainly, the charge is just. Keep cleaner books.

deck.precedent: Philip IV's arrest of Italian merchants throughout France on 1 May 1291, released against heavy fines; the Riccardi seized by Edward I, 1294
deck.source: J. R. Strayer, The Reign of Philip the Fair (1980); R. W. Kaeuper, Bankers to the Crown: The Riccardi of Lucca and Edward I (1973)

deck.title: The Apostolic Camera seeks a depositary
deck.text: The papal chamberlain needs a company to receive the tithes and annates gathered by collectors from Poland to Portugal, and to move them to the curia by letter of exchange. There is no rate, only the float, the exchange profit and the Church's favour. The Camera will also expect advances when the collectors are late.

advice.growth: The Church's money from every diocese passing through our ledger. Accept before the Alberti hear.
advice.prudence: The float is pleasant until the Pope wants an advance against Hungarian tithes that never arrive.
advice.court: No court protects its bankers like the curia. Its excommunications collect our debts for us.
advice.conscience: Serving the Holy Father is no sin. See that the exchange profits are honest exchange.

deck.precedent: Florentine companies (Bardi, Peruzzi, Acciaiuoli, later Alberti) served as depositaries and transfer agents of the Apostolic Camera at Avignon, 1316–78
deck.source: Y. Renouard, Les relations des papes d'Avignon et des compagnies commerciales et bancaires de 1316 à 1378 (1941)

deck.title: {city} laid under interdict
deck.text: A quarrel over a papal city has ended in a bull. The churches of {city} are shut, its citizens excommunicate, and every Christian prince is licensed to seize their goods and persons. Factors abroad are hiding ledgers with friendly hosts. Debtors abroad discover that paying the house is suddenly unlawful.

rumour.text: The papal legate rode out of the city this morning without giving his blessing.

advice.growth: Put the foreign accounts in our partners' names and keep trading. Seizures fall on the careless.
advice.prudence: Bring coin home before the princes take it, and expect every foreign debt to go unpaid.
advice.court: The Republic will not yield, and Rome cannot touch us. Seizures abroad will be trifling.
advice.conscience: Excommunicates die unshriven. Press the Signoria for peace, whatever it costs.

deck.precedent: Clement V's interdict on Venice over Ferrara, 1309–13, licensing seizure of Venetian goods abroad; Gregory XI's interdict on Florence in the War of the Eight Saints, 1376–78
deck.source: R. C. Trexler, The Spiritual Power: Republican Florence under Interdict (1974)

deck.title: A dying partner's confessor demands restitution
deck.text: The old partner is failing, and his confessor will not absolve him until his usuries are restored: to the borrowers if they can be found, to the poor if not. The friar has a list. The heirs have a lawyer. The town is watching to see whether the house's money is clean enough to bury him in consecrated ground.

choice.label: Restore in full and build a chapel
choice.result: The house pays heavily, and a painted chapel tells the city it has made its peace.

choice.label: A bequest to the poor, nothing admitted
choice.result: A modest gift to the hospital buys absolution without confessing what the ledgers mean.

choice.label: Refuse the friar
choice.result: The partner dies unabsolved, preachers name the house from the pulpit, and some clients cross the street.

advice.growth: A token to the hospital will do. Full restitution would publish our whole book of exchange.
advice.prudence: Restitution drains capital we need. Settle quietly with the friar for a fixed sum.
advice.court: The Signori fear scandal more than usury. Whatever you choose, keep it out of the pulpits.
advice.conscience: His soul outweighs the till. Restore what was taken, all of it.

deck.precedent: The Scrovegni Chapel in Padua (1303–05), built by a banker's son and long read as expiation for his family's usury
deck.source: A. Derbes and M. Sandona, The Usurer's Heart: Giotto, Enrico Scrovegni, and the Arena Chapel in Padua (2008)

deck.title: A bill comes back protested from {city}
deck.text: The house bought a bill drawn on a merchant in {city}. On presentation he refused to accept it, and a notary has drawn up the protest. The money comes back only through the drawer, with re-exchange and costs, if the drawer still exists. Meanwhile correspondents ask, politely, which other bad names sit in the house's portfolio.

advice.growth: One bad bill in a hundred is the price of the trade. Buy more, from better drawers.
advice.prudence: Know every drawer and acceptor. Buy no bill where both names lean on the same galley.
advice.court: Have the merchants' consuls enforce the re-exchange swiftly. Quick justice is reputation.
advice.conscience: Re-exchange is lawful damages, not interest. Claim only what was truly lost.

deck.precedent: Bills returned under notarial protest, with re-exchange claimed, in the correspondence of the Datini companies, 1380s–1400
deck.source: R. de Roover, L'évolution de la lettre de change, XIVe–XVIIIe siècles (1953)

deck.title: The factor in {city} has been keeping two books
deck.text: Letters from {city} have been cheerful for three years. A visiting partner has now found a second ledger: loans to the factor's in-laws, cloth bought from his own shop at double the price, and profits remitted that were never earned. The factor says the losses are temporary. The articles say he owes them personally. He owns a mule.

rumour.text: A merchant back from abroad says our factor has built himself a fine stone house.

advice.growth: He holds the best clients in the town. Fine him, keep him, and send a second man to watch.
advice.prudence: Recall him, audit every account, and from now on rotate factors every three years.
advice.court: The local lord will arrest him for us, for a fee. Use his court, not our own men.
advice.conscience: Mercy for a penitent, yes. But the depositors trusted their money to us, not to him.

deck.precedent: Medici branch managers in London and Bruges overlent and concealed losses from Florence, 1460s–1478; the agency problem is as old as the foreign branch
deck.source: R. de Roover, The Rise and Decline of the Medici Bank, 1397–1494 (1963)

deck.title: The convoy for {city} is lost
deck.text: A fast boat brings the news. The convoy bound for {city} met an enemy fleet off the Morea, and half the galleys are taken with their silver and cloth. Few were insured. The house's merchants financed their shares on its credit and now owe for goods that will never be sold.

rumour.text: Sailors in the taverns say an enemy fleet slipped past the guard at the straits.

advice.growth: Cargo that does arrive will fetch double. Lend on the survivors' goods.
advice.prudence: Never let more than a fifth of the book ride one convoy, and insure the rest.
advice.court: The Republic will arm a fleet of vengeance and want money. Offer before it is demanded.
advice.conscience: Do not press the widows of drowned crews for their husbands' notes.

deck.precedent: The Genoese destruction of the Venetian fleet at Porto Longo (Sapienza), November 1354, in the War of the Straits
deck.source: F. C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: The Pope forbids trade with the Sultan
deck.text: A new bull renews the ban on carrying anything to the Sultan's lands, on pain of excommunication and forfeiture. The Republic suspends its galleys to {city}. Pepper must now come the long way, through Armenia and Cyprus, at Cypriot prices. Merchants who financed Alexandrian voyages are asking for time.

advice.growth: The ban is for show. Send the galleys anyway; the Pope needs our ships for his crusade.
advice.prudence: Lend on the Cyprus and Armenia route for now. Dearer, but the cargo is not forfeit.
advice.court: Seek a papal licence through our friends at the curia. Licences go to those who ask well.
advice.conscience: Carrying iron and timber to the Sultan arms him against Christians. Obey.

deck.precedent: Papal prohibitions on trade with Mamluk Egypt after the fall of Acre (1291); Venice suspended its state galleys to Alexandria c.1323–44
deck.source: E. Ashtor, Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages (1983)

deck.title: A papal licence reopens {city}
deck.text: After long petitions and a fat donation to the crusade fund, the curia licenses a fixed number of voyages to the Sultan's ports. The galley charters are already at auction, and pepper on the Rialto has dropped on the news. Merchants want credit to bid for charters and to buy the silver that Alexandria craves.

advice.growth: Back the first convoy. Whoever reaches Alexandria first sets the year's price.
advice.prudence: Lend on the galley charters, secured on the cargo, not on the merchants' hopes.
advice.court: The Republic paid for this licence. Support its auction and it will remember.
advice.conscience: Licensed trade is lawful trade. Refuse only cargoes of iron and timber.

deck.precedent: Venice obtained a papal licence in 1344 and resumed state galley voyages to Alexandria in 1345
deck.source: E. Ashtor, Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages (1983)

deck.title: Crusaders sack {city}
deck.text: A crusading king of the islands, with knights from half of Christendom, has stormed {city}, looted it for three days and sailed away. The Frankish merchants left behind are in the Sultan's prisons and their goods in his treasury. The Republic is furious; the crusaders call it a victory. The pepper season is lost.

rumour.text: A great fleet is gathering at Rhodes, and no one will say where it sails.

advice.growth: When trade reopens spices will be dear. Buy the pepper already in the Rialto.
advice.prudence: Write off the Alexandrian advances now and bring the factor home before the next raid.
advice.court: The Republic will treat with the Sultan for its merchants. Support its envoys with a loan.
advice.conscience: A crusade is holy work, and our losses are a tithe to it.

deck.precedent: The sack of Alexandria by the crusade of Peter I of Cyprus, October 1365, followed by Mamluk seizure of Frankish merchants and goods
deck.source: K. M. Setton, The Papacy and the Levant, 1204–1571, vol. I (1976); Ashtor (1983)

deck.title: The Khan closes the Black Sea ports
deck.text: A brawl in a river town on the Don left a Tatar dead. The Khan has expelled the Italians, seized their warehouses and laid siege to the Genoese colony in the Crimea. Silk and slaves no longer come down to {city}, and grain is dear in the Aegean. The two republics talk of a joint embargo that will hurt them before it hurts the horde.

rumour.text: Merchants from the Crimea say the horde's envoys have stopped coming to the colony.

advice.growth: The Khan needs our silver. He will reopen within the season, so keep the factors and stock in place.
advice.prudence: Bring the factors home and lend nothing on Black Sea cargo until there is a treaty.
advice.court: Support the Republic's embargo. Whoever breaks it will be fined and barred from the galleys.
advice.conscience: The trade in Christian slaves is forbidden. This may be the moment to leave it.

deck.precedent: The Tana affray of 1343: the Khan of the Golden Horde expelled the Italians and besieged Caffa, 1345–46, while Venice and Genoa agreed an embargo
deck.source: F. C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: The wool-carders rise in {city}
deck.text: The day labourers of the cloth trade, who belong to no guild and may not combine, have burned the great masters' houses and taken the priors' palace. New guilds are proclaimed and new priors sworn. Cloth production has stopped, and masters who borrowed against their spring wool are not paying.

rumour.text: Bells rang at night in the poor quarters across the Arno, and the masters have hired guards.

advice.growth: Lend to the new guilds. Whoever governs the city will want a banker.
advice.prudence: Lend to no one this month. Wait until it is clear who holds the palace.
advice.court: The old families will be back within a few years. Stay quietly loyal to them.
advice.conscience: The carders are paid in debased silver. Their anger is not without justice.

deck.precedent: The revolt of the Ciompi in Florence, July 1378, and the guild regime that lasted until 1382
deck.source: J. M. Najemy, A History of Florence, 1200–1575 (2006)

deck.title: The men of Ghent take {city}
deck.text: Ghent's militia, starving under blockade, marched out and routed the count's army outside {city} on the day of the Holy Blood procession. Now they hold the town, plunder the count's partisans and fine the foreign merchants. The Italian, Hanseatic and Castilian nations are deciding whether to stay. The exchange square is very quiet.

rumour.text: Weavers from Ghent have been seen buying bread outside the walls.

advice.growth: Every revolt in Flanders ends with a pardon and a fine. Stay open.
advice.prudence: Coin onto a Hanse ship, ledgers to the Carmelites, and no new bills on Flemish names.
advice.court: The count's French overlord will avenge him. Lend to the side with the knights.
advice.conscience: Pay the fine without complaint. Looted factors fare worse than taxed ones.

deck.precedent: Ghent's militia defeated the Count of Flanders at Beverhoutsveld and took Bruges, 3 May 1382
deck.source: D. Nicholas, Medieval Flanders (1992)

deck.title: The wool staple leaves {city}
deck.text: By royal ordinance, all English wool for export must pass through a single staple town of the crown's choosing, and it is not {city}. Flemish clothiers must travel and pay more for their wool, and the Italian buyers follow the wool. Bills on {city} drawn against the wool trade are suddenly harder to place.

advice.growth: Follow the wool. Open a desk at the new staple before the Lucchesi think of it.
advice.prudence: Shorten our bills on Flemish clothiers. Their margins have just gone to the staplers.
advice.court: The staplers' company decides where the wool goes next. Lend them something modest.
advice.conscience: Nothing here troubles the soul, only the purse.

deck.precedent: The Ordinance of the Staple of 1353 moved the staple from Bruges to English towns; it was fixed at Calais from 1363
deck.source: T. H. Lloyd, The English Wool Trade in the Middle Ages (1977)

deck.title: The pestilence returns to {city}
deck.text: The sickness is back, and this time it takes the children born after the great mortality. The rich leave for their villas and the courts close. Debtors die, and their heirs cannot be found or refuse the inheritance. Notaries write wills all day, and the depositors who remain want their coin in their own chests.

rumour.text: Ships from the east were turned away from the harbour, and the gravediggers are hiring.

advice.growth: After the last mortality wages and rents rose. The survivors will be richer; lend to them.
advice.prudence: Coin in the till, partners scattered to safe towns, every loan backed by heirs who are alive.
advice.court: The Signori have closed the gates to foreigners. The sickness will not pass the walls this time.
advice.conscience: Remit the debts of the dead to their orphans. God's anger is not abated by collecting.

deck.precedent: The pestis secunda of 1361–63, which struck children hardest, and later waves in 1369, 1374–75, 1383, 1390 and 1400
deck.source: S. K. Cohn, The Black Death Transformed (2002)

deck.title: Rain on the harvest: dearth in {city}
deck.text: It has rained since Pentecost. The grain rotted in the fields and a measure of wheat costs three times last year's price. The Commune buys grain abroad with borrowed money, the poor sell their tools, and weavers buy bread instead of wool. Merchants who sold on credit to the countryside will not be paid before a good harvest, if then.

advice.growth: Finance the grain ships from Sicily and Apulia. The cities will pay anything.
advice.prudence: Bad harvests trouble peasants, not bankers. Keep lending as before.
advice.court: The Commune must buy grain abroad. Lend for it and the priors will owe us.
advice.conscience: Hoarding grain in dearth is a sin the preachers will name. Lend to feed, not to speculate.

deck.precedent: The Great Famine of northern Europe, 1315–17; Florentine dearths of 1329–30 and 1346–47 recorded by Villani
deck.source: W. C. Jordan, The Great Famine: Northern Europe in the Early Fourteenth Century (1996)

deck.title: The river bursts its banks in {city}
deck.text: Four days of rain in the mountains, and the river came over the walls by night, carrying away bridges, mills and the dyers' sheds along the bank. Ground-floor warehouses are full of mud and ruined cloth. Debtors whose stock was in those cellars come to the bench asking for time.

advice.growth: Rebuilding needs money. Lend to the bridge-builders and the mill owners.
advice.prudence: Write off the cellar stock now, and lend on no goods kept below the flood line.
advice.court: The Commune will levy for the bridges. Volunteer a loan before it becomes a tax.
advice.conscience: The friars call it a judgement on usury. Give alms to the drowned families.

deck.precedent: The Arno flood of 4 November 1333, which carried away the Ponte Vecchio and other Florentine bridges
deck.source: G. Villani, Nuova Cronica, bk XII, chs 1–2

deck.title: Base foreign pennies flood {city}
deck.text: Pennies from the Low Countries that look like the king's sterling but carry less silver pass everywhere in {city}; merchants take them at face because everyone else does. Now the crown has cried them down to half value and will forbid them altogether at Easter. Whatever sits in the till is worth half what the ledger says.

advice.growth: Keep taking them at face. The king will never punish his own merchants by refusing them.
advice.prudence: Weigh, don't count. Take coin by weight and run the base pennies to the exchange before Easter.
advice.court: Bring our bad coin to the king's exchange first; early comers get the crown's best rate.
advice.conscience: Do not pass bad pennies to the poor, who cannot weigh them.

deck.precedent: Continental crockards and pollards circulating in England were cried down to a halfpenny in 1299 and demonetised at Easter 1300
deck.source: M. Mate, 'Monetary Policies in England, 1272–1307', British Numismatic Journal 41 (1972)

deck.title: A failed rival's clients walk in
deck.text: A company across the square stopped payment last week, and its clients are looking for a bench that will still be there next year. They bring their deposits, their bills and their gossip about which of the dead firm's debtors are good. The house's habit of paying out promptly has been noticed.

advice.growth: Take them all, and have their deposits lent out by month's end.
advice.prudence: Take them, but keep a third of the new coin in the till. They ran once; they will run again.
advice.court: Ask the Signori to name us administrators of the fallen bench's estate.
advice.conscience: Do not buy the dead firm's debts for a pittance from its widows.

deck.precedent: After the Bardi and Peruzzi crash, the Alberti antichi rose to become the principal papal bankers, 1350s–1370s
deck.source: Y. Renouard, Les relations des papes d'Avignon et des compagnies commerciales et bancaires (1941)

deck.title: A partner dies, and his heirs want their capital
deck.text: The partnership dies with him, and the articles must be redrawn. His sons, who have never set foot in the counting house, want their father's share of the corpo paid out at book value, and book value carries the loans to princes at par. Paying them strips the till. Refusing them brings lawyers and gossip.

choice.label: Pay the heirs in full, now
choice.result: The till empties, but the house's name for honest dealing grows.

choice.label: Pay over five years from profits
choice.result: The heirs accept, and grumble in every tavern about the house's liquidity.

choice.label: Make the sons partners
choice.result: The capital stays in the house, and so do two young men with no head for exchange.

advice.growth: Make them partners. Capital is capital, and boys learn.
advice.prudence: Pay over years. Book value overstates what our royal paper would fetch in the square.
advice.court: Their mother is cousin to a councillor. Settle before the merchants' court hears of it.
advice.conscience: Pay what is truly owed, and tell them honestly what the royal loans are worth.

deck.precedent: Florentine compagnie were dissolved and re-formed on a partner's death or withdrawal; the Peruzzi company was reconstituted repeatedly, including in 1331
deck.source: E. S. Hunt, The Medieval Super-Companies (1994)

deck.title: A rumour starts a run in {city}
deck.text: Someone in the fish market says the house lost a fortune on a galley; someone else says the cashier was seen weeping. By noon there is a crowd at the bench in {city} demanding coin instead of transfers in the book. The story is false, but a bench that cannot pay at once makes it true.

rumour.text: They say the house's cashier was seen at the pawnbroker's.

advice.growth: Promise a gift to every depositor who leaves his money in. Confidence can be bought.
advice.prudence: Pay everyone, slowly and visibly, with coin stacked high on the counter.
advice.court: Ask the Commune to stand behind the bench. No Republic lets a sound bank fail.
advice.conscience: Swear no false oaths about the books to calm them. Answer only truthfully.

deck.precedent: The Venetian runs of 1499 that broke the Lippomano and Garzoni banks, recorded in Girolamo Priuli's diary
deck.source: F. C. Lane, 'Venetian Bankers, 1496–1533', Journal of Political Economy 45 (1937)

deck.title: Two popes, two Cameras
deck.text: The cardinals have elected a second pope and gone back to Avignon, and Christendom takes sides by kingdom. Each pope demands the collections of his obedience, excommunicates the other's bankers and invites the house to serve him. The Italian republics lean to Rome. The money of France, Castile and Scotland goes to Avignon.

choice.label: Serve the Roman pope
choice.result: The house stands with Italy and loses its Avignon clients.

choice.label: Serve the Avignon pope
choice.result: French tithes flow through the books, and the Signori look at the house sideways.

choice.label: Serve both, through separate partnerships
choice.result: Profitable and clever, until someone reads both ledgers.

advice.growth: Serve both through separate companies. Money keeps no obedience.
advice.prudence: Choose the obedience where our depositors live. A banker excommunicated at home has no clients.
advice.court: The schism will be healed by summer. Serve whoever pays and apologise later.
advice.conscience: Only one is Peter's successor. Choose truly, not profitably.

deck.precedent: The Great Western Schism, from the double election of 1378, which split the Camera's collections between Rome and Avignon until 1417
deck.source: W. Ullmann, The Origins of the Great Schism (1948)

deck.title: {court} pays something on an old debt
deck.text: A royal writ arrives: the exchequer will assign part of the customs at one port to the house in settlement of debts everyone had written off. It is a fraction of what was owed, paid in instalments, but it is coin. The clerk hints that further assignments depend on the house's attitude to new requests.

advice.growth: Coin from a debt we had buried. Put it to work in new business.
advice.prudence: Bank it. Do not let a few florins buy a new loan to the same king.
advice.court: Accept humbly. A grateful creditor gets paid before one who is right.
advice.conscience: If conscience bids, keep only the principal. The rest was interest dressed as gifts.

deck.precedent: After 1346 the English Crown made slow, partial assignments to the Bardi in settlement of Edward III's war debts
deck.source: E. Russell, 'The Societies of the Bardi and the Peruzzi and their Dealings with Edward III', in G. Unwin (ed.), Finance and Trade under Edward III (1918)

deck.title: A Holy Year fills {city}
deck.text: The Pope has proclaimed a jubilee, with plenary indulgence for pilgrims who visit the basilicas. Hundreds of thousands come, with coin of every mint in their purses and offerings for the altars. Changers sit at every bridge, and the clergy want the offerings remitted by letter of exchange. The house's exchange desk is busy from dawn to dusk.

advice.growth: Every pilgrim needs change. Open a second table by the bridge.
advice.prudence: Watch for clipped and counterfeit coin from distant mints. Weigh everything.
advice.court: Offer to remit the offerings for the Camera at a modest rate. Favour outlasts a fee.
advice.conscience: A holy business. Take a fair margin from pilgrims, and no more.

deck.precedent: The first Jubilee, proclaimed for 1300, whose pilgrim crowds and altar offerings Villani witnessed; repeated in 1350
deck.source: G. Villani, Nuova Cronica, bk IX, ch. 36

deck.title: Galleys sail direct to {city}
deck.text: The Republic now sends armed merchant galleys out past the Straits to Flanders and England: spices out, wool and cloth home. The long haul overland to the Champagne fairs is emptying. Bills on {city} are in demand, and correspondents there want credit to buy cargo for the return voyage.

advice.growth: Bruges will be the Rialto of the north. Open a branch there now.
advice.prudence: On a route a year old, one wreck wipes out all its profit. Spread the cargo across many galleys and many partners.
advice.court: Bid for the galley charters at auction. The Signori favour houses that keep the line running.
advice.conscience: A new route and honest trade. Nothing here troubles God.

deck.precedent: Genoese direct voyages to Bruges from 1277–78 and Venetian state galleys to Flanders from 1314 drew trade away from the Champagne fairs
deck.source: F. C. Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (1973)

deck.title: A shipowner asks the house to bear his risk
deck.text: A merchant in {city} wants the house to stand the loss if his cog sinks or is taken before port, against a payment now. Canonists frown on profit from sea risk, so notaries dress the deal as a loan the house has 'received' and must repay unless the ship arrives safely. The premium is handsome.

choice.label: Write it, dressed as a fictitious loan
choice.result: The premium is pocketed, and the contract is safe from the canonists unless the consuls look closely.

choice.label: Write a share openly, before a notary
choice.result: A smaller premium, shared with other underwriters, and a name for plain dealing.

choice.label: Decline
choice.result: The shipowner goes to a Genoese, who takes the premium and the client.

advice.growth: A premium for a promise. Take every line offered; most ships arrive.
advice.prudence: Share the line with three other houses. One wreck must never cost more than a month's profit.
advice.court: The Commune will want to tax assurances. Better it sees ours than catches them.
advice.conscience: Disguising a contract to evade the Church's judgement is a lie told to a notary and to God.

deck.precedent: The earliest known marine insurance contract, Genoa, 23 October 1347, for the Santa Clara to Majorca, drafted as a fictitious gratuitous loan
deck.source: F. Edler de Roover, 'Early Examples of Marine Insurance', Journal of Economic History 5 (1945)

deck.title: A free company threatens {court}
deck.text: Three thousand unemployed lances under a foreign captain have ridden into the countryside, burning mills and offering to leave for a price. The councils will pay; they always do. The question is who advances the coin by Sunday. The captain accepts bills of exchange on Avignon, and he is looking for a banker.

choice.label: Advance the ransom to the Commune
choice.result: The company rides off, the house is repaid slowly from a new gabelle, and the councils remember.

choice.label: Refuse; let others pay
choice.result: Another house advances the coin, and the councils note who did not.

choice.label: Bank the captain's own plunder
choice.result: His war chest earns the house a fat fee, and the city learns whose coffers the brigands trust.

advice.growth: The captain's war chest is bigger than ours. Bank it and charge him for the privilege.
advice.prudence: Advance only against a gabelle pledged by law, not against the councils' gratitude.
advice.court: Advance it. A Commune saved from the torch forgives its bankers many sins.
advice.conscience: Paying brigands feeds the next raid, and banking their plunder is receiving stolen goods.

deck.precedent: Siena bought off the mercenary companies dozens of times between 1342 and 1399; Florence and Pisa paid similar ransoms
deck.source: W. Caferro, Mercenary Companies and the Decline of Siena (1998)

deck.title: A client wants an exchange that goes nowhere
deck.text: A cloth merchant in {city} wants coin for six months. He proposes a bill on Bruges that the house's correspondent will not collect but redraw back at the Bruges rate, so the money returns with the spread between the two markets. No goods move, and no money reaches Bruges. Canonists call it dry exchange, and usury.

choice.label: Do the dry exchange
choice.result: Quick and profitable, and the friars have a fresh example for Sunday.

choice.label: Make it a real exchange, remitted in Bruges
choice.result: Slower and carrying true exchange risk, but the contract would survive any confessor.

choice.label: Refuse
choice.result: The merchant takes his business to a less scrupulous bench.

advice.growth: Everyone does it. The rate differs only because we bear the risk of the Bruges market.
advice.prudence: Real exchange carries currency risk; dry exchange carries a usury suit. Take the risk you can price.
advice.court: Councillors borrow this way themselves. No magistrate will prosecute what the priors practise.
advice.conscience: If nothing moves but time, the gain is the price of time, and that is usury.

deck.precedent: Exchange and re-exchange (cambio e ricambio) between Florence and Bruges in Italian merchant records of the late 14th and 15th centuries, condemned by canonists as dry exchange
deck.source: R. de Roover, 'What is Dry Exchange? A Contribution to the Study of English Mercantilism', Journal of Political Economy 52 (1944)

deck.title: New silver comes over the Alps
deck.text: Miners in the hills of Bohemia have struck the richest silver of the age, and a king there strikes a heavy new groat from it. Pack trains carry the bullion south to the German merchants' warehouse and the mint, where it buys gold, spices and the coin of the Levant trade. The house's dealings in bullion and copper turn a handsome profit this year.

advice.growth: Buy the Germans' silver as it arrives and ship it to Alexandria, where silver is dear.
advice.prudence: Bullion profits come once. Take them, and do not mistake a lucky year for skill.
advice.court: The mint-masters want silver. Sell to the Republic's mint and stand well with the Signori.
advice.conscience: Profit from honest trade in metal is no sin.

deck.precedent: The Kutná Hora silver strikes and the Prague groschen introduced by Wenceslas II in 1300, much of whose silver flowed south to Venice
deck.source: P. Spufford, Money and its Use in Medieval Europe (1988)

growth.name: Ser Bortolo Calbo
growth.title: Socio maggiore
growth.bio: Spent his youth on the Alexandria galleys and believes any ducat not at sea is a ducat wasting its life.

thin_till: The till is thin because the coin is working. Idle ducats breed nothing.
Let depositors wait a day. The Alexandria galleys will fill the chest by Lent.
flush_till: Ducats sleeping in a chest! Lend them to the spring muda before they grow mould.
A full till is a coward's pride. Put it to sea.
high_leverage: We write more in the book than lies in the chest. So does every bench on the Rialto.
The book is the bank, cassiere. Coin is for fishwives.
big_prince_exposure: The Commune never defaults. It merely delays. We can wait.
A forced loan to the Signoria still pays its five per cent. Mostly on time.
bubble_city: Every merchant on the Rialto wants credit. Shall we refuse the whole city?
Pepper never falls. Lend on it.
far_branches: One good correspondent in Bruges is worth ten in Padua.
News takes six weeks from Bruges? So do the profits. Patience.
loss_turn: A bad season at sea. The autumn convoy will mend it.
One loss and the cassiere wants to bury our coin in the garden.
good_turn: You see? The galleys came home. Double the stake next voyage.
Profit, sers. Now let us go and find more of it.
court_offer: Lend to the Doge and the Doge remembers. That alone is worth the interest.
A prestito to the Republic? Take it, and ask for the salt tolls as pledge.
new_tech: Double entry, they call it. Anything that writes faster sells faster.
If the Florentines already use it, we are late. Adopt it.
centre_moving: The money goes west? Then so shall we, by correspondent.
Bruges talks louder every year. We should be there to listen.
quiet: A quiet Rialto is a Rialto where somebody else is making money.
Nothing happening? Then something is about to. Be first to it.

prudence.name: Zuane Dolfinetto
